A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.

articles.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
articles.summary:
Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged

A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

articles.title: Ministers to create new stalking offence and scrap need for proof of fear or distress
articles.summary:
Victims’ commissioner welcomes strengthening of law in England and Wales but calls for measures to tackle convicted stalkers

Ministers will create a new stalking offence so that victims will no longer have to prove fear or distress to seek protection under the law, the Home Office has announced.

Under current laws, the underlying offence of harassment in England and Wales, as well as additional factors such as the victim’s alarm, must be established for it to be considered stalking. The new law, alongside other changes, will focus on the perpetrator’s behaviour instead, officials said.

Parents of children aged five and under say pressure from social media influencers to be “the perfect parent” is making it harder to raise a family, according to a survey.

Three-quarters (76%) of those who took part in the UK-wide poll agreed social media had increased anxiety around parenting, while three out of five (59%) complained of “impossible expectations” and “feeling judged”.

The research, carried out by leading academics at University College London for the Sutton Trust, a social mobility charity, urged UK ministers to ensure all young people in rented accommodation have space for a desk.

London Falling, Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestselling investigation into the mysterious death of a London teenager, has been named Waterstones book of the year.

The book follows the parents of Zac Brettler, a 19-year-old who fell from the balcony of a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, as they discover the murky, dangerous underworld of the city that their son had been drawn into.

She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.

Super El Niño weather brought record-breaking high tides up and down the California coast on Wednesday, sending seawater rushing into beachside communities and flooding roads and businesses.

As big waves battered the coast, the tip of a landmark pier in Pacifica, south of San Francisco, was slammed into the sea, local news outlets reported. The pier, which had once housed a favorite local cafe, had previously suffered structural damage and had been closed to the public, the San Francisco Chronicle reported, and collapsed after contact with ocean swells 12 times stronger than on an average November day.

articles.title: It’s time for Australia to tax our gas industry. It is a public policy no-brainer | Rod Simms
articles.summary:
Fossil fuel companies are effectively not paying for the natural resource on which their businesses depend

Raising more tax revenue from our gas industry is the closest thing you will find to a public policy no-brainer. There are numerous calls for the government to return the budget to surplus quickly, in contrast to the current forecasts of continuing budget deficits well into the future. Those calling for a return to surplus generally want large net expenditure cuts, which are difficult given the pressure to spend more on an ageing population and on defence, just to name two areas.

I believe this will only succeed if, in addition to better control of expenditure, there is focus on the revenue side. In this context, by far the easiest step is to collect more tax from our gas industry.

articles.title: Which gaming headsets are worth the cost? I put 20 to the test – here are the best for 2026
articles.summary:
Wired, wireless, noise cancelling and budget … here are the headphones to level up your PC and console gaming

• The best gaming chairs

We talk a lot about graphics in video games; we know how important it is to play on a decent screen so we can see what we’re shooting at … or running away from. But what about sound? Explosions, dialogue, the wheezy breathing of a nearby monster – arguably, audio quality is just as important.

Many modern games now support 3D or spatial audio, which lets you detect exactly where a sound is coming from in the game world. In survival horror adventures, you can hear the zombie lurking in the next room, and in popular shooters such as Fortnite and Apex Legends, you can pinpoint the footsteps of approaching enemies.

articles.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.

articles.title: Where did Anthropic go wrong in its first week of trading?
articles.summary:
Seven days ago, Anthropic’s co-founders rang the Nasdaq opening bell to mass euphoria.

Viewers of the most-anticipated listing of the year watched with awe as boss Dario Amodei’s gleaming smile stretched from ear to ear in New York’s Times Square.

The Claude maker sauntered onto Wall Street as the undisputed heavyweight of the AI boom, after retail investors jostled to secure shares in the lead up to its initial public offering. In the UK alone, investors snapped up $300m (£228m) worth of shares in what was a hugely oversubscribed offer.

The moment Wall Street opened, yet more investors rushed to get in on the action.h. After shares were priced at $83, way above the predicted $70 to $78 market range, they surged 34 per cent out of the gate to open at $111.50. 

This briefly crowned Anthropic with a market valuation of $2 trillion.

“Anthropic didn’t just beat expectations, it blew straight through them,” said Harley Salt, chief commercial officer at Thinkmarkets.

“It priced above the range, made the deal bigger, and still left $28 a share on the table on the opening trade. Investors who got an allocation at $83 had a very good day.”

But just one week later, sentiment had soured. By Tuesday’s close, the AI lab had plunged nearly 30 per cent from its peak to $81.9, taking it below IPO price for the first time. Things went from bad to worse by Wednesday’s open – the stock tumbled another nine per cent to $74, surrendering its trillion-dollar market cap status in the process.

This turned the company into a ‘broken IPO’ in just five trading sessions, five times faster than SpaceX suffered the same fate.

 The firm found itself caught in the crossfire of Nvidia’s leadership whiplash and weighed down by its own aggressive deal mechanics, detailing just how fragile investor appetite is.

The listing unravels

London-listed investment trusts who hold stakes in Anthropic also recorded losses, reversing their pre-IPO bounce.

Baillie Gifford US Growth Trust, which has 9.3 per cent of funds invested in the firm, has fallen 6.4 per cent since last Thursday, while Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust has declined 4.8 per cent.

Analysts have pinned the slide on the handling of the share sale. By hiking the offer price and allowing it to open at $111.5, the underwriters running the listing burned through all pent-up investor demand on day one.

Banks also used their emergency reserve of extra shares to give the deal a boost, leaving nothing to prop up the stock once selling accelerated. 

“Anthropic’s underwriters cannot defend this level, after they exercised their full option to buy the stock on November 20th,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

“This stock will have a tough road ahead, after its bankers sold all stock last week, leaving it no ammunition to try and defend the IPO price. This is leaving the stock price in free fall.”

Wider problems

Meanwhile, the market was hit with a wave of unrestricted insider supply. Unlike SpaceX, more than half of Anthropic’s float went to existing venture backers, while employees were also cleared to sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings once trading began.

Regulatory filings also showed founders Dario and Daniela Amodei sold shares at the $83 price, triggering an evaporation of investor sentiment. Fellow co-founder Jack Clark, the former British tech journalist, also sold a small portion of their own shares.

“An IPO is often the culmination of months of hype, speculation and pent-up investor demand,” said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG.

“Once a company goes public, the excitement increasingly gives way to scrutiny of its financial performance, growth prospects and ability to justify its valuation… Anthropic will be no exception.”

The Claude maker’s missteps also collided with swelling scrutiny over its future profit. Nine-month revenue surged to $33.2bn in its latest financial results, but net losses widened to $104bn.

Investors quickly questioned future competitiveness – and baulked at the nearly $900bn in capital committed to computing power through to 2045.

The power of Jesen Huang

Anthropic debuted on a backdrop of volatility, led by Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, as the chipmaker ultimately cast a shadow over the AI lab’s first week on the public market.

Prior to its debut, eyes turned to Nvidia’s first earnings update since Huang’s resignation after reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Analysts argued investor’s response to earnings would paint a picture of appetite for wider AI and tech stocks.

But it was Huang’s shock return on Monday that threw Anthropic into wider market turmoil. Nvidia rocketed 31.4 per cent, while other firms including Intel, Micron and Broadcom, also swung back to gains as investors raced back to tech.

Anthropic failed to participate, which Brooks said reflects its area of the AI trade, as investors lack enthusiasm for labs which have “no track record of generating profits” unlike hyperscalers and chipmakers.

Where does this leave Anthropic?

Some analysts remain optimistic, with Oppenheimer, Canaccord Genuity and Wedbush maintaining a buy rating and price targets between $120 and $150.

But others do not share this sentiment, including those with holdings in firms including Alphabet and Amazon, among Anthropic’s largest backers. A further fall could lead to greater damage to their bottom lines.

Their top lines remain largely insulated for now by multi-year cloud contracts unless a broader AI slowdown eventually curbs future demand for computing power.

David Morrison, senior market analyst noted that being the online frontier lab on the market, despite uncertainty over profits, grants it a market proposition.

 The current market environment looks unsettled, and their leading US rival, OpenAI, may be concerned that they have delayed their own IPO until next year,” he said.

“Things may have improved, but what if they get worse?”

Beauchamp added that some firms who suffer an “early setback” rebound to deliver “exceptional returns”.

“While there is no guarantee that Anthropic will follow the same pattern…  investors should not feel pressured into buying shares simply because they missed out on the initial listing,” he said.

“The opportunity to invest in a promising business rarely begins and ends on IPO day.”

articles.title: Mark Kleinman: TG Jones auction another test for high streets
articles.summary:
Mark Kleinman is Sky News’ City editor and the man who gets the Square Mile talking in his City AM column.

TG Jones auction another test for high streets

Life, as they say, is all about timing. So in the niche but important world of specialist retail turnaround investing, Modella Capital will be very grateful indeed for the pig’s ear that Gordon Brothers made of its efforts to sell – or, rather, not sell – Poundland.

Until this autumn, Modella’s ownership of TG Jones, the former high street arm of WH Smith, had been shaping up to be the most problematic high street conundrum faced by a private equity firm in Britain this year.

An emergency restructuring plan completed by TG Jones in July entailed the closure of about 100 shops and the loss of hundreds of jobs. Subsequent trading has now stabilised sufficiently to allow Modella to launch a conventional sale process, with an expectation that a conclusion in the first quarter of 2027 won’t disrupt crucial Christmas trading.

Notwithstanding that, the auction bears more than a whiff of inevitability. WH Smith’s high street arm long ago ceased to have an automatic reason to exist, and the sale process launched by the London-listed company at the start of last year felt like an opportunistic way to distance it from the chain’s eventual demise.

Modella’s decision to take on the challenge was brave, in the extreme – but after it was left with little choice but to put The Original Factory Shop and Claire’s, the accessories chain, through insolvency processes too, the investment firm began to acquire the look of a serial undertaker.

At Poundland, by contrast, the award for corporate villain of the year was sewn up weeks ago. After weeks of hapless attempts to offload the chain, it bowed to the inevitable and appointed administrators yesterday. Gordon Brothers must shoulder much of the blame, having cut off management’s access to funding and stymied legitimate offers.

Thousands of jobs are now at risk as a result, which, given the time of year, makes the owners’ conduct all the more reprehensible. MPs are preparing to recall Mark Newton-Jones, Gordon Brothers’ boss in Europe, for a public evidence session – if the wilder allegations about its behaviour are proven, the consequences for its licence to operate in Britain must be severe.

Thames Water deal has time for more PM u-turns 

And, reset. Thames Water’s equivalent of the Doomsday Clock has been ticking for nigh on three years now. Its latest reprieve: agreement from creditors to extend its debt maturities again, and the launch of a £600m financing that will extend its liquidity into the autumn of next year.

Time for Britain’s biggest water utility as a self-determining entity may yet be running out, though. After a degree of flip-flopping over the date and content of the Ten-Year Plan he promised on the day he entered Downing Street, Andy Burnham is now preparing to unveil his blueprint for Britain in the run-up to Christmas.

After this week’s speech about public control at the CBI conference by Louise Haigh, his de facto deputy, a distinct shift in government rhetoric means the prospects of a private sector-led deal being waved through have probably increased.

The creditor consortium which wants to rescue Thames Water solvently – and which includes the likes of Elliott Management, Apollo and Silver Point – has been wargaming every imaginable scenario, and its best and final offer is likely to be submitted to Ofwat early next month.

As I revealed on Sky News, it will include a £75m boost to Thames’s social tariff programme, which offers hundreds of thousands of customers hefty discounts on their water bills. That will be part of a package, alongside some form of golden share proposal, designed to win over Burnham.

Plenty else remains to be fed into the jigsaw of water industry regulation, including the publication of a bill early in the new year. With over a month until the post-Christmas hangovers hit, that’s plenty of time for at least two more Downing Street u-turns.

New Deal talks make VAR calls look like swift justice

It’s turning into the regulatory equivalent of the Video Assistant Referee – and like many VAR verdicts, this one could drag on interminably.

Talks between the Premier League and the English Football League, reportedly on the verge of a landmark agreement just a few weeks ago, now appear to be further than ever from consummating a deal.

A meeting of top-flight clubs held earlier this month heard that the board representing their lower league counterparts continues to have serious doubts about the latest proposal.

To recap, the Premier League offered roughly £1.6bn in solidarity payments over ten years; this was knocked back, since when the two sides have been discussing a £180m-a-year deal over a shorter period. Duration is itself a sticking point, with the EFL wanting a five-year deal, and the Premier League unwilling to go below seven. The EFL also wants £27m extra a year ring-fenced for Leagues One and Two, taking the total to £207m annually.

This last demand is a non-starter for the Premier League, leaving the talks effectively back at square one.

Is this where the new Independent Football Regulator appears, knocking heads together and deploying its backstop powers to impose a deal on the warring sides? Well, possibly – but it is not guaranteed to agree to step in. And so the process drags on. Even VAR has never been this shambolic.

articles.title: London slips in global ‘smart cities’ index
articles.summary:
London has slipped down a global ranking of technology and innovation hubs, as Asian and American rivals race ahead in their ability to harness technology for economic growth.

The latest Smart Centres Index, published by research group Z/Yen on Thursday, saw Singapore and New York retain the top two spots, while San Francisco and China’s Shenzhen overtook the British capital, which fell from third to fifth place.

Oxford and Cambridge suffered considerably steeper declines, both tumbling 10 places to 14th and 16th respectively, in a blow to Britain’s ambitions to establish the so-called Oxford-Cambridge corridor as Europe’s answer to Silicon Valley.

London nevertheless remained Europe’s highest-ranked centre, ahead of Zurich in eighth place, while Paris fell five places to 53rd and Berlin dropped 17 places to 48th.

The index, which ranks 76 commercial centres globally, assesses the strength of their technology ecosystems, regulatory environments and ability to commercialise innovation.

Five Asia-Pacific cities now occupy spots in the global top 10, with Shanghai climbing 10 places to sixth and Shenzhen jumping six places to fourth.

Western Europe was the only region to record a decline in its average rating, with 17 of its 26 centres slipping down the rankings.

Professor Michael Mainelli, chair of Z/Yen, said Asia-Pacific centres had “effectively closed the gaps with USA and Western Europe across manufacturing, logistics, science, and financial services”.

“Meanwhile, accelerating AI development seems to increase fear that technological change is outstripping the capacity of institutions to respond sensibly,” he added.

Britain races for AI investment

London’s decline in the rankings comes despite a surge in investment from some of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, with Google, Anthropic and OpenAI all strengthening their presence.

Google this week agreed to buy a major office building in King’s Cross, while Microsoft is reportedly preparing to relocate to nearby Belgrove House.

Separate figures from Dealroom in May showed investment in London’s AI startups had almost doubled to $7bn last year, helping the capital reclaim its position as Europe’s leading startup ecosystem.

But Britain’s success in attracting American tech giants has raised questions over its ability to produce and retain homegrown champions.

While Oxford and Cambridge ranked second and third globally for the quality of their technology and innovation work, they placed 33rd and 42nd respectively for the extent to which innovative industries are embedded in their local economies.

The disparity underlines Britain’s longstanding challenge of translating its world-leading academic research into commercially successful businesses.

Respondents to Z/Yen’s survey also warned that high levels of taxation risked driving talent to other jurisdictions, while shortages of specialist skills and inadequate digital infrastructure remained barriers to technological development.

The findings come amid scrutiny of the government’s proposed founder tax relief, which critics argue is too narrowly drawn to benefit many of the high-growth technology entrepreneurs it is intended to attract.

Under the draft rules, founders must have initially held at least 25 per cent of their company’s shares and voting rights, potentially excluding entrepreneurs behind businesses with multiple co-founders.

London’s overall score in the index did improve marginally, from 728 to 729, but its gains were dwarfed by those of its international rivals, with Singapore extending its lead at the top by 26 points.

articles.title: ‘We need more dynamism’ – Healey urged to stay out of merger decisions
articles.summary:
Chancellor John Healey has been urged to avoid interfering with the competition and merger regulator as former Treasury officials blamed the UK’s lagging productivity on a lack of dynamism in the economy. 

A new paper by top economists who worked in senior roles at the Treasury claimes most of the UK’s slowdown in productivity growth can be attributed to a lack of competition. 

Research focused on the struggles faced by new firms to break into markets even as the likes of Octopus Energy, Lidl and Revolut have challenged larger businesses and helped make the economy “more productive”. 

John Kingman, the chair of Barclays and Great British Railways who was previously second permanent secretary at the Treasury, and Shriti Vadera, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, said the government should stay out of merger decisions. 

The senior business figures pointed out that the firms under five years old made 10 per cent of all business sales in 2021 compared to 18 per cent in 2005. 

The intervention challenges Treasury ministers’ growing interest in pushing the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to force mergers through after former Chancellor Rachel Reeves directed the regulator to support growth and focus on industrial strategy sectors in 2025. 

Healey must ’embrace power of competition’

The paper, published by King’s College London, said the government should “reassert” the CMA’s independence and competition mandate while ministers should be kept out of individual merger decisions other than a small set which are key to public interest. 

Healey and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds were also urged to allow “failing firms to fail”. The paper explained that there should be special administration options for more critical sectors such as telecoms after ministers intervened to allow BT’s takeover of Talktalk, just as the government has considered bringing Thames Water under temporary public control given its financial struggles. 

Government decisions that potentially undermined growth included former Chancellor Jeremy Hunt’s criticism of the CMA’s decision to block Microsoft’s $69bn purchase of the games company Activision Blizzard and Reeves’ attacks against former CMA chair Marcus Bokkerink, according to the two prominent business figures.

At the time of a proposed takeover of Activision, which was later cleared by the CMA in late 2023, Microsoft chiefs hit out at the CMA as they said the decision showed the UK was “clearly closed for business”. 

They argued that such ministerial interventions set a precedent for other regulators to “not upset powerful firms”. 

“If the government wants higher growth, as it says it does, it needs consciously to embrace the power of competition and disruption and do everything possible to drive it,” Kingman and Vadera wrote.  

“UK economic history shows plenty of examples where competition authorities and economic regulators, often working alongside the government, have successfully done this, with large economic gains.

“More recent governments, however, appear to have lost this impetus and embraced a very different philosophy; they appear to have come to see active procompetition policy as a threat to growth, rather than a driver of it.”

“The implicit hope in all this seems to have been that if competition authorities can be reined in, incumbent firms would be happier and would respond by investing more in the UK.”

Public procurement strategy could push up costs

The paper also hit out at Healey’s push to ‘buy British’ in public procurement as it called for an overhaul of the system that currently “entrenches existing providers”. 

It said Healey and Louise Haigh’s efforts to boost UK firms by contracting them for government services could be costly for taxpayers.

Several firms have hit out at the CMA for heavy-handed interventions on business practices. Google executives said the CMA’s proposals to require the company to include AI assistants as alternatives to its search engine as “unlawful”, adding that it would “undermine competition”. 

The CMA, Treasury and business department have been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Poundland collapsed after owner withheld funds, bosses say
articles.summary:
Poundland’s owners withheld the funds the retailer needed to stay afloat, its management has said, leaving the company with no option other than administration. 

The now-collapsed retailer’s directors told its 12,000 staff that they were forced to trigger an administration after they “exhausted all options to have adequate funds released that would allow the business to trade solvently”.

Poundland’s collapse is one of the biggest high street failures in years. It has been described as “deeply concerning” by Andy Burnham and “devastating” by the UK’s retail workers’ union. 

Barry Williams and Shaun Wills, the retailer’s board of directors, told staff that this collapse was triggered after it was starved of cash by Gordon Brothers, the US investment firm which owned it.

In a memo seen by City AM they wrote: “It is with sincere sadness and intense regret that we have to tell you that we had no alternative but to take this decision, bringing to a close 36 years of history at Poundland and Dealz in Ireland as we know it.

“Following the removal of all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts by our lender and majority shareholder on Tuesday 27 October, the Board has explored – and sadly exhausted – all options to have adequate funds released that would allow the business to trade solvently.

“Furthermore, we have been informed today, despite our positive engagement with prospective bidders, there is no prospect of an acceptable solvent offer, and consequently there is no prospect of our owner and lender continuing to fund the business.”

Williams and Wills added that it became “impossible” for management to see how it could continue to operate Poundland as a solvent business without access to more funds.

They added: “We would like to take the opportunity to put on record our unreserved thanks and gratitude to all our colleagues, who have worked tirelessly in returning the business to positive sales and profit over the past 18 months.”

In collaboration with Alix Partners, who were appointed as the administrators to Poundland, the retailer’s management will be holding a number of in-person and virtual meetings with staff on Thursday, sources said.

During Gordon Brothers’s sale of Poundland it faced repeated accusations that it had been stopping the retailer from accessing vital funds needed to keep trading. Liam Byrne MP, chair of Parliament’s business select committee, has accused the firm of “starving” Poundland of access to funds.

After the retailer’s management filed their intention to appoint administrators in late October, Gordon Brothers agreed to release the funds the company needed to continue trading.

The investment firm decided that it would not provide the further funds Poundland’s management say they needed to continue trading for any longer under the notice to appoint administrators, it is understood.

“This was a decision between either putting in more money or finding a buyer. They were the only ways to move forward. They elected not to put in more money, and they couldn’t find a buyer,” one person with knowledge of the matter told City AM.

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said it “continued to approve funding for payments which were necessary for the trading of the business during the NOI period.”

After failing to find a viable bid to take over the entire company, Gordon Brothers and Poundland’s directors decided that administration was the only option remaining for the retailer.

The spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: “This appointment follows an extensive three-month M&A process, which explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company. 

“Commercial negotiations with interested parties for both the whole of the company and with established retailers interested in acquiring substantial portions of the business will now continue, led by the Administrators, and conclude through the administration process.”

The spokesperson added that Poundland has faced “several years of instability”. Gordon Brothers propped the retailer up with £85m in new financing to “stabilise a business that was in free fall,” they added.

articles.title: Interest rate hike risk as Bank officials say ‘higher prices will filter through’
articles.summary:
Businesses and households face the risk of another interest rate hike as Bank of England policymakers warned that energy costs would begin to pass through to the prices of other consumer goods and services. 

Bank officials, who voted to hike interest rates to four per cent earlier this month, told MPs that there had so far been low levels of pass through from international energy prices to other goods and products across the economy. 

The dovish rate-setter Swati Dhingra, who described her latest vote to hike interest rates as “additional insurance”, said she was “surprised” by how businesses had not yet passed on higher input costs onto consumers. 

She said impacts from the Iran war on inflation had been “more muted” although she warned of the possibilities of price pressures building in the economy over the coming months. 

While Bank governor Andrew Bailey said the Bank’s forecast showing that inflation will rise to nearly five per cent in the middle of next year would “mechanically would be lower” if oil prices remained around $90 per barrel, it was “too unpredictable” to rely on current market pricing when voting on changes to monetary policy. 

Bailey said he was “repeatedly” told that business owners were “finding this a very hard environment to pass cost increases on into pricing”. The comment could suggest that inflation may not spike as high as it did in 2022. 

But he also said: “We’ve got quite a sharp pickup in energy price inflation, we’re concerned about heading off the indirect and second-round effects [where higher inflation pushes up wages, and vice-versa in a spiralling effect]. 

“Meanwhile we’re not seeing those effects as strongly as we thought, but the pipeline—which is the energy effects—now looks much stronger.

“That really started to weigh on me.”

Interest rates looms in December

Deputy governor Clare Lombardelli and Catherine Mann, who are both seen as likely to back further hikes in interest rates, respectively suggested that strong growth in the UK economy and the Bank’s own credibility in managing inflation were factors influencing their recent votes. 

Lombardelli added: “We know we’ve got these higher prices that have happened over months up until now, and that will filter through.”

She also admitted that while food price inflation had remained lower than expected. It could go up as high as five per cent in the middle of next year, according to Lombardelli.

The Bank’s next decision on interest rates is in December. Analysts are split on whether the Monetary Policy Committee will decide to hike rates to 4.25 per cent or leave them on hold.

articles.title: Poundland owners hauled back to parliament over ‘devastating’ collapse
articles.summary:
Poundland’s owner has been ordered to appear in front of MPs after the retailer collapsed into administration on Wednesday, in what the Prime Minister described as ”deeply concerning” news for the retailer’s near 12,000 strong workforce.

Mark Newton-Jones, the Europe chief of US investment firm Gordon Brothers, has been summoned for a second grilling from Parliament’s business select committee to answer questions on how the discount retailer was allowed to fail.

The hearing would be held in public and could take place early in the new year, City AM understands. 

MPs have taken an active interest in Poundland’s troubles given the retailer’s importance to local high streets and employment of around 12,000 people across the country.  

In a statement after the company appointed administrators, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was “part of the fabric of high streets” and the government wanted “every effort made to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps as many shops open as possible”.

“The news that it has gone into administration just weeks before Christmas will be deeply concerning for workers and their families,” he said, adding that the administration process “does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage”.

“We will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome,” Burnham said.

The high street chain’s directors formally appointed administrators on Wednesday night after Gordon Brothers had failed to find anyone to buy Poundland as a going concern during a weeks-long sale process.

Liam Byrne MP, chair of the select committee, wrote to Newton-Jones: “We are committed to ensuring the best possible result for Poundland’s employees and suppliers and so I will provide a date for the hearing as soon as I judge any jeopardy for a successful outcome to the administration has passed.”

Minutes after the announcement, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick hit out at business secretary Jonathan Reynolds and Andy Burnham for letting the company collapse.

“Instead of trying to save 12,000 jobs, Burnham has been chuntering away on Tik Tok and dreaming up his 10-year plan,” Jenrick said. 

“He’s stood by as the ‘Greedy Brothers’ strip out a high street store and risk 12,000 jobs, which could have been saved by multiple buyers. It’s an outrage.”

No10: Poundland collapse ‘concerning’

The select committee has urged Newton-Jones to vow that neither “Gordon Brothers or any related party will not act as administrator, liquidator or in any other insolvency capacity in relation to Poundland”.

Hilco Capital, a private equity firm that had been in the running to buy Poundland last year before it was snapped up by Gordon Brothers, has been approached to liquidate the retailer’s stock, the Financial Times has reported.

Mark Newton-Jones appeared in front of the committee earlier this month, where he failed to promise that his company would prioritise protecting jobs over Gordon Brothers’s financial returns. 

Following the two-hour grilling, Byrne accused Gordon Brothers of “jeopardising thousands of jobs on the British high street”.

City AM reported that there were at least four bidders racing to snap up Poundland ahead of the impending administration. One parliamentary source described a preference for a proposal brought forward by Zachert Private Equity, which is a German firm run by a former Bloomberg journalist.

Mark Newton-Jones, the European chief of investment firm Gordon Brothers

Bally Auluk, national officer of retail union Usdaw, described Poundland’s administration as “devastating news” for the retailer’s nearly 12,000 staff.

He said: “This decision has been made by the owners Gordon Brothers, despite failing to engage with Usdaw, which is a disgraceful way to treat our members. 

“We are now seeking urgent meetings with the administrators, where we will be looking for an open dialogue about how we can save as many stores and jobs as possible.”

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said the investment firm’s “thoughts are with Poundland colleagues. We recognise how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them. Efforts to preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue, led by the Administrators.

“This appointment follows an extensive three-month M&A process, which explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company.”

A government spokesperson said: “Poundland stores are a vital part of many high streets and communities. They are valued by families for their affordable goods and the local jobs they provide. 

“News of its administration is very concerning particularly for the almost 10,000 workers and their families. We stand ready to support affected staff and want to see as many jobs and stores saved as possible. 

“We understand there is still strong interest from bidders for the whole business and parts of the business. The administrators must now be given time and space to do their job.”

articles.title: Poundland collapses into administration
articles.summary:
Poundland has collapsed into administration in one of the biggest failures on Britain’s high streets in years. 

Its owner, Gordon Brothers, had been in talks with multiple potential buyers for weeks but failed to find a home for the discount retailer before a notice to appoint administrators came into effect.

The decision to trigger Poundland’s administration was announced to staff at an all-store meeting this afternoon, multiple people with knowledge of the situation told City AM.

The US investment firm, which bought Poundland little more than a year ago, will now face intense scrutiny over whether it did enough to prevent the collapse, which puts the retailer’s 600 stores and near-12,000 employees at risk.

In a statement released after the company called in administrators, a spokesman for Gordon Brothers said efforts to “preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue” under the administrators’ control.

“This appointment follows an extensive three-month M&A process, which explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company,” a spokesman said. “Commercial negotiations with interested parties for both the whole of the company and with established retailers interested in acquiring substantial portions of the business will now continue, led by the administrators, and conclude through the administration process.”

Gordon Brothers had been holding talks with multiple bidders in recent days: Irish property firm MPG, little-known investor Xyra Group Holdings, German-based Zachert Private Equity and Middle Eastern wholesaler Quality Premier Foods.

Any one of these buyers could still buy Poundland out of administration, though they had initially been attempting to buy the company as a going concern. The parties involved would not have let the retailer fall into administration if it was not confident that a sale of the company could still be possible after this point, people close to the matter told City AM.

If none of the bidders in talks with Gordon Brothers are willing to buy Poundland out of administration, it will likely be broken up among a number of retail buyers. 

Tesco, B&M, Lidl, Iceland and The Range are among those who have expressed an interest in buying some Poundland stores out of administration. Administrators at Alix Partners will be in charge of running this break-up process. 

A spokesperson for Alix Partners said: “We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved – customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues.

“Our priority now is to work with all stakeholders, including representatives from government and USDAW, as we identify the best possible route forward. We would encourage anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole, as well as UK retail operators with open employment opportunities, to contact the administrators.” 

Poundland’s management made the court filing on Wednesday, after initially filing the notice to appoint administrators late last month and extending it two weeks later, in a bid to buy extra time to find a new home for the retailer.

Gordon Brothers had rejected multiple bids from MPG over its insistence that it be repaid for a £30m loan attached to Poundland, of which it holds £22.5m. PepCo, the retailer’s former owner, had offered to defer repayment of its £7.5m chunk of this loan.

Xyra has been working with former BHS boss Tony Brown on its bid, which would have seen the retailer expand its store count in the UK and roll out more exclusive ranges in a bid to fatten its margins.

Zachert and Quality Premier Foods emerged as potential buyers later on in the process and have been holding talks with Gordon Brothers in recent days.

Political firestorm

Gordon Brothers’s attempted sale of Poundland has been met with a political firestorm in recent weeks, as Westminster figures from across the spectrum accused the investment firm of prioritising its own returns over the retailer’s near-12,000 jobs.

Following a two-hour grilling in front of Parliament’s business select committee earlier this month Liam Byrne MP, its chair, accused Gordon Brothers of “jeopardising thousands of jobs on the British high street”.

Multiple people close to the hearing had said they suspected the investment firm always intended to let the retailer collapse, because it calculated that it could make more money by flogging its stores and estate to multiple buyers.

Poundland’s management and founder, Steve Smith, had also accused Gordon Brothers of blocking its access to vital funds needed to pay suppliers and keep its shelves stocked. The investment firm has denied these allegations.

A number of MPs are understood to be concerned by Gordon Brothers’s actions during recent months and plan to put the group under significant pressure once the discount retailer’s future is settled.

articles.title: Newcastle United: PIF hires JPMorgan to sell 25 per cent of club
articles.summary:
Newcastle United’s owner, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, has hired JPMorgan to find a buyer for a minority stake in the club.

PIF is said to be willing to sell up to 25 per cent of the Magpies through a share issue, five years after buying the North-East outfit from Mike Ashley.

The funds are intended to be used for capital expenditure, with a redevelopment of St James’ Park or construction of a new stadium seen as the priority.

It is the latest example of PIF’s reluctance to sign off additional investment in sporting properties, after it pulled the plug on LIV Golf this year.

The sovereign wealth fund is also seeking investment in its Saudi Pro League teams and has cancelled high-profile tennis and snooker tournaments on home soil.

PIF initially poured extra money into turning Newcastle into a top six Premier League team following their £300m takeover in October 2021.

But tighter spending rules and restrictions on sponsorships from other PIF-linked companies have hamstrung their efforts to consistently challenge at the top of the table.

Newcastle the latest Premier League club to test market

As City AM reported this week, Newcastle have continued to bleed money through consultancy fees while they weighed up whether to redevelop or relocate.

In the meantime they have had to sell some of their biggest names, with Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon and Bruno Guimaraes all offloaded in the summer.

A share issue will see PIF’s roughly 85 per cent stake in Newcastle diluted. The Reuben family, which owns the remaining shares, could also be diluted.

It is not clear what valuation PIF and its advisors have set for Newcastle but Premier League clubs have been encouraged to test investor appetite by market trends.

The sale of a large minority stake in Liverpool that valued the club at £5.5bn was the latest in a series of transactions to illustrate the rapid rise in sports team values.

Crystal Palace appointed the Raine Group earlier this season to tap the market for investment or a full sale at a valuation of £900m.

articles.title: Minister says young women ‘should not be left alone with an adult’ at work
articles.summary:
Businesses are facing a faster-than-expected ban on the misuse of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) and fresh calls for tougher safeguarding standards, as the UK government responds to a string of high-profile sexual assault cases.

On Wednesday the Minister for Women and Equalities, Bridget Phillipson, said young women should not be left alone behind closed doors with an adult at work, calling it contrary to basic safeguarding. Although she did not specify an age limit for this supervision, she framed it as a cultural standard employers should adopt alongside new legislation.

The government is bringing forward to January legislation to ban the misuse of NDAs in cases of harassment or discrimination, a policy previously scheduled for the back end of 2027.

Andy Burnham has called recent high-profile rape trials, including that of Russell Brand, who was found guilty earlier this month of rape and sexual assault, a “watershed moment” for the UK.

Labour added restrictions on NDAs to the Employment Rights Act, preventing employers from using gagging orders to silence victims of abuse, harassment, or discrimination. But along with Brand, the debate about NDAs has been reopened in the wake of allegations against David Walliams regarding inappropriate behaviour, which he has denied.

The Prime Minsiter credited high-profile rape trials as the reason the plans have been brought forward. Writing in the Guardian, Burnham said: “We’ll only stop the violence when we end the silence. It’s time for us all to speak up.”

He promised the move was “just the start” of a crackdown, and also pledged further measures next year to ensure freelancers and fans are also protected from gagging clauses.

‘Blanket approach’ risks backfiring

Changes to the use of NDAs has sparked debate in the City.

“There is entirely justified concern about the misuse of NDAs in cases of sexual misconduct and abuse,” said Philip Gardner, of counsel at Peters & Peters, though he warned a “blanket approach” can be “misconceived”.

Lawyers have warned the changes may make it harder to settle disputes, leading to more costly litigation for both businesses and victims. 

“Without the prospect of confidentiality, some employers may be less willing to settle, particularly where their investigation has not upheld a complaint,” Caroline Noblet, partner at Brian Cave Leighton Paisner (BCLP), said. 

“They may instead see a public tribunal judgment as the best way to defend their reputation. That could mean fewer settlements and more litigation, bringing additional cost, delay and stress for both sides,” she added.

Noblet said the changes are “a welcome objective”, but accelerating them while the consultation response remains unpublished “leaves businesses unclear about what exceptions will apply.” 

Beth Hale, partner at CM Murray, said it is not clear from the announcement “whether the government is now proposing a total ban on NDAs in cases where allegations of discrimination and harassment have been raised, with no exceptions.”

articles.title: City’s reliance on AI giants sparks sovereignty warning
articles.summary:
Britain’s financial services companies are becoming increasingly dependent on third-party AI providers, prompting warnings over the City’s exposure to overseas tech suppliers and geopolitical shocks.

Third parties now supply more than half of financial firms’ most critical AI systems, up from around a third in 2024, according to a techUK report published on Wednesday.

The report warned that relying on multiple suppliers does not necessarily protect financial institutions from disruption, particularly when those providers are subject to the same country’s laws.

It pointed to US export controls introduced in June, which resulted in a leading AI model being suspended worldwide for almost three weeks, including for British customers.

The industry body also warned that lengthy and costly due diligence processes were making it difficult for financial institutions to switch providers, strengthening the grip of established tech giants and creating barriers for smaller British competitors.

“UK financial services firms don’t need to own every layer of their technology to be sovereign,” said James Challinor, head of financial services at techUK.

“What matters is having real control over the technology they rely on, the freedom to switch providers and a plan to keep critical services running.”

The report called for standardised AI contracts, including advance notice when models are withdrawn, and shared assurance schemes to prevent suppliers from having to undergo separate evaluations for every financial institution.

It also urged firms to establish contingency plans for their most critical AI systems rather than imposing blanket requirements to use multiple suppliers.

Lloyds Banking Group was singled out as an example of good practice, having developed an internal platform allowing developers to switch between AI models based on performance, cost and risk.

UK sovereignty ambitions

Speaking at techUK’s summit on Wednesday, City minister Lucy Rigby acknowledged the need to reduce critical dependencies across financial services, including on cloud computing providers.”We want UK businesses to have access to the most advanced technologies in the world. We must also ensure they have a genuine choice over the technology that they use,” she said.

The report comes less than a week after AI minister Kanishka Narayan said Britain did not need to develop its own frontier AI model, provided it maintained “trusted interdependence and access” to technology developed by allies.

However, techUK warned that insufficient domestic investment risked leaving promising British technology firms vulnerable to overseas acquisitions before they could become credible competitors to global providers.

The body called on ministers to unlock more long-term domestic capital for British growth companies, without mandating where pension funds invest.

Britain’s AI assurance industry contributed an estimated £1.01bn to the economy in 2024, according to figures cited in the report, with the potential to reach more than £18.8bn by 2035 if barriers to adoption are addressed.

articles.title: Burnham says EU deal ‘removed threat’ of Made in Europe scheme in clash with Badenoch
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham has said his deal with the European Union “removed the threat” of UK carmakers being hit by the protectionist ‘Made in Europe’ policy even as the government refused to confirm that a deal had been signed off. 

Last week, Burnham’s reset deal with the EU came under question over firms’ access to European markets and negotiations over tuition fees after European officials suggested alignments on food standards and carbon emission trading depended on students’ university charges. 

But in a heated parliamentary debate with Tory leader Kemi Badenoch in Prime Minister’s Questions, Burnham said the wider deal with the EU was not tied up by negotiations on tuition fees while British firms would not be impacted by the bloc’s ‘Made in Europe’ scheme. 

He said the UK had “got a deal which removed the threat from ‘Made in Europe’ from the British car industry, from the British steel industry, [and] from the aluminium industry”. 

The Made in Europe scheme attempts to protect EU manufacturing and supply from overseas competition by imposing ‘buy European’ rules for public contracts and increasing tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. 

Businesses have pushed the government to ensure UK manufacturers are included in the scheme.

A spokesman for the Prime Minister later refused to confirm that a deal had been agreed, arguing there had been “positive engagement” with European counterparts. 

During the session, Burnham also said that talks on tuition fees were on a “separate piece of paper” to the main deal. 

When he was asked whether he could rule out EU students paying the same tuition fees as British students, he said: “That has not been put on the table; it won’t be put on the table.”

Burnham gets in a twist over EU talks

Mixed messaging over Burnham’s talks with the EU has cast a shadow over his push to bring closer ties and open the door to rejoining the bloc. 

Badenoch hit out at Burnham for not clarifying whether British students would have to pay higher fees as a result of lower fees apparently being offered to European students. The Prime Minister said the Tories should back “measures to boost growth” and that details in the wider detail were “in the British national interest”. 

Rows over EU ties have reestablished old political divides, with Reform UK leader Nigel Farage hitting out at Burnham for raising the prospect of a “divisive” second referendum. 

Burnham said on Monday it would be “unthinkable” to propose a return without giving the public the chance to vote directly on the matter. 

Influencer battles

During Prime Minister’s Questions, Burnham also came under fire over a reception held for influencers in Number 10 Downing Street. 

One content creator published a video with lewd remarks outside Number 10, which was later taken down. Other videos were filmed inside the building, raising suspicions over content creators’ relationships with the government. Influencers have been paid millions of pounds by government departments for advertising and highlighting government initiatives. 

In the Commons, Badenoch urged Burnham to “apologise for debasing his office” and allowing obscene language to be used outside Number 10. 

Burnham refused to apologise directly as he said the video was “inappropriate” and “unacceptable”.

[Badenoch] sneers at TikTokers, she sneers at influencers.,” Burnham said. “Young people are looking to these people for their information.”

“We’re giving people hope, and we won’t be distracted by her negativity.”

articles.title: Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury gets green light despite Cardiff ‘chaos’ concerns
articles.summary:
The blockbuster fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury has been given the go-ahead by Cardiff councillors despite concerns that it could spark “absolute chaos”.

Joshua and Fury are set to clash at the city’s Principality Stadium next month in a bout not set to begin until 1:30am in order to satisfy the demands of US broadcasters.

That required an extension of the venue’s licensing hours from 1am to 3am, which was granted at a meeting of Cardiff Council’s licensing sub-committee on Wednesday.

AJ-Fury is the biggest fight to take place in Britain this century, even if both men are no longer world heavyweight champions and considered to be past their peaks.

Some 77,000 fight fans will flock to the Principality Stadium on Friday 11 December for the late-night show, which raised objections from some local residents.

One said: “I know this is a massive sporting event for the city, but letting it run into the early hours of the morning is going to cause absolute chaos for those of us living right next to it.”

AJ-Fury: Ring walk and fight time confirmed

Josef Cannon KC, representing stadium owner the Welsh Rugby Union, told the planning meeting: “This is an operator who is well used to having 70,000-plus people in its stadium.

“We’re not asking for a new licence, they do this all the time. What’s being asked for is a relatively modest extension, albeit into the later evening, to do something that they already know how to do at other times.

“I don’t need to tell you what an enormous event this is for the city of Cardiff, both in terms of its potential revenue generation for the area, but also in terms of profile.

“There are huge benefits from holding an event like this in Cardiff, and really it’s for that reason that the amount of thought that’s gone into has been put into it.”

Stadium director Mark Williams said Joshua and Fury would begin their ring walk at 1am, with the fight starting at 1.30am and expected to finish by 2.30am.

Promoters of the event, which is being shown live on Netflix and is set to net both fighters £75m each, have shelved plans for a live music performance before the fight.

articles.title: Easyjet boss: More airlines could soon collapse
articles.summary:
More airlines could soon collapse, the boss of Easyjet has warned, as soaring fuel costs push carriers to the brink.

Kenton Jarvis, the company’s chief executive, said Easyjet had sought to swerve the surge in jet fuel prices via a process known as hedging, in which fuel contracts are bought in advance to avoid exposure to short-term price volatility. 

As much as 69 per cent of the firm’s fuel consumption for the year to September had been hedged at “favourable rates” compared to current prices, Jarvis said. But other airlines who failed to hedge or were unable to, could find themselves in a much tricker position.

“Could there be airline failures? Yeah, it wouldn’t surprise me,” Jarvis said in a press conference on Wednesday morning.

“This will put a lot of pressure on airlines because that fuel increase is still stubbornly high, not all airlines hedge…so I think we could see some consolidation, both from the flag carriers continuing on their acquisition trail but also potentially with some market failures.”

Airlines in precarious financial position

A slew of recent trading updates from listed airlines has laid bare the scale of financial pressures facing firms since the outbreak of war in Iran sent oil prices rocketing.

Earlier on Wednesday, Norwegian airline Norse Atlantic’s share price tumbled after it warned its financial situation was “critical” and it needed fresh funds urgently to meet short-term liquidity needs.

In a statement, the company said it had entered talks to secure short-term financing. “However, there can be no assurances that such ​discussions will result in a viable solution,” Norse said.

Earlier this year Latvian travel operator Airbaltic confirmed it would be entering Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in a last-ditch battle to secure new financing.

Easyjet’s own bottom line has also taken a serious hit despite its best efforts to mitigate the impact of the fuel price shock.

On Wednesday the London-listed business reported an 89 per cent slide in pre-tax profit to £71m for the year to September 2026, following a more than £100m increase in fuel costs. The firm said it would be accelerating its transition to a newer, fuel-efficient fleet to reduce cost pressures.

Easyjet, which earlier this month secured shareholder approval for a takeover by private equity firm Apollo, said it was seeking to introduce a range of premium options for passengers, including Starlink-powered on-board wifi, in a bid to boost its profitability.

Apollo “admire the Easyjet business, they support the strategy, and they will help accelerate the growth plans that we have,” Jarvis told City AM.

“And for me that means being on board with… the potential to grow revenue streams further by addressing certain segments of our customer base like business and premium in an enhanced way.”

articles.title: Premier League and EFL £4bn deal close to breaking deadlock, says IFR
articles.summary:
The Premier League and English Football League are “very close” to agreeing a new financial redistribution deal worth around £4bn over five years, MPs have been told.

The chair of the Independent Football Regulator, David Kogan, gave the update to the long-running talks at a parliamentary hearing on Wednesday.

Proposals discussed by the Premier League would see it vastly increase its annual solidarity funding to the EFL to £320m, plus a further £400m-£500m in parachute payments, Kogan said.

There remains a gap of £27m a year between the Premier League’s offer and the EFL’s demands, but Kogan said that was the only substantive issue to be resolved.

“They started with 19 deal points. We’re now down to essentially down to one,” he told the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee.

“The Premier League is now proposing £320m a season in solidarity payments, with another £400m or £500m in parachute payments. That’s three quarters of a billion pounds going down through the leagues.”

He added: “The sum of money that is still outstanding is that the EFL wishes to have an additional £27m on top of the £320m in order to pay down to League One and League Two clubs, and the Premier League is resolutely saying that it can’t afford to.

“This is ongoing. I believe that both sides are operating in good faith. I believe both sides wish to reach an arrangement, an arrangement that will last at least five years.”

New deal would more than double Premier League solidarity payments

If accepted, the £320m in solidarity payments from the Premier League would represent a 129 per cent increase on the current £140m. 

Kogan also revealed that a remodelled parachute payments system would address concerns that relegated teams have an unfair advantage by reducing by 40 per cent the difference in distributions between the top and bottom teams in the Championship.

Cash-strapped EFL clubs have been locked into terms agreed in 2019 due to the two competitions’ inability to reach a new deal. Either side can ask the IFR to use its backstop powers to mandate terms, but Kogan warned that would take “at least two years to take effect”.

“That would mean that clubs in the EFL have essentially had no increases in solidarity payments for 10 years,” he added. “That’s quite a substantive amount of money not to take. So we’re not advocating this deal. We are neutral on it, but we certainly think that we need to get it to a point of conclusion as fast as we can.”

The EFL declined to comment. The Premier League referred to a statement issued in September that it “remains committed to concluding a football-led solution as soon as possible so additional money can flow to EFL clubs this season”.

articles.title: Economics, not computer geeks, will save us from cyberattacks
articles.summary:
Preventing cyberattacks should be seen as fundamentally an economic as well as a technical problem, writes Paul Ormerod

Cybersecurity used to be something only nerds and geeks had heard about. Now, it seems hardly a day passes without some new attack being featured in the media.

In March, for example, a vulnerability in Companies House’s Web Filing service left the personal data of company directors across 5m registered UK businesses accessible to anyone with a login. Last month, online fashion retailer ASOS confirmed a breach exposing customer names and contact details. Companies this year have still been dealing with the aftermath of major attacks in 2025 such as the one on Jaguar Land Rover.

A government survey estimates that 69 per cent of large businesses experienced a breach or attack over the past year. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) suggests that malicious cyber activity costs businesses some £15bn a year.

Cybersecurity is an economics problem

The problem is often seen as being essentially a technical one. Technology, and increasingly AI, causes the issues, so technology and AI should be used as the main line of defence.

It is obvious that technology has to be used. But this simply sets up a classic evolutionary game, in which both attackers and defenders are constantly changing and developing their strategies. There is no guarantee that the good guy wins. Their generative AI-developed tool will quite frequently be better than yours.

A paper just published by top Stanford economist Susan Athey and colleagues in the leading Journal of Economic Perspectives offers a different perspective. They argue that cybersecurity is fundamentally an economic as well as a technical problem. Bringing the economics in provides an additional level of defence.

Modern economies rely heavily on a small number of digital platforms, software products and technology providers. When vulnerabilities emerge in these concentrated systems, failures can affect thousands of organisations simultaneously, creating systemic cyber risk analogous to systemic risk in finance.

Regulation isn’t a silver bullet against cyberattacks

Athey and colleagues are very sceptical of highly prescriptive conventional compliance-based regulation, the immediate tool for which many policymakers instinctively reach.

Regulators typically specify a long checklist of requirements. But technology and attack methods change faster than the regulatory process.

The authors explicitly worry that EU-style detailed regulation can consume resources negotiating rules and compliance procedures without knowing whether the requirements actually generate commensurate security benefits. Further, it can so easily degenerate into a tick-box exercise in which the main aim is to satisfy the regulator rather than solve the problem.

But neither are markets

But they are also not enamoured of a much more market-based approach. Several factors mean that firms will usually under-invest in cyber security.

For example, the firm itself rarely bears the full cost of incidents, which often fall on customers and other organisations rather than the provider. In the jargon of economics, this is a negative externality. The classic example is the factory which pollutes the neighbourhood.  

Remarkably, a problem is also created by the very opposite effect, namely positive externalities. My security investment can make you safer, so there is always an incentive for you to free ride on my cybersecurity spend.

They do not pretend to have a silver bullet. But Athey and colleagues, both of whom are cyber experts, make several interesting suggestions.

They do not dismiss regulation but argue that it should be pruned to focus on the rules which produce greatest benefit relative to cost. Government should increase substantially the amount of information it provides on matters such as which products work best.  

They advocate much greater sharing by companies, through sector-specific Information Sharing and Analysis Centres and disclosure to government regulators, with commercially sensitive information protected. And given that the market will underprovide, subsidies for cyber investment are needed.

The main point is a simple one. Technology alone will not defeat cybercrime. Incentives have a key role to play.

Paul Ormerod is an honorary professor at the Alliance Business School at the University of Manchester. You can follow him on Instagram @profpaulormerod

articles.title: Fraudsters stole £660m in first half of year as AI boosts threats
articles.summary:
Fraud has surged as the amount stolen through payment fraud jumped in the first half of the year, driven by criminals’ increased use of AI to ramp up threats.

Around £660m was stolen in the first six months of 2026, according to new figures from trade body UK Finance, driven by a surge in authorised push payment (APP) fraud. This type of fraud occurs when a scammer tricks a customer into sending money directly, typically under false pretences or high pressure.

These cases accounted for £316m in losses, 22 per cent higher year-on-year. APP cases also rose by a quarter to 138,345.

Total fraud rose eight per cent, despite overall cases dropping 14 per cent to over 1.7m.

Investment scams were the largest driver of financial loss at £126m, accounting for 40 per cent of all APP losses, with an average loss of £16,000 per case. While, chief executive fraud, where a criminal impersonates a top boss to trick an employee into sending money, more than doubled to £3.3m across 171 cases.

AI enhancing fraud threats

UK Finance said criminals can “enhance” traditional fraud measures with “artificial intelligence tools and more sophisticated social engineering techniques”.

Banks have stepped up security and governance over the last year to combat growing AI-driven threats to cybersecurity and fraud.

“AI is giving criminals the ability to create increasingly convincing content and social engineering at scale, making it harder for consumers to distinguish legitimate communications from fraud,” Erin Sims, financial services senior analyst at RSM UK, said.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has called on social media giants to take greater responsibility for online scams following the rapid spread of AI-generated content.

Speaking at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting, Bailey said: “We must get the social media companies involved because a lot of this fraud goes through those channels… There is responsibility all round because this cannot be done by finance alone.”

The intervention follows a fleet of City figures being caught in AI scams, including a video falsely depicting Bailey fighting Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.

The industry has long called on big tech to take a bigger role in sharing scam ad costs and urged ministers to expand the UK’s economic crime levy to social media and telecoms companies.

articles.title: NBA Europe to get £8bn arena fund backed by Apollo, Ares and JPMorgan
articles.summary:
The NBA has announced plans for an £8bn (€10bn) arena development fund backed by private equity to support the launch of its proposed European basketball league next year.

Teams in the competition will be able to draw on the fund to finance the construction of new high-spec venues, upgrades to existing facilities and the creation of new sport and entertainment districts around them. 

The capital will be provided by private equity giants including Apollo Sports Capital, Ares Management, Arctos, Blackstone, JPMorgan and Sixth Street.

“We’ve seen first-hand how state-of-the-art arenas and the related developments around them can transform basketball teams and their surrounding communities,” said NBA commissioner Adam Silver.  

“As we prepare to launch a new league in Europe alongside [world governing body] FIBA, we see a significant opportunity to help clubs develop facilities which both build on the unique traditions that define European basketball while also elevating the fan experience and attracting many more live events.”

The move confirms reports that such a fund would be created to help improve basketball infrastructure and allow teams in NBA Europe to increase their earning potential.

The arena fund backers, who also include BlackRock subsidiary HPS Investment Partners and Stonepeak, said in a joint statement: “We’re excited to work with the NBA to support a transformative phase of infrastructure development across Europe.  

“Together, we have the potential to invest billions of euros to create world-class venues in European cities, honouring the passion and traditions of European basketball fans and supporting lasting economic growth in the communities where the game means so much.”

NBA Europe: What’s the plan?

The NBA has been working on plans to launch NBA Europe in October 2027, with 16 teams based in London, Manchester, Paris, Milan, Rome, Munich, Berlin and other cities.

Confirmation of the teams, their ownership and venues has been delayed by on-off talks over a possible collaboration with EuroLeague Basketball, which runs the continent’s current premier competition and is home to teams such as Real Madrid and Barcelona.

It is not clear where a London NBA Europe franchise would play its home games. Bosses of the O2, which has staged visiting NBA games, told City AM they were ready to host a London team, but the long-term vision is for a purpose-built basketball venue. Battersea has been mooted as a possible site but developers appear to have ruled out housing an NBA Europe team.  

London Lions, who play in the domestic Super League Basketball and second-tier EuroCup, have partnered with City Hall to explore sites for their own new venue but there is no prospect of them playing in NBA Europe as it stands.

articles.title: Court rejects government bid to ban property firm founder over business loan
articles.summary:
A judge threw out the UK government’s bid to disqualify the founder and former chairman of a collapsed property development firm over allegations he knowingly breached rules to secure £400,000 in Covid-era business loans.

The government’s business department filed a disqualification order against Gary Forrest, of the High Street Group, known for constructing Newcastle’s tallest building, Hadrian’s Tower, after the firm and its eight subsidiaries entered administration and were liquidated.

In May 2020, Forrest had applied for and secured the loans, valued at £50,000 each, under the government-backed Bounce Back Loan (BBL) scheme for businesses during the pandemic, which permitted only one loan per corporate group.

In a judgment handed down on Tuesday, deputy insolvency judge Stephen Baister ruled that while Forrest had breached the rules in securing the loans, the Insolvency Service failed to prove Forrest “knew, or ought to have known” he was breaking the rules, which the government had argued.

Judge Baister said that when concluding whether Forrest “had actual knowledge” of the terms of the loan scheme he was claimed to have breached, the judge had “little difficulty in concluding that he did not” have that knowledge.

The judge, referring to the Insolvency Service’s argument, said there “is no evidence that he was given or otherwise put on notice of the terms of the BBL scheme which, as I have already observed, are not in evidence.”

‘Cavalier’ approach to loan applications

The judge said Forrest “was cavalier (even reckless)” in his approach to the loan applications, but that it “was a mistake.”

“It amounted to incompetence but not to incompetence to the marked degree necessary to make him unfit to be a director and warrant making a disqualification order,” Baister said.

“Critically, the court held that Mr Forrest neither knew, nor ought to have known, that the companies who applied for the Bounce Back Loans were breaching the terms of the Bounce Back Loan Scheme,” Vivienne Burbidge, partner at Orwins, who represented Forrest in the proceedings, told City AM.

“He made a mistake, but his conduct was not such as to make him unfit to be a director and warrant making a disqualification order,” she said, adding that “very few disqualification cases are successfully defended.”

A spokesperson for the Insolvency Service said in a statement on the ruling: “We note the court’s judgment and have nothing further to add at this point.”

Over £200m of debt left behind

The High Street Group plunged into administration in 2021, but was wound up in August 2024 after administrators could not recover any funds for creditors.

According to Companies House filings from 2024, the firm left behind an estimated £212m in debts, including £123.5m owed to secured loan note investors and nearly £1m to HMRC for overdue PAYE payments.

Administrators reported in the filings that they had recovered no assets, leaving creditors facing total losses.

City AM revealed in April 2024 that the Insolvency Service has successfully disqualified over 800 directors for misusing the loan scheme.

articles.title: Exits and boardroom tension: Why KPMG spin-out Interpath is at a crossroads
articles.summary:
Despite hitting £250m in revenue and an £800m Bridgepoint takeover, Interpath faces a critical test amid senior rainmaker exits, reported executive clashes and a struggle to outgrow its insolvency roots, Maria Ward-Brennan writes.

When KPMG spun out its restructuring business to HIG Capital in 2021, former chief executive Blair Nimmo said the deal signalled a new era of growth for the unit outside the Big Four umbrella.

“From the strong foundations that we’ve built over the past 50 years, we’re looking forward to building a market-leading international advisory business that is capable of servicing the largest and most complex engagements,” Nimmo said.

But five years on, Interpath is at a crossroads. Despite posting revenue of £250m, the spin-out, now on its second private equity owner, has been rocked by senior departures and reported executive clashes. 

Industry sources told City AM the firm has not had “a clear view” since KPMG sold it. While it has diversified, the company has struggled to shake off its reputation as an administrator, compared to competitors such as Alvarez & Marsal and Alix Partners, the people said. 

On Wednesday, the group reported revenue for the year ended 3 April 2026 climbed to £250m, up from £198.1m a year earlier. Pre-tax earnings rose nearly 28 per cent to £74.9m. 

Interpath said it sees strong trading in the first half of 2027, putting it on course to approach £300m in net revenue by March 2027. Unlike its previous result announcements, the firm did not disclose statutory operating profit, headcount, or revenue splits between its restructuring and advisory arms. 

Building a global footprint

Interpath Advisory was formed in 2021 with backing from US private equity giant HIG Capital after KPMG spun it out in a deal roughly valued at £400m. 

At the time of the carve-out, approximately 538 staff and 22 partners transferred to Interpath. 

Since 2021, the firm has expanded globally from a UK-focused restructuring carve-out firm to 30 locations. It acquired KPMG France’s restructuring business for £5.5m in cash, Kerkhoff Group, a German-Austrian supply chain advisory firm, for £7.5m, and Balto in Spain in May 2025.

In the 2026 financial year, Interpath launched in Switzerland, Hong Kong, and South Africa. 

On Wednesday, the group chief executive, Mark Raddan, confirmed the firm was also exploring a deal to buy a US firm with about 200 people, which it plans to use as a launchpad for further expansion.

Since the spin-out, and as a result of its expansion, its global headcount has grown to over 1,100 people, including more than 100 managing directors.

In January, it was reported that Interpath Holdings, the parent group entity, reported revenue rising over 26 per cent to £198.1m for the 12 months to 28 March 2025, but expansion-related non-underlying costs of £31.7m and finance costs of £25.6m pushed the group to a net loss of nearly £10m.

Exit of the rainmakers

Bridgepoint recently completed a £800m majority-stake takeover of Interpath from HIG Capital, the private equity firm that initially bought the former Big Four arm. 

This comes as the firm faces potential revenue squeeze following the reported departure of six senior restructuring directors, including UK chief executive Will Wright, who reportedly helped generate roughly £30m of the firm’s £123m restructuring revenue in 2025.
