articles.title: Ex- Ukraine prosecutor general accuses Zelenskyy's office of interfering in anti-corruption investigation
articles.summary:
Ukraine's former prosecutor general is accusing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's administration of interfering in a criminal investigation involving the head of the country's anti-corruption bureau after the president demanded his removal from office in September.

In an extensive interview with Fox News Digital, Ruslan Kravchenko alleged that Zelenskyy's decision to remove him came under pressure from the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), whose officials he said his office had been investigating.

"The signature on the resignation letter was mine. The decision was his," Kravchenko said. "You do not have to put handcuffs on the president himself to tie his hands. It is enough to put the people he relies on at risk."

BILLIONS IN US AID TO UKRAINE UNDER MICROSCOPE AS CORRUPTION ROCKS ZELENSKYY’S INNER CIRCLE

Kravchenko's most serious allegation concerns what happened afterward. He claims the president's office instructed prosecutors to close a criminal case involving NABU Director Semen Kryvonos.

"The Office of the President began issuing instructions to the Office of the Prosecutor General to immediately close the criminal case against the head of NABU," he said. "In my assessment, that amounts to deliberate interference in an investigation."

"The authority to investigate crimes becomes the ability to determine government policy and even geopolitics," he argued.

Kravchenko did not identify who allegedly issued those instructions or provide documentary evidence of the communications in the materials supplied to Fox News Digital. His allegation of presidential interference has not been independently verified.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'

Kravchenko's departure followed a September investigation known as Operation Carthage, in which NABU and SAPO accused officials connected to the Prosecutor General's Office of helping protect fraudulent call centers and laundering criminal proceeds.

According to a Sept. 8 report in The Guardian, the investigation centered on fraudulent call centers whose employees impersonated banks, police officers and investment advisers to steal money from victims in Ukraine, Russia and Europe. NABU alleged that a senior official in the Prosecutor General's Office protected the operation and helped launder its proceeds. 

Law enforcement sources told Ukrainska Pravda that individual call centers paid approximately $7,000 a month in protection money. Investigators also released recordings suggesting that the principal suspect had overseen repairs at Kravchenko's home while allegedly collecting bribes.

Kravchenko, who has not been charged in the investigation, denies wrongdoing and rejects the allegations against his office. He claimed the operation was intended to seize investigative materials concerning misconduct by anti-corruption officials and prevent him from pursuing those cases.

He said he initially refused to resign but changed his position following a Sept. 7 meeting with Zelenskyy, attended, according to Kravchenko, by Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the president's parliamentary faction.

"When the president wants your resignation and the leader of his parliamentary faction, which commands a majority, is sitting beside him, believe me: a prosecutor general's room for maneuver is extremely limited," he said.

Zelenskyy publicly confirmed that he had demanded Kravchenko's removal.

"There is only one path for this Prosecutor General: removal from office. That is what I told him," Zelenskyy said in a Sept. 14 statement, according to Reuters.

Zelenskyy also said that if Kravchenko considered the decision political pressure, he was free to characterize it that way. The president suspended him on Sept. 14, and parliament approved his dismissal the following day.

ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH

The confrontation intensified when Kravchenko announced on Sept. 14 that he had signed a notice of suspicion against Kryvonos over alleged misconduct predating his appointment as NABU director.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office disputed the validity of the notice, stating that Kryvonos had not been formally notified of suspicion under Ukrainian law and that relevant entries in the investigative register had been deleted.

Kravchenko alleges those actions followed pressure from the president's administration. The claim remains unverified.

NABU and SAPO have rejected Kravchenko's broader accusations, describing them as a campaign against independent anti-corruption institutions. In a Nov. 4 announcement, the agencies said Operation Carthage had uncovered an alleged criminal network involving senior law-enforcement officials accused of protecting fraudulent businesses. Those allegations have not been proven in court.

The controversy comes amid widespread public concern about corruption. A September survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that 72% of Ukrainians held Zelenskyy politically responsible for corruption among his associates, although the findings did not suggest respondents believed he was personally involved.

Zelenskyy has publicly condemned the widening investigation's allegations. In a Nov. 7 address, he described alleged misconduct involving senior security officials as "frankly shameful, absolutely unacceptable," according to Reuters, and called for a full investigation.

His former chief of staff, Andriy Yermak, defended him in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, amid an earlier corruption scandal in November 2025, describing Zelenskyy as "not corrupt" and saying he had allowed independent anti-corruption investigations.

Zelenskyy's office did not respond to multiple requests from Fox News Digital for comment on Kravchenko's latest allegations.

The former prosecutor general maintains that his removal prevented him from pursuing investigations into the leadership of the anti-corruption agencies. Ukrainian authorities, meanwhile, have publicly defended the investigation that preceded his dismissal.

articles.title: Former Florida mayor urges American Jews to fight back against rising antisemitism
articles.summary:
As antisemitism surges across the United States and around the world in the wake of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, massacre, policy strategist and public speaker Gabe Groisman is urging American Jews to stand their ground and fight for the future of their community — and the soul of the nation.

In his new book, "The Jewish Fight for America," Groisman, a former mayor of Bal Harbour, Florida, explores the history of American Jews and their contributions to the country, arguing that despite rising antisemitism, they should confront the tide of hate and stand firm in their rightful place.

"The first fight we have to take on here in the U.S. is to strengthen the community, to try to teach our brothers and sisters about who we are as a people," Groisman told Fox News Digital. "Then we can get to the part of why the Land of Israel is important to us, why Jewish sovereignty over the Land of Israel, which is the State of Israel today, is an integral part of who we are as Jews in America or anywhere in the world."

CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND

One of the book’s chapters opens with quotes from Genesis. Groisman explained that powerful forces are seeking to distance American Jews from Israel. On the left, he said, a movement is seeking to "unlearn Zionism," while on the right, critics attack Zionism through the lens of dual loyalty.

"These days, people are afraid to connect things to the Bible, but it is critical to do so. It is the only way to honestly understand where our connection to that land begins. It begins with the Bible and the words of God himself," Groisman said.

He noted that only 26% of American Jews say they believe in "God as described in the Bible," per a Pew Research Center study published in May 2021. According to the study, another 50% believe in some other spiritual force.

"Most American Jews don't hold a biblical or Judeo-Christian understanding of God, and I think that's a huge reason why most don't look to the Bible for their connection to the land," said Groisman.

"When they are asked to defend their connection to the Land of Israel or to the State of Israel, they can’t begin to respond in a proper way because they don’t believe in God," he added.

Groisman has practiced law for more than 20 years, litigating cases nationwide and participating in legal challenges on behalf of the Jewish community.

A NEW CHAPTER FOR AMERICA’S 250TH: 'J250' INITIATIVE PUTS JEWISH CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE SPOTLIGHT

During his tenure as mayor, Groisman passed what he describes as the nation's first anti-Israel boycott ordinance, as well as the first municipal ordinance adopting a definition of antisemitism.

Groisman said the book seeks to address a question American Jews across the country are asking privately: What is the future of Jews in America, and is it time to leave? His answer, he said, is an emphatic no.

"Jewish American history is not well taught, not even in Jewish circles. We need to understand that this community has been here since before day one and has played integral roles in this country. The religious liberties established in this country from the beginning were meant to benefit groups explicitly like the Jews, who were here from day one," he said.

For American Jews, Groisman said, the solution lies in helping young people reconnect with their identity. He argued that a strong sense of identity and purpose, rooted in their Jewish religion and national heritage, can help them become confident American Jews and thrive in the United States.

"America is not about freedom from religion; it’s about freedom of religion. You are allowed to be who you are as an American and still be as American as everybody else," he said.

In his book, Groisman examines developments over the past several years that he believes have contributed to the surge in antisemitism, including the rise of intersectionality and critical race theory on the left and their growing influence in academic and intellectual circles, which he says have received significant funding from foreign actors.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Groisman pointed to foreign funding flowing into American universities, warning that "that money comes with strings attached" and is intended "to create chaos in our country." He argued that foreign actors unable to defeat the United States militarily seek to weaken it by creating internal divisions, with antisemitism serving as "a useful tool" in that effort.

"When we saw actors in this country, in the aftermath of Oct. 7 and even before Israel responded in Gaza, being coordinated and directed by foreign actors in the United States, all the way down to small chapters on college campuses across the country, that requires years and years of coordination," he said.

Groisman said his book offers a message of optimism, emphasizing his faith in America, its political system and the American people’s ability to confront these challenges.

"For the American Jewish community, this book will hopefully help swing the pendulum back, encouraging people to recalibrate and put our country — and the American Jewish community as an integral part of it — back on track," he said.

articles.title: Iran flogs female singer 74 times for performing without hijab in viral YouTube concert
articles.summary:
Iranian authorities subjected a female singer and four members of her concert team to 74 lashes each Monday after she defied the Islamic Republic’s restrictions on women by performing without a hijab in a viral YouTube concert, their lawyers said.

Parastoo Ahmadi, 29, and her four male co-defendants were flogged in the Iranian city of Qom, defense attorney Mostafa Nili told Iranian news outlet Emtedad, according to Reuters.

The five were also banned from traveling abroad and engaging in artistic and musical activities for two years.

IRAN'S REGIME CAME FOR TEENAGE TWINS. THEIR FATE OFFERS A GLIMPSE OF TEHRAN'S WIDENING DEATH CAMPAIGN

One of the defendants’ lawyers told the BBC Monday that efforts to overturn the ruling, reduce the punishment or suspend its enforcement had failed. Defense attorneys also sought to postpone the flogging, but authorities insisted on carrying out the sentence immediately.

The punishment sparked outrage among Iranian artists and human rights advocates, who condemned the regime’s restrictions on women and artistic expression.

Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the U.S.-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), told the BBC that Ahmadi’s flogging was "a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights" and demonstrated the authorities’ determination to suppress women’s freedoms and punish those who challenge discriminatory laws.

Those flogged alongside Ahmadi were musicians Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri and Amirali Pirnia and producer Mohsen Lashkari.

IRAN REGIME'S EXECUTION SPREE CONTINUES AS TWINS FACE DEATH PENALTY, DECADES IN PRISON AFTER ALLEGED TORTURE

The case stems from a Dec. 11, 2024, performance in which Ahmadi appeared in a sleeveless black dress with her hair uncovered, accompanied by male musicians at the historic Deir Gachin Caravanserai in Qom province.

With no audience physically present, Ahmadi shared the performance, known as the "Imaginary Concert," on her YouTube channel.

The video of the concert has garnered over 3 million views on YouTube.

Iran’s judiciary swiftly opened a criminal case over the performance, and Ahmadi was arrested three days later. Two musicians involved in the concert were also arrested. All three were subsequently released on bail, according to the Norway-based Hengaw Organization for Human Rights.

In June 2026, a criminal court in Qom sentenced Ahmadi and eight others involved in the production to 74 lashes each on charges of "offending public decency by producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online," according to Hengaw.

The defendants denied the charges. An appeals court upheld the flogging sentences in September, clearing the way for their enforcement, Iran International reported Sept. 25.

IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY

Amnesty International urged Iranian authorities in October to abandon plans to carry out the sentences, arguing that judicial flogging amounts to torture and violates international human rights protections.

Ahmadi, a native of Nowshahr in northern Iran who studied film directing at Soore University, had previously faced restrictions from Iranian security authorities over her performances of protest songs and regional folk music during the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, according to Hengaw.

The movement erupted in September 2022 following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Iranian Kurdish woman detained by the country’s morality police for allegedly violating mandatory hijab rules.

Many Iranian women have since openly defied the compulsory dress code, despite periodic arrests, warnings and other enforcement measures.

Of the nine people originally sentenced over Ahmadi’s concert, five were reported to have been flogged Monday. The status of the remaining defendants’ punishments remains unclear.

Ahmadi’s punishment comes amid a broader human rights crackdown in Iran that has intensified since nationwide anti-regime protests erupted in January. In addition to years of restrictions on women, artists, journalists and political dissidents, Iranian authorities have increasingly resorted to mass arrests, torture in detention and executions to suppress opposition, as previously reported by Fox News Digital. 

Human Rights Watch reported in February that Iran’s executions in 2025 had reached levels unseen since the late 1980s, while rights groups have documented a further escalation in political repression throughout 2026.

Earlier this month, the Norway-based Iran Human Rights organization reported that at least 121 people arrested in connection with January’s protests had been sentenced to death, including at least 30 whose sentences had been upheld by Iran’s Supreme Court.

Iranian authorities did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s risk jumps 53% for millions living with common blood sugar condition
articles.summary:
People living with type 2 diabetes may face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease compared to those without the condition, a new study suggests.

Researchers from Curtin University's School of Population Health in Australia reviewed 40 observational studies including people with Alzheimer’s disease and type 2 diabetes.

After accounting for other health and lifestyle factors, the researchers found that individuals with this condition have a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer's. That translates to roughly 4.7 new cases for every 1,000 people tracked over a year.

3 THINGS TO AVOID IN MIDDLE AGE COULD MEAN 13 MORE YEARS WITHOUT DEMENTIA, STUDY FINDS

"It doesn't add newer experiments or show that diabetes directly causes Alzheimer's disease, but how we should read it is that someone with diabetes has about one and a half times more chance of getting Alzheimer's disease compared to someone without it," Dr. Caghan Kizil, professor of neurological sciences at Columbia University Department of Neurology and recipient of the Catalyst Cure One, Cure Many Award in Neuroinflammation from the American Brain Foundation, told Fox News Digital.

The findings were published in the journal Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy on Nov. 9.

ALZHEIMER’S BLOOD MARKER COULD PREDICT COGNITIVE DECLINE RISKS, MAYO CLINIC SAYS

Unlike earlier reviews that often combined different forms of diabetes and dementia, the new analysis looked specifically at type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease to calculate the rate of new cases, according to lead study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, a researcher at the Curtin School of Population Health.

"Reporting both relative risk and incidence measures helps explain not only whether risk is higher, but how frequently new cases occur," Adewuyi told Fox News Digital. "What stood out was the fuller picture that emerged when we examined how often Alzheimer’s disease developed alongside how risk compared between groups."

Experts point to a few key ways that poor blood sugar control harms brain cells over time.

POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PREVENT PREDIABETES FROM TURNING INTO DIABETES

Excess blood sugar can stiffen and narrow blood vessels in the brain, causing a decrease in blood flow and oxygen to brain cells, according to Dr. Nikhil Palekar, director of Stony Brook Medicine's Center of Excellence for Alzheimer's Disease in New York.

"Insulin resistance prevents the brain cells from utilizing glucose, resulting in reduced cellular energy and neuronal functions," Palekar, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.

Maintaining optimal blood sugar levels can reduce the risk for Alzheimer’s, the doctor confirmed.

"GLP-1 agonists have been shown to lower elevated blood sugar levels as well [as] decrease brain inflammation, which is a risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease," Palekar said.

There were some limitations, including extreme variation across the studies.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Because the individual studies reported vastly different rates — ranging from fewer than one to nearly 30 new cases per 1,000 people each year — the researchers could not pinpoint a single, exact risk rate.

Additionally, the analysis relied on real-world observational data rather than controlled clinical trials.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Importantly, these are population-level findings," Adewuyi said. "They cannot predict whether a particular person will develop Alzheimer’s disease."

Variations in where the studies were conducted, how long patients were tracked and which outside health factors were considered all influenced the outcomes.

Alzheimer's is one of the most prevalent dementia types, comprising almost 70% of all cases, Kizil noted, which is why the studies are heavily focused on that condition.

However, as diabetes can deprive the brain of essential nutrients, it can contribute to a wide range of neurological diseases beyond just Alzheimer’s.

For people who have diabetes along with an increased risk of developing dementia, Kizil recommends undergoing cognitive screenings much earlier, alongside blood sugar control and other measurements.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

People with diabetes or any type of cardiovascular risk factors, including high blood pressure, should work proactively with their doctors on metabolic control and earlier cognitive monitoring, he advised.

Adewuyi emphasized that the study provides no basis for changing medication or adopting tighter blood glucose targets specifically to prevent Alzheimer’s disease. 

"If someone notices persistent changes in memory or thinking – particularly if these are affecting medicines, glucose monitoring or daily activities – they should discuss them with their healthcare team," he advised.

The early signs and symptoms of Alzheimer’s are most often related to becoming more forgetful, according to Palekar.

Some of those include "short-term memory loss, such as forgetting recent events or conversations, misplacing things routinely, having difficulty managing finances or performing complex daily tasks," the doctor told Fox News Digital.

To support brain health, Palekar recommends following a primary care physician’s guidance to closely monitor blood sugar levels alongside key lifestyle modifications — "specifically, moderate-intensity aerobic exercise 150 minutes a week and a balanced diet, such as the Mediterranean diet."

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone strike on Russian warship in Libya risks ‘serious escalation,’ former official warns
articles.summary:
The Ukrainian sea drone strike that capsized and sank a Russian warship in Libya on Sunday risks a "serious escalation" of the nearly five-year war, a former U.S. national security adviser warned Monday, calling the operation a "giant tantrum" by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Morgan Murphy, a former press secretary to the secretary of defense, also told Fox News Digital that the nighttime attack on the Russian corvette Mercury in the Libyan port city of Benghazi could further strain relations between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump, while echoing frustrations that he said also plagued former President Joe Biden's administration.

"The strike on the Russian corvette Mercury in North Africa — in Libya specifically — is a serious escalation of the war in Ukraine," Murphy claimed.

"Calling the Benghazi strike a giant tantrum could be one interpretation of it, and it's not unusual behavior for him," Murphy said of Zelenskyy.

RUSSIAN WARSHIP SINKS OFF LIBYA AS SUSPECTED UKRAINIAN STRIKES TAKE WAR BEYOND BLACK SEA

Murphy also argued that Zelenskyy's willingness to pursue military objectives that complicate Washington's diplomatic priorities has frustrated previous administrations.

"This is why I think the Biden administration was frustrated with Zelenskyy, and why the Trump administration has been frustrated with Zelenskyy: he's acting like an independent player and not an ally," Murphy said.

Biden had reportedly lost his temper during a June 2022 phone call after Zelenskyy requested additional military assistance shortly after the White House announced a $1 billion aid package for Ukraine.

In his recently released memoir, Biden also revealed private frustrations with Zelenskyy, describing the Ukrainian leader as moody, stubborn and less grateful than expected.

UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

Murphy went on to suggest the Benghazi drone strike could also complicate Trump's efforts to broker an end to the war, particularly after the president met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit without Zelenskyy.

"The President just had a successful meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, and he met them without Zelenskyy present, as is the right of the President of the United States to meet with whom he likes when he pleases," Murphy said.

"Zelenskyy was clearly upset about that, and this attack is him showing the President of the United States that he's still very relevant."

The operation, coordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and armed forces, targeted the Russian vessel in port, raising questions about where the drones originated and whether the conflict could spread further beyond Ukraine's borders.

Zelenskyy praised the strike Monday in a post on X, calling it "An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."

Murphy argued that the Ukrainian leader is increasingly under pressure to demonstrate Kyiv can still deliver significant military victories as Trump pursues a diplomatic resolution.

"What he's looking for here is, I believe, a victory, because Ukraine has found more aid and sympathy on the world stage when it's winning," Murphy said.

Ukraine initially drew widespread international support after resisting Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, defying expectations that Moscow would quickly overwhelm Kyiv.

"Ukraine performed much better against an enemy five times its size, and human nature loves an underdog."

"There was a deep outpouring of sympathy — and more importantly, support — for Ukraine after that initial flop of a Russian invasion," Murphy said.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

But as the conflict has dragged on, Murphy argued, Ukraine has struggled to sustain the enthusiasm that followed Russia's initial setbacks, with the fighting descending into what he described as a "stalemate and a war of attrition."

"Zelenskyy is having a harder time building support," he said of the current state of play.

"As he saw the President meet with Russia and meet with Xi Jinping in China, he needed a victory, and he needed a dramatic attack — so an asymmetric attack was on the board."

The Benghazi strike also underscores Ukraine's expanding ability to target Russian military assets thousands of miles from its territory, although questions remain about how the operation was carried out.

"Ukraine has taken credit for it, but they've been coy about where it was launched from," Murphy said.

"There's some speculation that it was launched from within Libya. Others say that it came from a mothership, which is totally plausible — that they took an innocuous-looking cargo ship and launched these drones out of it."

Murphy said the operation reflects a broader transformation in modern warfare, with military planners still grappling with the implications of increasingly sophisticated drone attacks.

"What we are watching unfold in real time is a total shift in the nature of warfare. It's really unheralded," he said.

UKRAINE’S DRONE REVOLUTION SHOWS RUSSIA IS DANGEROUSLY UNPREPARED. BUT, SO IS AMERICA

"It will take time — planners' time and nations' time — to understand how to react to this kind of aggression."

Beyond the military implications, Murphy warned that the strike could undermine diplomatic efforts in Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict.

"There is a very concerted group of diplomats and thought leaders in D.C. who want to see a diplomatic end to this conflict sooner rather than later," Murphy said.

"They see that as being in the best interest of the United States and the world, but most importantly, they see it in the best interest of the Ukrainian people."

Murphy said those pushing for a negotiated settlement would likely view the reported strike in Libya as a setback to Trump's peace efforts.

"A lot of thinkers in Washington want this to end, and they'll see this escalation in Libya as counterproductive to what the President is trying to do."

articles.title: NATO warns Putin could strike before European army responds, points to US as military model
articles.summary:
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned Monday that creating a separate European army could undermine the alliance’s ability to respond quickly to a Russian attack, as Moscow continues to ramp up its military capabilities during the ongoing war in Ukraine.

Speaking at the 72nd annual session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, Rutte cautioned that competing military command structures could hold up decisions in a crisis, warning that Russia’s "war machine" is running at full throttle and could also pose a threat to Europe long after the war ends.

"What I would counsel against is having all the nations with their own militaries working together in NATO and then on top of that having a big European structure, because then if Putin attacks, we will first need two or three weeks to agree who will do what, and then he will probably end up in Rotterdam before we have decided. So that has been my argument," Rutte said, according to Ukrainska Pravda.

NATO JETS SHOOT DOWN DRONE IN LITHUANIAN AIRSPACE AS RUSSIA GROWS 'INCREASINGLY RECKLESS,' RUTTE SAYS

Rutte pointed to the United States as a model for an integrated military, arguing that European countries would also need to move beyond separate national forces to establish a unified army.

"My point has always been that if you have a European military, you cannot also have national militaries. The United States has one military."

"There is not a specific army or navy for the state of New York or for the state of California. It is an integrated United States military. If Europe is able to pull that off, fine," Rutte said.

Rutte said it was Russia's expanding military production and cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea that pose a long-term threat to NATO, regardless of how the war in Ukraine ends.

"We face great dangers coming from Russia and the fact that Russia works so closely together with Iran, China, and North Korea, we know that Russia's war machine at the moment is running at full speed," Rutte also said at the assembly in Berlin.

FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE

"Its war economy keeps growing, and it won't stand still when the war against Ukraine hopefully will end one day. That whole machine is there and will continue."

Rutte also rejected the idea that only countries bordering Russia or Ukraine face a direct military threat, warning that Moscow's long-range missiles put capitals across Europe within striking distance.

"Let me say once again to everyone here who is not on the eastern flank: I have news for you. You are on the eastern flank too. These latest Russian missiles need only five minutes longer to reach Lisbon, Rome or The Hague, my hometown, than to reach Tallinn, Warsaw or Helsinki," Rutte said.

"So we are all on the eastern flank here. Let's put an end to this discussion about whether or not you are on the eastern flank. We are all on the eastern flank."

The NATO chief's remarks came amid plans to deploy an early-warning aircraft to Poland after Polish prosecutors said three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles landed on Polish territory Friday during strikes against Ukraine.

NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK

Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said that NATO would deploy an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to strengthen surveillance along the alliance's eastern flank, according to Reuters.

"This is a very good system that gives us even deeper... operational awareness which allows us to respond better to this kind of threat," Zalewski told reporters following a NATO meeting in Brussels.

The aircraft can monitor large areas of airspace and provide allied forces with a shared picture of potential aerial threats, improving NATO's ability to detect and respond to missile and aircraft activity.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also warned Monday night that intelligence indicated Moscow was preparing a new wave of strikes against Ukraine.

Beyond Russia's ongoing military threats, Rutte said that Europe's interconnected infrastructure, including energy networks and communications systems, is vulnerable.

RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT

"We are all targeted, that we are all affected when it comes to our pipelines, our cables, our energy grids, and our economies."

"They are all interconnected, and that means that we are all in this for the long term. And therefore, we must step up to the plate to ensure that we stay ahead of danger."

Rutte said defending NATO countries demands civilian preparedness, pointing to northern European nations that have begun teaching residents about their responsibilities in the event of war.

"This really takes the whole of society," he said.

"And that's in the end, I think, still Norway and Sweden, and Denmark and Finland, and maybe one or two others who are really ahead of the pack here, and having made clear to their citizens what they need to do in case war breaks out, at least not to get in the way of the military, but to be helpful and also how they make sure that the police and the ambulance services and fire, the fire fighting departments work together, supporting the military wherever possible."

Rutte's warnings come amid uncertainty over Ukraine's long-term security arrangements and whether Western allies will offer guarantees resembling NATO's Article 5 collective defense commitment as part of a future peace agreement.

U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner said Sunday that President Donald Trump was willing to consider Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine as part of a broader postwar security arrangement for Europe.

articles.title: Russia warns of 'preventive nuclear attack' as Medvedev claims Ukraine, NATO crossed line
articles.summary:
Russia warned Monday that it could carry out a "preventive nuclear attack" under certain circumstances, with former President Dmitry Medvedev claiming Ukraine and NATO allies have already crossed certain thresholds that could push Moscow to consider using nuclear weapons.

"The massive use of non-nuclear means that cause catastrophes makes a preventive nuclear attack by the Russian Federation possible," Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote in an article published Monday in the Moscow Journal of International Law and excerpted by the state news agency TASS.

Medvedev also warned that "secret or hidden supplies of nuclear weapons from the West to Kyiv will provoke a legitimate preventive nuclear attack by Russia."

MOSCOW THREATENS NUCLEAR RESPONSE OVER TINY FORTRESS WEDGED BETWEEN US ALLIES AS CLASH FEARS GROW

"Kyiv and its allies must remember that the Russian Federation not only has the right, but in various situations has the obligation to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.

Medvedev's warning came amid continuing tensions between Moscow and the West over the nearly five-year war in Ukraine and NATO's military support for Kyiv.

He argued that Ukraine and its Western allies have already created circumstances under which Russia could consider a nuclear strike, though he said Russian President Vladimir Putin carefully weighs the consequences before making such a decision.

"Formally, in a number of cases, the parties collectively opposing us (Ukraine, NATO countries, and several Western countries outside the alliance) have already created situations in which Russia considers the possibility of launching a nuclear strike," Medvedev wrote in the article, titled "State Sovereignty and Nuclear Weapons: International Legal Aspects of Ensuring National Security".

TRUMP HOLDS THE NUCLEAR CARDS TO PLAY AGAINST CHINA AND RUSSIA ON ARMS CONTROL

Despite those warnings, Medvedev wrote that Putin "is always guided by a comprehensive analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage inflicted and the retaliatory measures."

Medvedev also said Russia has not used nuclear weapons during the war with Ukraine because it has not considered them necessary, though he warned that calculation could change.

"Obviously, so far the course of events in the Ukrainian crisis has not created a state of direct necessity to use nuclear weapons," he wrote.

"The decision on Russia's use of nuclear weapons during the special military operation was not taken due to the lack of a direct necessity to do so," he added, using the Kremlin's preferred term for the war in Ukraine.

Medvedev argued that while Russia's nuclear doctrine does not explicitly authorize preventive nuclear strikes, certain scenarios — including catastrophic attacks using conventional weapons or the transfer of nuclear arms to Ukraine — could justify preemptive action. 

He said any final decision rests solely with Putin.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

"In making such decisions, the Russian president is always guided by a complete analysis of all factors and the proportionality between the actual damage caused and the retaliatory measures," Medvedev wrote.

"The Kyiv regime and its sponsors must not harbor dangerous illusions," he warned.

"If the scenarios mentioned above were to occur, the head of state not only has the right, but also the obligation to use nuclear weapons. All those who are currently fanning the flames must fully realize this".

Medvedev's remarks came within days of President Donald Trump meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Nov. 19 in Shenzhen, China, where the leaders of the three nuclear powers agreed to pursue talks aimed at reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

While the summit produced no major breakthrough on arms reductions, the leaders reaffirmed in a declaration that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.

TRUMP WILL FACE REPORTERS AFTER HISTORIC XI-PUTIN TALKS AS WAR QUESTIONS LINGER

To support his argument, Medvedev cited a 1996 International Court of Justice advisory opinion, contending that international law does not categorically prohibit the use of nuclear weapons when a state's survival is at stake.

The court concluded that the threat or use of nuclear weapons would generally violate international humanitarian law, but it did not definitively resolve whether such use would be lawful in extreme circumstances of self-defense.

Medvedev, who served as Russia's president from 2008 to 2012 and later as prime minister under Putin, has become one of Moscow's most outspoken voices on nuclear escalation since Russia invaded Ukraine.

Medvedev accused NATO members of undermining nonproliferation efforts, criticizing Germany's participation in nuclear deterrence arrangements and arguing that NATO's nuclear-sharing policies do not represent a universally accepted interpretation of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)

On Monday, he also accused the U.S. of applying double standards toward Iran and said Washington used nonproliferation fears to justify military action against Tehran while following its own objectives.

articles.title: Russia could launch nuclear-capable satellite within weeks, Western intelligence warns: report
articles.summary:
Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit within less than 60 days according to new Western intelligence assessments reported Monday, raising fears that Moscow is preparing to deploy a weapon capable of crippling thousands of satellites used by the United States and its allies.

The intelligence reports emerged just four days after President Donald Trump met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a high-profile summit in Shenzhen, China, where nuclear arms control was a central topic.

The three leaders issued a joint declaration affirming that nuclear war should never be fought, but stopped short of announcing binding arms-control commitments.

NEXT GENERATION OPIR GEO: BUILDING AMERICA’S GATEWAY TO THE FUTURE OF SPACE-BASED MISSILE WARNING AND TRACKING

On Monday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz publicly addressed the reports, while the Kremlin dismissed the allegations.

According to a joint investigation published Nov. 23 by German broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, Western intelligence agencies believe Russia has assembled a satellite known as "Sputnik-S," which has reportedly been stored in the Moscow region for several years.

Intelligence warnings shared among several NATO countries in early November indicated that the satellite, reportedly designed to carry a nuclear warhead, could be launched within 60 days. Germany's military Space Command reportedly assessed that a December launch was possible.

The German investigation also reported that military officials had briefed senior government figures, including German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, about the threat.

The reports prompted an immediate response from European leaders.

Speaking alongside Rutte in Berlin on Monday, Merz described the allegations as "shocking," while noting that concerns about Russia's nuclear space ambitions were not entirely new.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

Rutte, meanwhile, stressed that NATO was continually assessing its defensive capabilities.

"I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory," Rutte said, according to Reuters.

He added that the alliance's defense planning included threats in space and said NATO had response options that were not always visible to the public.

The Kremlin rejected the allegations. Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov questioned the credibility of the intelligence reports, saying they contained numerous unsubstantiated claims that were "hardly worth taking seriously," according to The Moscow Times.

"We haven’t seen the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that it’s certainly hardly worth taking them seriously," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.

Russia's Embassy in Berlin separately dismissed the reporting as part of a propaganda campaign and maintained that Moscow's space activities were peaceful and consistent with international obligations.

The latest warnings follow an earlier assessment by the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency , which publicly identified Russia's development of a nuclear-capable satellite in October. "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon," the DIA stated in its 2026 Challenges to Security in Space assessment.

NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK

As Fox News Digital reported on October 29, the agency warned that such a weapon could cause the rapid loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by governments and private companies.

Unlike a conventional anti-satellite weapon targeting an individual spacecraft, a nuclear detonation in orbit could potentially disable large numbers of satellites through radiation and electromagnetic effects.

The consequences could extend far beyond the military. Satellites support GPS navigation, international communications, financial transactions, weather forecasting and critical infrastructure.

The threat also has implications for Ukraine, whose military relies heavily on satellite communications, including SpaceX's Starlink network, during its war with Russia.

The concern was initially addressed on February 2024 when the Biden administration publicly acknowledged that Russia was developing a troubling anti-satellite capability, although officials said at the time that no such weapon had been deployed.

Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which prohibits stationing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in space.

The latest German reporting suggests the threat could be approaching a more immediate stage, but critical questions remain unanswered, including whether the satellite already carries a nuclear warhead and whether Western intelligence has independently verified the reported launch preparations.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House, Pentagon, U.S. Space Command and German Embassy for comment.

articles.title: Who owns your body parts after surgery? Doctors uncover the complicated rules
articles.summary:
Most people want to forget their time in the operating room, yet some surgical patients insist on bringing their removed body parts home as souvenirs.

While hospitals usually throw away removed tissue as medical waste, a small number of patients asks doctors to pack up their organs, teeth and worn-out joints after surgery, according to TIME magazine.

Doctors say these patients want keepsakes for many reasons, from marking personal milestones to honoring cultural traditions.

ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS

Examples included a patient who kept her removed uterus in a jar after a hysterectomy as a reminder of the pain she survived, and another who dried her removed fallopian tubes to display in a box with flowers, according to the report.

Other saved items included a pulled wisdom tooth fashioned into a calligraphy pen and a piece of medical tubing saved from a hospital stay and later given to a future spouse, the magazine said.

Dr. Robyn Power, a gynecologic surgeon in South Florida, told TIME that only about five of her patients finished the paperwork to take tissue home over the past year, though more people are asking about it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

She said patients living with painful conditions like endometriosis sometimes want the removed tissue as physical proof of what disrupted their lives.

"It means something different to everybody," Power said.

Taking a body part home takes more than asking a surgeon in the recovery room.

Dr. Kenneth Perry, an emergency room physician based in South Carolina, told Fox News Digital that rules surrounding who owns removed tissue vary widely.

"As odd as it sounds, the ownership of tissue and other things removed from a person’s body is actually not settled law," Perry said. "Each state and each institution will have its own views on how to handle different tissues."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

In the emergency room, Perry said doctors often let patients take home low-risk items like passed kidney stones, salivary gland stones or splinters, as long as the objects are not tied to a police case, like a bullet. 

Larger organs or body parts carry more risk because doctors must rule out infection or serious disease before releasing them.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"For instance, if an extremity or an organ has been removed due to infection or bleeding, it is often required that it goes through pathology testing to ensure it is safe," Perry said.

He added that for pregnancy-related tissues, such as a placenta or remains from a miscarriage, hospitals typically have different rules and separate steps involved for families who ask to take them home.

Some surgical patients have taken to Reddit to share their confusion and experiences with trying to keep removed body parts.

"Seeing as the hip bone is coming from my own body, I don't understand why I cannot," one user wrote ahead of a hip replacement in Washington State after a surgeon claimed that state law rejected his request to keep the bone.

"My best friend's son got to keep one of his tonsils to take to school for show and tell," the user added.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Others pushed back, pointing to health hazards and hospital rules.

"It's considered medical waste. Yes, bones can carry risks," one commenter wrote.

"It really depends on the state laws, but most will not allow it," wrote another user who said they worked in pathology. "You can have a funeral home bury it if you like, but probably not take it home."

articles.title: Captain who abandoned passengers on sinking Costa Concordia cruise ship released early from prison
articles.summary:
After nine years in a Rome prison, the captain of the Costa Concordia, Francesco Schettino, was released early from prison. Italian newspaper Quotidiano Nazionale reports he will serve the remaining 7 years of his 16-year sentence for manslaughter on supervised probation.

Schettino’s lawyer, Francesca Carnicelli, told Fox News, "I can confirm that Mr. Schettino is currently finishing his sentence under a program that allows him to live outside of prison," saying, "he has a job as an office worker, must be home by 10:00 p.m. and is not allowed to leave the province where he resides."

CRUISE COMPANY FOUNDER SAYS HE'S 'THE VILLAIN' AFTER 200-PLUS PASSENGERS ARE STRANDED

Almost 15 years ago, on Jan. 13, 2012, the Costa Concordia slammed into rocks off Tuscany’s Giglio island. Schettino reportedly veered off course to perform a "sail-by salute." There were 4,200 passengers and crew on board, and 32 people were killed.

Schettino faced backlash after abandoning the ship, while hundreds of passengers were waiting to be rescued. At the time, Schettino told Italian La Repubblica that while helping others he tripped and ended up in one of the lifeboats.

'THIS WAS A MIRACLE': CRUISE PASSENGERS DESCRIBE FRANTIC ESCAPE AS TANKER STRIKES SHIP

A Netflix documentary titled, "Shipwrecked: Nightmare at Sea," was released earlier this year.

American Nicholas Taliaferro, who survived the tragedy, told Fox News, "We have an opportunity to ask ourselves, a very important question was justice truly served? and that question is not only for those watching the documentary, but especially the victims and the survivors and the families who have had to live the consequences of the captain and everybody else that was involved for nearly 15 years, because serving a sentence and delivering justice aren’t necessarily the same thing."

JULY 17, 2013: COURT HEARS HOW 32 DIED IN COSTA CONCORDIA SHIPWRECK

Prosecutors argued the captain was cowardly in his actions and refused the Italian Coast Guard’s orders to go back onboard and help with the evacuation.

Taliaferro said: "Whether you’re in United States or in Italy, or anywhere, the captain is the last one to get off the boat and he was the first one and now you’re the first one to get out, I mean it just seems a little disrespectful to the families and the survivors".

articles.title: Israel’s leading contender for prime minister clashes with Netanyahu over Iran strikes
articles.summary:
The politician tasked by Israel's president to form a new government, Gadi Eisenkot, said Monday that Iran poses no immediate threat requiring military action before a new government is formed, drawing a sharp response from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as President Donald Trump considers renewed strikes against Tehran.

The dispute comes amid a political power struggle following last month's Israeli election. Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister, but Eisenkot's allies now control the leadership of the Knesset and key parliamentary committees as negotiations over a new government continue.

"Today I see no direct and immediate threat to Israel that requires action before a government is formed," Eisenkot, who previously served as the IDF chief of staff, told his party's Knesset faction, according to an English translation of his Hebrew remarks provided to Fox News Digital.

ISRAEL'S POLITICAL SHAKE-UP ENTERS NEW PHASE AS FORMER PM PLAYS KINGMAKER — AND DEADLINE LOOMS

He stressed that Iran remains Israel's gravest security threat, particularly its nuclear program.

"In my view, the gravest threat from Iran is its stockpile of 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60%," Eisenkot said. "It has yet to be destroyed or removed."

He called for the material at a minimum to be placed under strict monitoring.

Netanyahu pushed back hours later, accusing political rivals of downplaying the Iranian threat for political reasons.

NETANYAHU'S BLOC FALLS SHORT AS LONGTIME ALLIES REPORTEDLY WEIGH MOVE THAT COULD END HIS RULE

"The Iranian threats are real," he said before a Likud faction meeting, according to TPS-IL. He renewed his call for a national unity government, signaling room for compromise on ultra-Orthodox military conscription while rejecting a coalition dependent on Arab-led parties.

The status of Iran's uranium remains uncertain. The International Atomic Energy Agency last verified approximately 440.9 kilograms enriched to 60% before attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025, but inspectors have since lost continuity of knowledge about the material. The U.S., Britain, France and Germany highlighted that verification gap in a Nov. 19 statement.

Adding another perspective Monday, former Mossad director David Barnea urged military action against Iran "as soon as all conditions allow."

Speaking at The European Leadership Network Jerusalem conference, Barnea warned that "a diplomatic agreement with the Ayatollah regime will never succeed," according to The Times of Israel, although he also acknowledged the option of giving sanctions more time.

TRUMP WARNS OF NEW STRIKES AGAINST IRAN AFTER NEW YEAR, CALLS NEGOTIATORS ‘PROFESSIONAL TAP DANCERS’

The competing assessments followed Trump's comments Sunday to Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst that he was inclined to resume strikes against Iran after the new year if talks failed.

Trump called Iranian negotiators "professional tap dancers" and warned that ships challenging the U.S. naval blockade could be sunk.

In a response to Fox News Digital, a U.S. official said the administration believes its economic pressure campaign has been effective enough that major military operations are not currently necessary, while emphasizing that Trump retains all options. "As President Trump and Secretary Rubio have stated, our economic pressure campaign is devastating Iran to such an extent that the president does not have any need to conduct major combat operations," the official said on background.

"However, President Trump has all options at his disposal to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. President Trump holds all the cards and will do whatever is best for the United States."

An Israeli source familiar with discussions within the opposition told Fox News Digital that there are assessments that anti-government demonstrations in Iran could intensify as the blockade adds to economic pressure.

According to the source, those assessments are contributing to an argument for waiting before launching another major military operation. The forecast has not been independently verified.

IRAN VOWS ‘ASTONISHING’ STRIKES AND LIFTS MISSILE-RANGE LIMIT AS US TARGETS LAND ROUTES

The blockade has already significantly curtailed Iranian oil exports. Reuters reported Monday that visible Iranian crude exports had dropped to near zero in recent months.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran would use all available means to oppose the restrictions, calling them military aggression, according to Reuters.

The disagreement over Iran is unfolding as Eisenkot attempts to turn an electoral advantage into a governing coalition.

Israel's Oct. 27 election left no bloc with a governing majority. Eisenkot's four-party alliance won 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Netanyahu's traditional right-wing and religious allies secured 53, including 13 held by the ultra-Orthodox parties. But those alliances have since shifted. United Torah Judaism, which holds seven seats, declined to endorse Netanyahu and has entered coalition negotiations with Eisenkot, leaving the prime minister with just 46 lawmakers formally backing his bid to remain in office. 

Eisenkot, meanwhile, received the support of 67 lawmakers, including 19 from Arab-led parties, although significant disagreements remain over the composition of a future government.

Unlike Congress, Israel has a single-chamber parliament. Although Netanyahu remains in charge of the caretaker government, the new parliamentary majority can advance legislation and exercise oversight without first forming a government.

Eisenkot ally Matan Kahana is now Knesset speaker. Former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman heads the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, Liran Avisar Ben Horin chairs the provisional Finance Committee, and Yashar lawmaker Roy Folkman leads the Arrangements Committee, which helps organize parliamentary business.

IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY

Those appointments have practical consequences.

At a Nov. 17 Finance Committee meeting, officials said approximately 1.5 billion shekels in coalition funds remained unallocated. Avisar Ben Horin instructed the Finance Ministry to submit requests involving those funds separately so lawmakers could scrutinize them, according to an official Knesset announcement.

The new majority is also advancing legislation to reverse changes to judicial appointments and other measures adopted under Netanyahu, though the bills have not become law.

The Israeli source said opposition leaders view control of the committees as an opportunity to restore parliamentary oversight after years in which Netanyahu's coalition dominated the legislative agenda.

The source said they also hope to put Eisenkot in a stronger position should Israel return to the polls.

Eisenkot said any coalition must respect his core principles, including establishing a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 attacks and expanding mandatory military service.

"There will be no compromise on establishing a state commission of inquiry," he said. "There will be no compromise on mandatory service for all."

The debate over when to act against Iran now unfolds alongside another unresolved question in Jerusalem: who will lead Israel when that decision is made.

Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Taylor Swift ISIS concert plot foiled with Israel’s help, ex-Mossad chief says
articles.summary:
Former Mossad chief David Barnea revealed Monday that Israeli intelligence played a key role in thwarting an ISIS-inspired terrorist plot targeting Taylor Swift's concerts in Vienna in 2024, an attack he said could have killed hundreds of young people.

Speaking at the European Leadership Network ELNET conference in Jerusalem, Barnea disclosed that Austrian intelligence had initially identified the threat before turning to Israel's Mossad, which helped uncover the network behind the planned attack.

"The initial threat warning came from our Austrian partners," Barnea said, according to the transcript of his speech.

SPY LAW USED TO STOP TAYLOR SWIFT ATTACK TO LAPSE AS CONGRESS SKIPS TOWN, WORLD CUP NEARS

Once Austrian authorities shared the information, the Mossad used its intelligence capabilities to analyze the threat, uncover the network and help bring about the suspects' arrests, Barnea said. The joint effort prevented "mass murder, up to hundreds of young European men and women," he said.

The disclosure sheds new light on the international intelligence cooperation behind the foiled plot, which forced the cancellation of three sold-out shows during Swift's record-breaking "Eras Tour" in August 2024.

More than 170,000 spectators were expected to attend the concerts, according to estimates from the Austrian news agency APA cited by The Times of Israel.

Austrian authorities arrested the principal suspect, then 19, on Aug. 7, 2024, just one day before Swift was scheduled to perform at Vienna's Ernst Happel Stadium. Swift later described the cancellations as devastating and thanked authorities for preventing a tragedy. "Thanks to them, we were grieving concerts and not lives," she wrote on Instagram in August 2024.

FBI ARRESTS WOMAN WHO ALLEGEDLY PLOTTED ISIS-LINKED ATTACK ON NEW YORK STATE CAPITOL BUILDING

Investigators said the suspect had pledged allegiance to ISIS and was preparing a suicide attack intended to inflict mass casualties. Authorities discovered chemicals, machetes and electronic devices at his home. Austrian intelligence officials believed the suspect intended to attack crowds gathered outside the stadium, where an estimated 20,000 fans without tickets were expected to assemble.

The investigation also involved American intelligence agencies. The Biden administration acknowledged in August 2024 that the United States had shared intelligence with Austrian authorities to help disrupt the threat. Then-White House national security spokesman John Kirby confirmed that American officials had provided information to their Austrian counterparts.

The Vienna concert plot was not the only operation Barnea discussed. According to his remarks, he described Mossad's cooperation with European agencies against alleged Iranian-directed assassination plots and Hamas networks accused of preparing attacks on Jewish and Israeli targets.

Barnea said Israeli intelligence helped expose an alleged Iranian network in Greece and North Macedonia and uncover cells in France and Germany. He also claimed that joint investigations with German, Austrian and Danish authorities revealed Hamas infrastructure and concealed weapons stockpiles in Vienna, Bulgaria and Poland. These were separate operations from the ISIS-linked Swift plot.

FBI BRINGS IRAQI MAN ACCUSED OF COORDINATING NEARLY 20 TERROR ATTACKS IN EUROPE TO FACE TRIAL IN NEW YORK

Fox News Digital reported on one of those investigations in Nov. 2025, documenting coordinated counterterrorism raids in Germany and Austria. According to Israeli officials cited in that report, Austrian intelligence discovered pistols and explosive materials in a Vienna cache allegedly connected to Muhammad Naim, a son of senior Hamas figure Bassem Naim.

A senior Israeli intelligence official told Fox News Digital at the time that active cells remained across Europe and warned that security agencies needed to remain vigilant.

In Sept. 2026, Fox News Digital also reported that German prosecutors had indicted seven suspects accused of procuring weapons for Hamas, including an automatic rifle, 13 pistols and more than 700 rounds of ammunition.

Barnea presented these separate cases as evidence of the value of cooperation between Israeli intelligence and European law enforcement.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: NIH funded foreign labs with troubling safety lapses, including deadly bat virus experiment
articles.summary:
FIRST ON FOX: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) awarded millions of taxpayer dollars to foreign animal research facilities where significant biosafety, containment and staffing failures allegedly took place — including a bat virus experiment in Australia that was abruptly halted after animal containment broke down, according to federal records obtained by People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) and reviewed by Fox News Digital.

The internal agency records and noncompliance reports show that federal health officials repeatedly approved funding or failed to identify major safety and oversight vulnerabilities until after taxpayer-funded animal experiments were already underway.

In response to the findings, PETA on Monday sent a formal complaint to NIH Director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, demanding that the agency immediately halt all federal funding for animal experiments conducted outside the U.S.

The newly released information comes amid mounting scrutiny on Capitol Hill regarding foreign research oversight and renewed calls for the bipartisan Cease Animal Research Grants Overseas (CARGO) Act, which would permanently prohibit NIH from bankrolling animal experiments in foreign countries.

GABBARD SAYS DECLASSIFIED BIOLAB RECORDS VALIDATE CONCERNS PREVIOUSLY DISMISSED AS MISINFORMATION

According to federal documents, the NIH funded a study on Hendra virus — a lethal, bat-borne pathogen — at the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness, operated by Australia's national science agency, CSIRO. The project, "Shining a light on bat cellular immunity following virus infection," was suspended by the facility’s Animal Ethics Committee after serious operational failures surfaced.

Internal records show the facility suffered from insufficient appropriately trained personnel capable of conducting animal procedures at the required biocontainment level, an absence of adequate contingency planning, unclear protocols and prolonged confinement of flying fox bats without proper enrichment.

RIDGLAN FARMS BEAGLES BEGIN LEAVING WISCONSIN FACILITY AFTER RESCUE GROUPS STRIKE DEAL FOR RELEASE

After a single flying fox tested positive for Hendra virus, staff were forced to kill all eight bats housed together because the room could not be elevated to Biosafety Level 4 (BSL-4) containment. A ninth flying fox housed separately at BSL-4 was later killed after also testing positive.

The primary investigator alerted the NIH to the infections in May 2023, leading the ethics board to suspend the study weeks later. However, the NIH’s Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare (OLAW) did not receive even a preliminary report of the suspension until April 2024 — more than 10 months after the shutdown, according to records.

The documents show the Australian bat study was not an isolated incident. At Newcastle University in the United Kingdom, where researchers conducted NIH-funded brain and stroke research on nonhuman primates, a 2025 federal review ordered the facility to reevaluate its personal protective equipment standards, tuberculosis screening and emergency procedures for testing potential human exposures to the deadly Herpes B virus.

Following past international scandals — including a shuttered Colombian facility that received $17 million in U.S. funding while keeping monkeys in squalor — the NIH pledged to implement "enhanced oversight" of foreign institutions in line with Government Accountability Office (GAO) recommendations.

However, PETA’s review of 124 federal files obtained through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) shows the NIH’s oversight relies almost entirely on self-reporting and scripted virtual site visits.

Records show that virtual visits were announced months in advance, allowing overseas facilities ample time to prepare. At Newcastle University, the facility received notice in May 2025 for a virtual visit that did not happen until December. 

Notification letters outlined prearranged planning sessions, document reviews and camera tours where foreign personnel controlled what government monitors could see on screen.

The format gave federal regulators no ability to conduct unannounced walk-throughs, inspect arbitrary rooms, review records in real time or conduct confidential staff interviews, according to records. 

Out of 70 annual reports examined regarding active NIH-backed animal research across foreign labs between 2023 and 2025, 67 self-reported zero violations, reflecting a system almost entirely dependent on foreign labs self-policing their own programs.

HARVARD-CHINA LINKS UNEARTHED AS CONGRESS FINDS 140 PAPERS CO-AUTHORED BY CCP MILITARY UNIVERSITIES

The records also document widespread administrative failures, including grants flowing to institutions that lacked basic federal authorization:

The NIH awarded a $13 million tuberculosis vaccine adjuvant contract to the University of Sydney in 2022, but the animal testing was outsourced to the Centenary Institute in Australia, an entity lacking the required NIH Foreign Animal Welfare Assurance. 

The unauthorized setup went unnoticed by the NIH for years until the university inquired about the death of an experimental mouse in 2025.

HUNDREDS OF ACTIVISTS FACE PEPPER SPRAY IN VIOLENT CLASH WITH DEPUTIES AT WISCONSIN BEAGLE RESEARCH FACILITY

The NIH also confirmed that it could find "no records of an assurance" for multiple foreign entities carrying out U.S.-funded animal studies, including Australian biotech firm Kinoxis Therapeutics, which conducted opioid withdrawal experiments on 80 dogs, 314 rats and 1,485 mice under a grant active through May 2026. 

Similar record absences occurred for grants involving animal testing at institutions in Canada, Kenya and Israel.

At the Research Center in Clinical Biochemistry and Immunology in Argentina, the NIH funded a multi-year Chagas disease study. A 2026 preprint co-authored by the lead researcher detailed mice experiencing continuous whole-body tremors and hind-limb paralysis — conditions mandating euthanasia under the approved protocol.

However, the lab reported that untreated animals died over an extended 120-day timeframe and admitted it does not generate animal monitoring or veterinary records, leaving federal regulators with no documentation of how animal deaths were tracked.

WHITE HOUSE REBUKES CBS INTERVIEW AFTER HOST BATTLES NIH DIRECTOR OVER LOSS OF TRUST IN PUBLIC HEALTH

In her letter Monday to Bhattacharya, Dr. Magnolia Martínez, PETA’s lead projects manager and congressional liaison, argued that the NIH's foreign monitoring regime is fundamentally broken.

The organization noted that an Animal Welfare Assurance represents a baseline administrative requirement that does not ensure animal welfare or clinical applicability to human health, urging the agency to halt funding foreign animal tests and redirect resources toward human-biology-based research methods.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on Monday told Fox News Digital the NIH "received the report today and will investigate its claims thoroughly to determine whether any animal welfare policies were violated."

"Under the leadership of Director Dr. Bhattacharya, the agency has taken unprecedented steps to strengthen oversight and increase transparency in research conducted by foreign institutions," HHS press secretary Emily Hilliard wrote in a statement.

Lawmakers in Washington are similarly ramping up efforts to cut off foreign funding through the CARGO Act, emphasizing that American taxpayers should not be underwriting unaccountable and hazardous research in foreign jurisdictions.

Fox News Digital reached out to bipartisan sponsors of the CARGO Act — including Sens. Rick Scott, R-Fla., Cory Booker, D-N.J., and Dina Titus, D-Nev. — asking whether the newly revealed foreign laboratory failures will prompt renewed legislative action and oversight hearings to permanently ban federal funding for overseas animal experiments.

articles.summary: A powerful storm forecast to bring fierce winds and heavy rain to the northeastern United States has forced the unprecedented postponement of the city's 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade, with the event rescheduled for Saturday. articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
articles.summary: Andy Taylor, whose guitar riffs helped shape Duran Duran's distinctive sound and propel the British band to global fame in the 1980s, has died aged 65 after a long battle with prostate cancer, the band and his family said Wednesday.

articles.title: PSG's perfect Champions League record ends as Roma snatch 2-2 draw with late penalty
articles.summary: Donyell Malen's 78th-minute penalty earned Roma a 2-2 draw at Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday, ending the defending champions' perfect record in this season's Champions League. The result also halted PSG's 12-game winning streak in all competitions, leaving Real Madrid as the only team with a 100% record after five league-phase matches.

articles.title: Le Pen party leaks: prefect dismissed, Paris deputy prosecutor placed under investigation
articles.summary: Two senior figures in France have been caught up in an investigation into suspected leaks to the far-right party of Marine Le Pen, the National Rally. The prefect of the Loiret, Hugues Moutouh, a former top official at the Interior Ministry, has been removed from his post after being suspected of passing on confidential information about investigations. And a deputy prosecutor in Paris, who was found at the party's headquarters during a police search, is now under administrative inquiry. FRANCE 24's Camille Knight reports.

articles.title: Israeli lawmakers advance October 7 inquiry opposed by Netanyahu
articles.summary: Israel's new parliament on Wednesday took a first step to set up a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to Hamas's unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack, a move long opposed by caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. FRANCE 24's Selina Sykes reports.

articles.title: New US tariffs: 'Trump lashing out really indiscriminately', expert says
articles.summary: The United States on Wednesday unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney, Dean Baker, Senior Economist at the Centre for Economic and Policy Research, says that "there has to be some mechanism for better coordinating China's involvement in the world trade system and ideally the US, the EU, Canada would have a common front, some clear ground rules that we could agree to, that China could agree to, to be mutually beneficial. It's not a step in that direction, we have President Trump lashing out really indiscriminately. It's very hard to see his approach being very productive".

articles.title: Did GTA 6 really recreate Charlie Kirk's assassination?
articles.summary: Just days after its release, Grand Theft Auto 6 has become a vehicle for political misinformation. Viral footage falsely claims the game features a mission recreating Charlie Kirk’s assassination, while pro-Russian accounts are sharing fake screenshots containing anti-Ukrainian messages. Meanwhile, Russia’s own Defence Ministry has exploited the game's popularity to promote military recruitment. Vedika Bahl explains how GTA 6 is being used to push real political agendas in Truth or Fake.

articles.title: Campaign rules for influencers? French regulator targets content creators
articles.summary: Ever since 1965 when the French first got to cast a ballot by universal suffrage for their president, they've valued campaign rules that guarantee ‘equal time’ for candidates. But what does equal time mean when you're closing in on 2027? Last week a bombshell announcement ahead of next Spring’s presidential elections: major online content creators will have to respect the same balanced air time rules as traditional TV and radio broadcasters during the campaign period. Here at France 24, we’re already testing the stopwatches and combing ove the guest list spreadsheets. Should podcasters, YouTubers and influencers be subjected to the same rules as us?

articles.title: EU says 'strongly' rejects premise of new US tariffs
articles.summary: The EU said Wednesday that it rejected the premise of new tariffs on its exports proposed by the United States and expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year. The recommendations, which came as Israel's longest-serving prime minister fights for his political survival, were immediately cheered by Netanyahu's right-wing allies who demanded the trial be brought to an end. Poland backs Ukraine as it fights off Russia's near five-year invasion and has repeatedly accused Moscow of seeking to target Kyiv's supporters with drone incursions and other methods. The no-fly zone is intended to allow Polish forces to quickly identify any Russian military aircraft and shoot them down if necessary. FRANCE 24's Selina Sykes reports.
