articles.title: 'Nothing will ever be the same' for Jensen Huang and Nvidia after his return
articles.summary: PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, November 24: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia dominates the papers. In other news, leaked records shed new light on Russian military losses in Ukraine. Also, the UK will host the 2035 Women's World Cup. Finally, a devilled eggs world championship crowns its winner.

articles.title: Nvidia's position as cornerstone of AI trade confirmed by market reaction to Huang's return
articles.summary: Tech shares in Asia and Europe rebounded on Tuesday, following in the footsteps of Nvidia's shares closing on Wall Street 31 percent higher on Monday. The return of CEO Jensen Huang, 11 days after his resignation over an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has reassured investors in the AI trade. In this edition, we look at Nvidia's central role in this trade, and Huang's central role at Nvidia. Also, French President Emmanuel Macron proposes to enshrine fiscal rules in the constitution.

articles.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
articles.summary: In a stunning U-turn, Nvidia's board has reinstated Jensen Huang as the company's president and CEO. The announcement came just days after the board rejected a petition calling for the tech titan's return. US President Donald Trump said had personally got in touch with the board to advocate for Huang's return. Nvidia's stock surged 32 percent on the news, adding nearly $1 trillion to its market cap while the rest of Wall Street also rallied.

articles.title: 'It can take years': Why the AI Riemann proof is far from settled
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence claimed another major scalp in maths on Friday, as Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge published what he says is proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a Millennium Prize Problem, in 17 million lines of code that no human has read in full. Physicist Tony Padilla tells Tech 24 that verification could take years, and that Alpöge should share how he got there.

articles.title: 'GTA VI': When the biggest-ever entertainment release becomes the biggest headline
articles.summary: This week FRANCE 24's media show "Scoop" looks at how the press covered the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI". Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than $2.3 billion. What does the game and the franchise's success mean for the future of entertainment? Our guest is Margaret Wallace, a video game developer and an associate professor of the practice of media innovation at Boston University.

articles.title: Anthropic shares slide on second day of trading as AI jitters fuel tech sell-off
articles.summary: Anthropic's much-hyped arrival on Wall Street fizzled out on Friday as ​nosediving tech stocks showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. Shares in the AI firm dipped below $90, one day after soaring to over $110 during a record-breaking Nasdaq debut.

articles.title: Anthropic goes public after blockbuster IPO but fails to revive AI trade
articles.summary: Anthropic has become the first pure-play AI developer to be publicly traded on the stock market, following a record-setting IPO. The stock opened 34 percent higher, briefly valuing the company at more than $2 trillion, before ending its first day of trading up 17 percent. However, Wall Street indexes closed sharply lower as investors took profits, reflecting underlying market jitters about the AI trade.

articles.title: How much do businesses want to pay for AI?
articles.summary: Four years after ChatGPT went mainstream, generative AI is transforming how we live and work. It's also been a major driver of economic growth, with massive amounts of money poured into expanding global computing capacity. But now, there are signs of a slowdown in AI spending as companies take a reality check: are they getting sufficient returns on their investments and how much artificial intelligence do they actually need?

articles.title: Anthropic blows past $2 trillion in Nasdaq debut, beating SpaceX's June listing
articles.summary: Anthropic hit $2 trillion in market value as its shares soared in their Nasdaq debut on Thursday, with investors rushing to own a stake in the maker of the Claude chatbot, the world's first publicly traded frontier AI company. Shares began trading at $111.5, 34% higher than the IPO price of $83.

articles.title: AI lab Anthropic sets stock market record with $81 billion IPO
articles.summary: Anthropic becomes the first "pure play" AI lab to go public, with an eye-watering $1.5 trillion valuation, a bellwether moment amid growing concerns of a financial bubble in the sector. Meanwhile, a scientific study shows US data centres are emitting as much greenhouse gas as entire nations.

articles.title: Peter Magyar meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Viktor Orban era
articles.summary: After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their countries' ties.

articles.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
articles.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?

articles.title: German firms eye Africa as global trade shocks hit traditional markets
articles.summary: German businesses are optimistic about Africa, but Berlin's cautious approach to risk is holding them back from cashing in on the opportunities that their competitors from countries like the UAE and Turkey are seizing.

articles.title: Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia's war on Ukraine
articles.summary: Whether through deception or desperation, Indians continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine. What can New Delhi do to protect its citizens from ending up fighting in Ukraine?

articles.title: In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
articles.summary: Millions of women in Afghanistan, particularly pregnant women, are suffering under Taliban restrictions and are increasingly losing access to life-saving medical care.

articles.title: Fact check: Deepfakes and 'US abandons Taiwan' claims spread ahead of vote
articles.summary: Ahead of local elections, Taiwan is seeing a surge in AI-generated attacks on mayoral candidate Puma Shen, alongside disinformation portraying the US as abandoning the island.

articles.title: Climate loss and damage fund exists, but the money doesn't
articles.summary: Climate-vulnerable countries fought for years to create a loss and damage fund. Four years on, demand far outstrips funding, pledges are scarce, and disaster-hit nations are still waiting for support.

articles.title: German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
articles.summary: German auto workers profited during the industry's boom years, but are now increasingly being asked to trade past gains for future job security.

articles.title: Ukraine's bid for NATO membership and more air defense remains controversial
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling for the rapid acceptance of his country into NATO. However, the necessary unanimity for this is lacking, as shown during the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

articles.title: EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?
articles.summary: Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's behind them.

articles.title: Why Iran's medicine supply chain is failing
articles.summary: Pharmacies in Iran are closing, hospital deliveries have stalled and patients are rationing doses or turning to black markets.

articles.title: Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
articles.summary: A North Korean troop buildup Ukraine warned about months ago has yet to materialize, even as strategic cooperation continues. Analysts say Pyongyang is balancing its ties with Moscow and Beijing.

articles.title: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble
articles.summary: From Nvidia to Coreweave, AI and tech stocks have swung sharply in recent months. Some investors still see plenty of room to run, while others are trying to diversify — and finding it harder than expected.

articles.title: What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?
articles.summary: Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is possible.

articles.title: After Japan's APEC snub, what's next for its China ties?
articles.summary: Japan has long-running concerns over Chinese military expansionism, and Beijing has bristled at Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan. The frosty ties were on full display at the APEC summit.

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates former CEO Jensen Huang despite China espionage scandal
articles.summary: Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring back the disgraced CEO, who resigned this month amid news of his affairs. He's suspected of having had a relationship with a Chinese intelligence asset.

articles.title: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
articles.summary: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

articles.title: COP deadlock prompts calls for a reset of climate diplomacy
articles.summary: COP31 has been branded a failure after countries couldn't reach a final agreement, divided over a reference to "fossil fuels." But was the decision to walk away from a watered-down text actually a show of strength?

articles.title: 'I've lost her forever' — Why German voice actors are refusing to sign Netflix's AI contract
articles.summary: For decades, Germans have known Hollywood's biggest stars through the same familiar voices. Now an AI clause in Netflix contracts is splitting the industry over whether it protects performers or exposes them.

articles.title: Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?
articles.summary: Germany plans to pay €10 a month into investment accounts for children to encourage long-term retirement saving. Economists say the measure may help build wealth but won't solve the country's pension funding challenge.

articles.title: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use
articles.summary: After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

articles.title: COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading
articles.summary: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

articles.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
articles.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.

articles.title: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
articles.summary: From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?

articles.title: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
articles.summary: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.

articles.title: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
articles.summary: Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.

articles.title: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
articles.summary: As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington.

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

articles.title: Why Jean-Luc Mélenchon has it in for Germany
articles.summary:
PARIS — It’s an unusual way to prepare for a trip to Berlin: suggesting Germany might pose a military threat to your country.

But that’s exactly what French presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon did ahead of his visit this week.

“I’m not ok with Germany’s pledge to build the largest conventional army in Europe,” the far-left leader said earlier this month, on Armistice Day, a holiday that in France commemorates the end of the intense fighting between France and Germany in World War I. “Because if it does, I have to ask: Who does it want to go to war against?”

The comments up the ante on Mélenchon’s long-standing defiance toward France’s neighbor, which he accuses of acting as a hegemon in Europe. His hostility toward Berlin — part longtime obsession, part political positioning — is one of the many ways the far-left leader clashes with his country’s establishment, which has traditionally worked closely with Berlin to shape the continent. 

Unsurprisingly, his comments have riled many in Germany, given that the rearmament effort was a response to Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“Mélenchon paints a distorted picture of Germany and Franco-German relations,” said Roland Theis, a German lawmaker from the conservative Christian Democratic Union who chairs the Bundestag’s Franco-German Parliamentary Group and sits on its Defense Committee. 

U.S. President Donald Trump speaks with Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz during a work lunch as part of the G7 summit, in Evian on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Christian Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images

The leftist veteran is polling in second place ahead of next year’s presidential election, putting him within reach of a runoff against the far-right front-runner, Marine Le Pen. For some in Berlin, neither prospect is particularly reassuring.

“On security and European affairs, his political positions are at least as dangerous as Le Pen’s,” Theis said.

A critic of Berlin’s traditional positions on fiscal and European affairs, Mélenchon is the author of a 2015 book subtitled “The German Poison.”

His France Unbowed party has long criticized joint Franco-German defense projects, arguing they favor German interests at the expense of French defense companies. The party also mistrusts the United States — Mélenchon has pledged to leave NATO — and his lieutenants have described Berlin as Washington’s “Trojan Horse” in Europe.

He intends to double down on his criticisms at an event in Berlin on Friday night, where he will present a German translation of another book: “Now, the People! — Revolution in the 21st Century,” which lays out his vision for France, Europe and the world.

In his presidential platform, Mélenchon pledged to radically overhaul the EU, disobeying its rules if necessary. 

“We are being honest,” said Hadrien Clouet, a lawmaker from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed who will accompany him to Germany. “We have to say what we think: Chancellor [Friedrich] Merz is a problem for Europe.” 

The event is being organized with the support of the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, which is affiliated with Germany’s far-left Left Party. Mélenchon is expected to meet privately with party representatives Saturday. 

Aurélien Taché, the party’s point person on the French National Assembly’s foreign affairs committee, said Mélenchon’s problem wasn’t with the German people. 

“We think there is a very strong German influence [in Europe], with an ordoliberal vision that we strongly reject,” Taché said. Concerns about hybrid warfare by Russia “don’t justify recreating a Wehrmacht as Europe’s leading military power,” Taché said, using the German word for Nazis’ armed forces.

Germany jitters

While Mélenchon has taken his antipathy toward Berlin further than any other leading French politician, doubts around the Franco-German relationship aren’t limited to the far end of the political spectrum. 

In a November poll conducted by the French branch of the European think tank More in Common, 71% of respondents described Germany as an ally. While that was more than any other international partner, it was down 6 percentage points from last year, led by a sharp drop among conservatives, traditionally among the most pro-German part of the electorate. 

Even mainstream French politicians have begun to temper their enthusiasm for Franco-German industrial cooperation after Germany decided unilaterally to pull the plug on a joint effort to design and build a next-generation fighter jet and in the face of cooled support by Berlin for a similar project for tanks.

Leading center-right candidates such as Edouard Philippe, a German speaker, have said that Paris should look beyond Berlin to form new partnerships and beef up its security. Le Pen, who has long shared Mélenchon’s defiance, said on Thursday she wanted to end the era of “German Europe.” 

“German rearmament strikes a chord historically for many voters,” said Paul Maurice, an expert on Franco-German relations at the French Institute of International Relations. “It speaks to the collective psyche.” 

Beyond security fears, German defense spending also plays on French insecurities as the country grapples with a prolonged public finances crisis. 

“When [voters] look at Germany today, they see what France is not capable of doing any more,” Maurice said. Tellingly, he added, “Mélenchon is the first candidate to go to Berlin” during the campaign. 

And, so far, the only one.

articles.title: 5 budget battles to watch at the EU summit
articles.summary:
5 budget battles to watch at the EU summit

From farmers’ subsidies to tech taxes, leaders are expected to disagree over almost everything at the European Council.

By GREGORIO SORGI
in Brussels

Illustration by Natália Delgado/ POLITICO

EU leaders are bracing for a huge fight over the bloc’s next seven-year budget as they gather in Brussels on Thursday for a summit that none of the rival governments expect to conclude with an agreement.

European Council President António Costa is trying to muster support for his budget proposal that was presented on Saturday and envisages €44 billion in additional cuts from a previous plan.

All leaders will discuss the EU budget and a €45 billion loan to Ukraine at lunchtime on Thursday, after which they will hold several hours of meetings in smaller groups or one-on-one later in the day.

They’ll reconvene Thursday night to see whether the discussions helped them make progress — but no deal is expected before the final summit of the year starting Dec. 17.

“Europe cannot demand more of itself while at the same time choosing to invest less,” Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in a statement from his office on Wednesday evening. “There can be no strong Europe with a weak European budget.”

Over a dozen diplomats preparing for the summit said they expect flare-ups and tensions among leaders, who have signaled they are unwilling to make compromises at this stage of the negotiations.

European Council President António Costa and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz address a press conference at the Chancellery in Berlin on Sept. 9, 2026. | John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images

“It is not the summit for convergence. It is not the time to climb down,” said an EU diplomat who, like others quoted in this story, was granted anonymity to discuss confidential negotiations.

“Costa knows he probably needs a bad EUCO [European Council] before he can have a good one” in December, said a second senior EU diplomat.

Here’s what’s going to be on the leaders’ minds:

1. The actual size of the thing

This is the mother of all battles.

A bloc of northern states, including Germany and the Netherlands, is pushing for a smaller budget geared toward what they consider “modern” priorities like defense and competitiveness. They are challenged by a rival camp of governments from Europe’s south and east, including Italy and Poland, demanding the EU spend more and maintain its focus on what the bloc has traditionally spent money on, like farming and its poorer regions.

Tensions are so high that EU governments can’t even agree on how much larger the proposed budget is than the current one.

While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz claimed that Costa’s proposal is 40% higher than the last seven-year budget agreed in 2020, rival governments said this ignores the rise in inflation and the repayments of the EU’s post-Covid debt, which eats up roughly 10% of the total.

“Some keep pretending that the budget still increases as compared to the current MFF [Multiannual Financial Framework],” EU budget commissioner Piotr Serafin told the European Parliament Wednesday. “But that is only because they do not factor in inflation — and that is simply not convincing.”

Expect more flashpoints during the summit.

2. Protecting the farmers

So far, farmers have been among the few stakeholders sheltered from efforts to shrink the budget.

But that’s still not enough for France, home to a powerful farmers’ lobby and facing elections in April and May, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading the polls.

The latest budget proposal comprises up to €297 billion in direct payments for farmers from 2028 to 2034.

President Emmanuel Macron is pushing to increase ringfencing of this figure from 80% to 90% — to the annoyance of several other countries.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico arrive for working session during the informal EU leaders’ retreat at the Alden Biesen Castle, in Rijkhoven, on Feb. 12, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images

“France also has to be able to make compromises,” said a third EU diplomat. “They feel like they are doing everyone a favour if they agree so they want all their priorities addressed.”

3. New taxes

Costa faces an uphill battle to convince the EU’s 27 leaders to support new EU-wide taxes to bolster the budget and reduce contributions to Brussels directly from national governments.

The latest proposal would see five new taxes, to generate €60 billion per year. But given the sensitivity of the EU acquiring new taxing powers, leaders won’t give any approval until the whole budget deal is finalized.

Each government wants to get rid of the tax that would disproportionately affect it. Poland opposes using revenues from the emissions trading scheme to target polluting firms. Luxembourg objects to funneling tobacco tax proceeds. Ireland is skeptical about a levy on tech giants over fears it will ignite U.S. retaliation.

4. Link to Ukraine

Germany’s Merz is using the budget as leverage to pressure four countries — Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Bulgaria — to help repay the borrowing costs associated with a €45 billion loan to Ukraine. Berlin, which pays around one quarter of the total EU budget, has threatened to slash its contributions if they hold out.

But behind closed doors, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria are open to contributing to the loan while Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico is more reluctant, said two EU diplomats with knowledge of proceedings.

A potential solution could involve paying the borrowing costs of the Ukraine funding that doesn’t finance military spending, a Bulgarian official said. 

But most countries reject this idea. “There isn’t a menu in Europe where you decide what to pay and what you don’t,” a fourth senior EU diplomat said.

5. European preference

Macron is leading a rearguard push to lock non-EU firms out of defense funding under the new budget.

Costa proposed giving access to companies from allied countries including the U.K., Canada, Norway and Ukraine — but left out the U.S.

While this compromise is acceptable to most governments, it’s still not enough for Macron, who wants to raise the issue during the summit, an EU diplomat said.

On the other hand, Romania is pushing in the opposite direction. It insists that U.S. arms companies gain more access to the European market.

“We need the American technology in Europe, and from my perspective we should identify ways to collaborate and to have the American presence,” Romanian Defense Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea told POLITICO.

articles.title: How to watch the Spanish election like a pro
articles.summary:
Almost 39 million Spaniards are eligible to vote in Sunday’s election, which is tipped to shift the country’s political trajectory to the right and end Pedro Sánchez’s eight-year Socialist premiership.

Turnout is projected to be high, with many voters seeing the contest as a potential turning point — not least because the conservative People’s Party is expected to form a governing coalition with the nationalist Vox party, ushering the far right into power for the first time since democracy was restored in the 1970s.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the PP, has vowed to bring “the necessary change” to Spain, telling POLITICO that his party and Vox agree that “sanchismo [Sánchez’s rule] is going to end in our country.”

Sánchez himself is framing his long-shot bid for reelection as an existential choice between joining a “far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs” or having Spain “remain a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility.”

Here is everything you need to know about how the election will work and what to expect after the result and coalition haggling begins.

What are people voting for?

Spaniards are voting to fill the two chambers of the Spanish parliament, or the Cortes Generales: the Congress of Deputies and the Senate.

Spain’s Congress of Deputies wields significant political power: it examines all proposed bills, has the final say on which laws are passed, and can bring down governments.

The Congress will ultimately decide who governs Spain, and the next prime minister needs the votes of 176 of its 350 members to win.

In Spain’s last general election, the PP won the most seats in Congress, but Sánchez retained power by striking a deal with a key regional party.

When will we know who wins?

On election day, polls open at 9 a.m. and close at 8 p.m. The Interior Ministry will publish turnout updates at 2 p.m. and 6 p.m.

When polls close at 8 p.m., counting begins, with congressional ballots counted first.

At 9 p.m. (8 p.m. in the Canary Islands), official results will start to come in. National media will publish the most recent polling data they have, instead of a traditional exit poll. The results come in quickly on election night, with the winner clear within a matter of hours.

The final count is conducted by provincial electoral boards starting from three days after the election and the official results are those published in the Official State Gazette.

How are the lawmakers chosen?

The 350 MPs are elected across 50 provinces and the two autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa. Each city elects one representative, using a first-past-the-post system. Every other province elects a minimum of two lawmakers, with the rest of the seats allocated based on the size of the population.

Madrid and Barcelona elect 38 and 32 lawmakers, respectively, while provinces that appear large but are not densely populated, often described as España vaciada (“Emptied Spain”), can account for just a handful of seats.

Voters select a party on their ballots, and candidates are then assigned to seats based on their position on a closed list drawn up by each party.

Seats are given to each party in proportion to the share of votes it receives in each province. Specifically, this calculation uses the D’Hondt system to allocate seats among parties that have received more than 3% of the valid votes (which include blank votes in Spain.)

Which regions matter most?

The most important battlegrounds vary across elections, depending on prospective coalition alliances — for instance, this year Andalusia and Catalonia will be key places to watch — but the structure of Spain’s electoral system means that winning over rural voters is particularly advantageous.

This is because the two-seat minimum requirement means that rural areas are actually over-represented in the legislature, while voters in the capital have less relative power.

If all of Spain’s eligible voters voted for the 350 MPs in the upcoming national election, each lawmaker would represent about 110,000 people. But in reality, the number of voters a deputy represents can vary massively across provinces.

Spain’s two main nationwide parties tend to win a larger share of seats than their actual national voter share. This is, in part, because in the majority of constituencies that only have a handful of seats available, smaller parties would need to get a significant share of the vote — well above the formal 3% threshold — to be in contention to win seats.

What about the Senate?

Some 209 senators will also be elected directly by voters, with four coming from every province on the mainland and additional representatives elected on Spain’s islands and North African exclaves. Regional parliaments appoint the remaining senators.

The Senate is less powerful than the Congress, providing second readings of proposed legislation and territorial representation. The body has a reputation for being a dumping ground for sidelined party grandees and a refuge for politicians whom Spain’s political groups seek to shield from judicial investigations through parliamentary immunity.

However, its support is vital for constitutional reform, and the chamber has the power to appoint magistrates to the Constitutional Court. Although the Senate doesn’t normally get much attention during elections, right-wing parties are hoping to secure three-fifths of the seats this year, enough to push through appointments that could shift the Constitutional Court’s ideological balance without consulting the left.

In the hopes of gaining control of the chamber, the Socialists and the PP have both struck deals with like-minded parties to withdraw candidates from constituencies where they would run against each other.

What happens after election day?

Once all the votes are counted and seats in Congress are assigned, coalition negotiations and vote-whipping for investiture debates formally begin. This can take months and has become increasingly long-winded in recent years as Spanish politics has become more fragmented.

The process is, in theory, simple: The candidate who wishes to become prime minister meets with the king, who tasks them with forming a government. This candidate then presents themselves to the Congress for an investiture debate and vote, in which they need at least 176 votes from their peers to be elected.

If they fail to win support in the first investiture vote, another one is held with a lower bar: a candidate only needs more votes in favor of their leadership than against. If they fail at the second vote and no other prospective leader can get enough support to become prime minister, another election is called.

Assuming the PP wins the largest share of the national vote and, combined with Vox’s seats, a working majority in Congress, Feijóo is expected to become prime minister relatively quickly — perhaps in January. The key question will be whether the two parties enter a formal coalition agreement together, or whether they agree to more limited cooperation supporting each other in congressional votes.

If Sánchez manages to win the largest share of the national vote, things could become more complicated. He would have a mandate to go to the king to ask to form a government, and could try his luck at negotiating with smaller parties to govern together. Assuming PP and Vox still end up controlling a majority of seats in Congress, it is expected Sánchez would fail to win the investiture votes, at which point Feijóo would have his opportunity to put himself forward as leader and repeat the process.

This would be similar to the scenario after the last general election, in which Feijóo’s PP won the largest share of the public vote but failed to win support to form a government in Congress.

If neither the PP and Vox nor Sánchez and his left-wing allies are able to form a majority, the situation could become extremely complex, with a possible repeat of the failed attempts to form governments after the 2015 and April 2019 elections.

Aitor Hernández-Morales and Ángel Villarino Pérez contributed reporting.

articles.title: This Riviera mayor wants to bring Javier Milei’s chainsaw politics to France
articles.summary:
PARIS — When he presented his plan to slash French public spending in April, David Lisnard brought a paper shredder.

It was a more safety-conscious take on uber-libertarian Argentine leader Javier Milei’s chainsaw. The right-wing mayor of Cannes fed it sheets representing France’s labor, environmental and urban planning laws. He vowed to shred large chunks of French legislation, cut 400,000 civil service jobs and reduce public spending by at least €200 billion.

The proposals are an unusual pitch for a country deeply attached to a strong centralized state. And yet Lisnard’s popularity ratings have shot up, shaking up a presidential race in which the far right’s Marine Le Pen and the far left’s Jean-Luc Mélenchon have made the early running.

“Lisnard is very different, very free,” said Geoffroy Boulard, a mayor and vice president of Lisnard’s New Energy party. “Some say he’s nothing but an online bubble, but there’s a surge of popular enthusiasm around him.”

Partly thanks to his stunts, the plain-speaking, athletic 57-year-old has become a social media phenomenon, with supporters posting AI-generated videos that portray him as a Marvel superhero, a World War I soldier or even a member of the Ghostbusters team.

Lisnard, a former member of the conservative Les Républicains party, openly praises Milei’s methods in Argentina. He argues that France needs its own “radical and cultural break” with the “infernal spiral” of debt, tax hikes and deteriorating public services.

POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts Lisnard at 11% in the first round, neck and neck with the center-right Edouard Philippe and the center-left Raphaël Glucksmann. Even Le Pen is under pressure to react to the emergence of a fresh face in the race, attacking him for failing to defend workers.

The Lisnard buzz is “a bubble,” said one of President Emmanuel Macron’s ministers who, like others quoted here, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But like Emmanuel Macron was at the beginning. We all laughed at him when he would lose his voice at his first political rallies.”

“Maybe the bubble will burst,” the minister added. “But it could also be the beginning of something.”

Crowning moment

Lisnard has never been elected to parliament or held a ministerial post. But he is not exactly an outsider, either. As mayor of a world-famous conference resort, he has plenty of networking opportunities, and since 2021 he has led the powerful French mayors’ lobby.

On Wednesday, Lisnard was re-elected president of the Association des maires de France with 72% of the vote. The question on everyone’s mind is whether his re-election will be a springboard to the Elysée Palace.

At the AMF’s annual gathering, the mayor of Cannes was in his element. Lisnard is “energetic, outspoken,” said Olivier Maurin, the mayor of a village in southern France who joined the New Energy party last month. “He’s got a positive attitude,” said David Pommier, a conservative mayor from near Lyon.

Argentinian President Javier Milei gestures while delivering a speech at an economic forum in Madrid on Oct. 21, 2026. | Thomas Coex/AFP via Getty Images

But others are fed up with what they see as his use of the organization — which is supposed to be a pluralistic forum for more than 34,000 mayors — to boost his presidential bid.  “It’s starting to get awkward,” said Françoise Gonnet-Tabardel, the mayor of a small rural town.

Before his re-election, Lisnard said on the sidelines of the conference that “not that many people are bothered” by his bid for the Elysée. “It’s being weaponized by my opponents,” he said. He refused to take questions about his presidential bid.

The newcomer

Lisnard’s big advantage in the campaign is that he is not in any way associated with Macron’s decade in power.

“Lisnard’s strength is that he is new,” said the minister quoted above. “People like the fact that he embodies order … But they don’t buy the libertarian politics.”

The son of small-business owners in Cannes, Lisnard has spent most of his life in local politics. He ran the city’s Palais des Festivals before becoming mayor in 2014. That role gave him the chance to rub shoulders with Hollywood stars and with leaders in the advertising and real estate industries, who spend lavishly at marquee trade events each year in the Mediterranean resort.

Lisnard is also capable of rubbing people the wrong way. He recently clashed with a journalist who chided him live on TV for arriving late for his morning interview. He also said that he didn’t “give a damn” when a student questioned him about the Oct. 17, 1961 massacre in Paris, when French police turned on Algerian demonstrators, and dozens were thrown in the Seine and drowned. “I wasn’t born then,” he said.

A long-distance runner and a fan of Nina Hagen and The Clash, Lisnard claims political inspiration ranging from Argentina’s Milei to British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, arguing that she “liberated the creative energy of her country.”

Targeted

As the newcomer in the presidential race, Lisnard is taking hits from across the political spectrum.

National Rally President Jordan Bardella called him a “masked Macronist” who would bring the centrists back to power. Meanwhile, Lisnard’s rivals accuse him of preparing an alliance with the far right in France.

Candidates are often asked who they would vote for if they fail to qualify for the second-round runoff, and while Lisnard said in a television interview Sunday that he would vote for Philippe against Mélenchon, he did not say whether he would pick his center-right rival against Le Pen.

Lisnard “finds it difficult to say whether he will vote for Le Pen or myself,” the center-right Philippe told reporters on the sidelines of the AMF conference.

“It shows that you can like chainsaws, but don’t know where to draw a line,” he said.

Philippe’s allies say that once the public finds out about Lisnard’s policy ambitions — which, in addition to radical spending cuts, include eliminating regional health agencies and pushing back the retirement age — voters will come back to earth. On immigration, the mayor of Cannes also wants to hold a referendum and introduce strict immigration quotas.

For now, the Lisnard bubble shows no sign of bursting. He says he already has enough endorsements from elected officials to run in the presidential election and this week the New Energy party said its membership had crossed the 150,000 mark.

He is the fourth most influential politician online at the moment, behind Le Pen, Mélenchon and far-right leader Éric Zemmour, according to Visibrain, a social media monitoring platform. Over the past three months, Lisnard has drawn 2.2 million likes and mentions across social networks, 14 times more than Philippe.

A centrist former minister said the emergence of France’s version of Milei shows that candidates who are former members of Macron’s governments are now seen as tainted:

“Voters don’t want a baby Macron.”

articles.title: Tusk government ‘facing armageddon’ as European court resumes cases against Poland
articles.summary:
Europe’s top human rights court resumed proceedings against Poland on Wednesday, putting fresh pressure on Prime Minister Donald Tusk to deliver on his promise to restore the independence of the country’s courts.

The European Court of Human Rights said it has around 1,600 cases pending over judicial changes introduced by Poland’s former nationalist Law and Justice government. It suspended proceedings in 2023 to give Warsaw time to restore judicial independence.

Tusk’s promise to restore the rule of law helped unlock billions in frozen EU funding following his return to power in 2023. But his efforts have been hampered by two successive PiS-backed presidents, most recently Karol Nawrocki.

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has estimated that compensation payments could exceed €12 million. Speaking by phone Wednesday evening, he said the bill could grow considerably as judges appointed under the disputed system continued to hear cases, creating fresh grounds for compensation claims.

“So we’re facing armageddon,” Żurek said. He blamed PiS for undermining Poland’s judicial system and accused Nawrocki of obstructing efforts to repair it.

The decision comes amid a wider confrontation between Tusk and Nawrocki over Poland’s courts, including the Constitutional Tribunal.

At the heart of the ECHR cases is a 2017 overhaul that gave lawmakers greater control over judicial appointments. Nawrocki vetoed a bill in February aimed at reversing those changes, arguing it would usher in a “new phase of chaos.”

Nawrocki’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The ECHR has already sided with applicants ranging from a distributor of sex-enhancing supplements to former Polish President and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa.

Wałęsa had won a defamation case against a former associate who accused him of collaborating with the communist secret police, only to see that victory overturned years later by a newly created chamber of Poland’s Supreme Court.

The ECHR awarded him €30,000 in damages in a landmark 2023 ruling that prompted the suspension of similar cases. It twice extended the suspension but let it expire Monday.

Another bill addressing the status of thousands of judges appointed under PiS-era rules has been on Nawrocki’s desk since Nov. 9. Żurek said it would address the ECHR’s main concerns but that he feared another politically motivated veto.

articles.title: “Les COP, c’est une blague” : les critiques enflent contre les sommets climatiques après l’échec à Antalya
articles.summary:
Le processus des Nations unies pour coordonner la réponse mondiale au changement climatique se fissure discrètement depuis des années. Aujourd’hui, même ses partisans historiques se rebellent ouvertement et exigent une refonte des négociations internationales.

L’élément déclencheur : l’échec retentissant des négociateurs à conclure un accord mondial dimanche. De l’Afrique à l’Europe, les représentants des pays ont exprimé leur méfiance face à un processus qui a permis aux pays riches en pétrole de passer outre les appels à inclure dans le texte final une mention sur la sortie progressive des énergies fossiles — une mesure que les scientifiques réclament depuis des années.

Les divisions se sont avérées si profondes lors des pourparlers à Antalya, en Turquie, que les gouvernements n’ont pas pu conclure d’accord de haut niveau pour la première fois depuis 2009. Cela a conduit les ministres, les négociateurs et d’autres responsables à réclamer des changements dans un processus qui, depuis des décennies, nécessite un consensus entre près de 200 pays pour avancer.

“Si nous parvenons à donner le meilleur de nous-mêmes, à nous organiser, au cours des douze prochains mois, la COP31 nous paraîtra rétrospectivement comme un moment cathartique de prise de conscience”, a positivé Rachel Kyte, envoyée spéciale du Royaume-Uni pour le climat, lors d’un entretien accordé à POLITICO, ajoutant que les pays devaient corriger le processus qui, ces dernières années, a peiné à produire des résultats.

Ceux appelant à une refonte du processus réclament une réforme du format COP, voire sa suppression pure et simple, sans que l’on ait réellement d’idées sur la manière de mettre en œuvre l’une ou l’autre de ces options. Reste que l’échec des organisateurs à négocier un accord final a libéré un flot de critiques.

Selon ses détracteurs, le processus actuel, dans lequel les pays pétroliers font obstacle aux initiatives visant à mentionner explicitement les énergies fossiles, n’est plus viable dans un monde qui se dirige à toute vitesse vers une aggravation des conditions climatiques.

“Nous avons tous été pris en otage par les producteurs de pétrole, mais aussi par les plus grands consommateurs de pétrole”, a pointé auprès de POLITICO le ministre panaméen du Climat, Juan Carlos Navarro.

La faute aux pays pétroliers, mais pas que

Ces négociations chaotiques en Turquie interviennent onze ans après que, pour la première fois, tous les pays se sont mis d’accord sur la nécessité de lutter contre le changement climatique en signant l’Accord de Paris. Depuis, des progrès poussifs ont laissé les pays à la traîne par rapport à leurs objectifs. Au point que l’ONU a annoncé le mois dernier qu’il n’y avait plus aucun espoir d’éviter un réchauffement de 1,5 °C.

L’échec de ce week-end contraste fortement avec les négociations de l’année dernière au Brésil, où les gouvernements étaient parvenus à un accord malgré les attaques à distance contre le processus du président Donald Trump, et sa décision de retirer les Etats-Unis de l’Accord de Paris.

Alors que les négociations entraient en prolongation le week-end dernier, l’Arabie saoudite et un groupe d’autres pays producteurs d’énergies fossiles se sont battus pour empêcher que les négociations ne reprennent les termes convenus il y a trois ans lors de la COP28, qui appelaient à accélérer la sortie des énergies fossiles.

“Ce que nous voyons ne doit pas devenir la norme”, insistait le 18 novembre Jiwoh Abdulai, ministre de l’Environnement et du Climat de la Sierra Leone, avant l’échec des négociations. “Il y a un manque de confiance. Je pense que l’essentiel est de trouver un mécanisme permettant de rétablir la confiance.”

Certains responsables estiment que les politiques climatiques peuvent être menées par d’autres moyens, par exemple via des accords commerciaux et des partenariats d’approvisionnement en minerais. Une grande partie de ce travail est déjà en cours, consolidant des changements concrets dans l’économie mondiale et dans la lutte contre les gaz à effet de serre.

“Les COP, c’est une blague et ce depuis des années. Elles devraient être supprimées”, a tancé mardi sur X Rohan Patel, ancien conseiller à la Maison-Blanche en matière de politique climatique et énergétique sous Barack Obama. “Au mieux, cette conférence apporte un élan moral à un problème qui ne cesse de s’aggraver et auquel nous avons tardé à nous attaquer à bien des égards. Mais en général, c’est un énorme fiasco et tout le monde le sait bien (même ceux qui y participent chaque année).”

D’autres pays ont joué un rôle dans cet échec. Les gouvernements des pays riches ont refusé d’accorder des financements aux pays pauvres pour leur permettre de s’adapter au réchauffement climatique. De grandes puissances comme la Chine sont restées en retrait. Plusieurs diplomates ont déploré en privé l’absence des négociateurs américains, qui, historiquement, ont toujours fait pression sur les récalcitrants pour qu’ils fassent des compromis.

Des participants de longue date ont estimé que les négociations se sont trop concentrées sur l’élaboration de déclarations de haut niveau, au détriment de progrès concrets pour réduire les émissions de gaz à effet de serre. D’autres ont suggéré que l’échec du week-end dernier pourrait servir à revoir le processus et à le rendre plus efficace dans un monde fragmenté.

“Je reçois des appels de partout, me disant : ‘C’est une occasion à ne pas manquer, il faut la saisir’”, a confié Rachel Kyte, l’envoyée britannique. “Donc, tout bien considéré, ça a été une décision difficile [de rejeter l’accord], mais je pense que c’était la bonne.”

Des progrès passés inaperçus

Par ailleurs, de nombreux diplomates soulignent avoir constaté des progrès discrets à Antalya, mais ils ont été éclipsés par les dernières heures catastrophiques des négociations.

L’Allemagne, la France et les Pays-Bas ont publié des feuilles de route détaillées pour abandonner le pétrole, le charbon et le gaz. Le fait que 130 pays, dont l’Union européenne, se soient opposés au texte après le retrait de la mention sur la sortie des énergies fossiles a mis en évidence une large coopération, ont soulevé certains. Plus de 80 pays ont signé un engagement lors de la COP31 visant à électrifier 35% de leur consommation finale d’énergie d’ici 2035, bien que celui-ci n’ait jamais été adopté en raison de l’échec des négociations.

En outre, les particuliers achètent de plus en plus de véhicules électriques et les pays développent rapidement leurs capacités de production d’énergies renouvelables. Cette tendance va se poursuivre, a affirmé la semaine dernière l’Agence internationale de l’énergie. Toutefois, celle-ci a également souligné que la demande d’énergie croît, ce qui signifie que la consommation de pétrole, de gaz et de charbon se poursuivra pendant des décennies.

“Le sujet, ce n’est pas des feuilles de papier. C’est décarboner réellement l’économie mondiale”, a résumé dans son podcast Christiana Figueres, qui a dirigé les négociations de l’Accord de Paris en 2015.

Chris Bowen, le ministre australien du Changement climatique et de l’Energie, qui a coprésidé la COP31 avec la Turquie, a jugé que les négociations de cette année s’étaient déroulées dans un climat particulièrement tendu. La sécurité énergétique constituait une préoccupation majeure, étant donné l’angoisse des populations face aux pénuries d’approvisionnement en carburant et à la flambée des prix due à la fermeture du détroit d’Ormuz. Les guerres au Moyen-Orient et en Europe ont encore davantage mis à rude épreuve la coopération internationale.

Les pays économiquement dépendants des énergies fossiles, comme l’Arabie saoudite et la Russie, ont adopté des positions intransigeantes face au désordre mondial. L’Union européenne, le Royaume-Uni et des dizaines d’autres pays ont considéré qu’il valait mieux rejeter un mauvais accord plutôt que de faire marche arrière.

“Il est profondément décevant qu’aucun consensus n’ait été trouvé lors de la COP31. Ce moment, après l’été que le monde vient de vivre, appelait à faire preuve d’ambition. Au lieu de cela, on nous a présenté un accord qui constitue un recul en matière de climat, et nous ne pouvions pas le soutenir”, a justifié lundi le Premier ministre britannique Andy Burnham devant la Chambre des communes.

Les négociations annuelles constituaient autrefois le mécanisme permettant de parvenir à un accord international sur les moyens de lutter contre le changement climatique. Aujourd’hui, il vaut mieux les utiliser comme une tribune pour faire pression sur les pays afin qu’ils agissent plus rapidement pour réduire leurs émissions, considère Alden Meyer, du think tank E3G.

“Je dirais que la coopération pour mener des initiatives de décarbonation sur le terrain dans tous les secteurs de l’économie revêt une importance bien plus grande que l’existence ou non d’un consensus sur une décision-cadre qui se limite au plus petit dénominateur commun”, a-t-il écrit dans un SMS.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Marie Thirion et Jean-Christophe Catalon.

articles.title: Don’t ‘backslide’ on defense spending, senior US lawmaker tells Europe
articles.summary:
A senior U.S. lawmaker has urged the European Union not to cut defense spending in its next seven-year budget as Europe’s leaders struggle to agree on the almost €2 trillion pot of cash.

Brendan Boyle, a Democratic member of the U.S. House of Representatives who will chair its Budget Committee in 2027, warned that Russia was an “enormous threat” to Europe and said the bloc must continue increasing its defense spending.

“This is not a time when we can backslide,” Boyle told POLITICO in an interview, pointing to the approaching five-year anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Earlier this week, Boyle was also elected president of NATO’s parliamentary assembly, which is made up of delegates from the alliance’s 32 member countries.

His comments come as EU leaders prepare to discuss the bloc’s next seven-year budget at a summit Thursday and Friday. The latest draft defense budget tabled by European Council President António Costa would see tens of billions cut from the European Commission’s earlier proposal, drawing the ire of some EU countries — though the total is still double the previous seven-year budget.

Boyle said he was “heartened” that all NATO allies were now spending more on defense than the alliance’s longstanding 2% of GDP target agreed at the 2014 Wales summit. “I’m glad that that is a floor and no longer considered a ceiling,” he said, while acknowledging that European governments face “similar budget constraints” to the U.S.

He said Europe building up its own defense industry after decades of relying on American weapons was a net positive for the NATO alliance, but warned against the bloc breaking that dependence too fast. EU countries are currently only spending about 15% of their defense procurement budgets on European-made equipment, despite calls from the Commission to raise this to at least half by 2030.

“Where it would become a negative is if suddenly there was a hard turn away from totally buying U.S. systems,” Boyle said. “That would be a mistake.”

articles.title: French presidential hopeful Teddy Riner says Ukraine is ‘not our war’
articles.summary:
PARIS — Teddy Riner, the legendary judoka running for president in France, sparked controversy on Wednesday after declaring that Ukraine was not his country’s conflict.

“I don’t understand why we’re sending troops to Ukraine when it’s not our war,” the five-time Olympic gold medalist told reporters.

Riner was referring to the deployment of French troops in Ukraine, which was criticized by opposition parties for having been decided without parliamentary approval. Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said the troops are “dedicated to training and equipment maintenance.”

“If I become president tomorrow, I would like to be the kind of person who brings people together, who smiles and shakes hands to put an end to this war,” Riner added about Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin also practices judo and was honorary president of the International Judo Federation before launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The 37-year-old Riner has unveiled few policy proposals and had not yet weighed in on foreign affairs since announcing his candidacy earlier this month. The two leading candidates for next April’s election in France — far-right chief Marine Le Pen and far-left veteran Jean-Luc Mélenchon — have both been critical of current President Emmanuel Macron’s Ukraine policy. Macron’s government has sent funds and weapons to Ukraine and co-led the coalition of the willing, a group of Kyiv’s most significant allies and supporters.

Riner, however, had been more closely associated with the pro-Macron camp based on early campaign statements, making his Ukraine comments more surprising. Early surveys have shown him polling at about 4%, drawing mostly from voters who opted for Macron in the last presidential election.

Center-right MEP Nathalie Loiseau, who handles foreign affairs policy for presidential candidate Edouard Philippe, seized on Riner’s remarks to attack the election rival.

“Teddy Riner’s world would be so simple: you don’t get involved in anything, you shake hands with everyone, and there’s peace and love all over the world,” she wrote on X.

Riner was speaking from the French mayors’ congress currently taking place in Paris, where he was seeking out endorsements needed to run for president.

He still has a long way to go before actually getting onto the ballot: Riner said he had obtained more than 100 signatures from local officials in support his candidacy — far from the 500 needed to confirm his candidacy under French law.

articles.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
articles.summary:
A northern gannet (Morus bassanus) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail

Steve Votier

Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Advertisement

Read more

Most large fishing boats go untracked as ‘dark vessels’

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets (Morus bassanus) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters (Puffinus mauretanicus) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.

Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.

A tagged northern gannet coming in to land in Wales

Steve Votier

“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.

In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.

The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.

Powerful images show dark side of South-East Asia’s fishing industry

Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro, also at BirdLife International.

Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.

“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

Science Advances

articles.title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
articles.summary:
MARK SYKES/SPL/Alamy

There is a story, possibly apocryphal, that when the mathematician G. H. Hardy was about to undertake a dangerous sea voyage, he sent a postcard to a colleague declaring “I have solved the Riemann hypothesis”. Hardy, a staunch atheist, joked that this would prevent his ship from sinking, as God would never let him claim the credit for such a major result without revealing the details of his proof.

Hardy would probably be both astonished and aghast that we now have what seems to be a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has vexed mathematicians since the 19th century, but that no one yet understands it. The consensus among mathematicians is that the proof, produced with the aid of AI, will hold, but that it will take much more work to make it comprehensible to humans.

However you feel about AI, this is a watershed moment, and one that demonstrates just how little we still understand about the capabilities of the technology. As recently as last month, leading mathematician Terence Tao speculated that AI would eventually solve the Riemann hypothesis, but that it may not happen before 2050. Now, some mathematicians are considering whether their hardest and most infamous remaining problems could be settled within months. In a year that has left mathematicians reeling, this may be the knock-out blow.

Advertisement

This is a watershed moment, and it shows just how little we understand about AI’s abilities

For non-mathematicians, the fall of the Riemann hypothesis is harder to interpret. In the past year, AI has seen incredible advances in both maths and coding, but it is perhaps no coincidence that in these arenas, with nothing more than computer code, answers can swiftly be checked and iterated upon, allowing for rapid improvement. When it comes to other human endeavours though, from art to zoology, such verification is far harder, involving either the messy physical world, or unknowable human taste – or both. Whether this verification gap can be closed may become the biggest question of our age. Answers on a postcard, please.

What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?

It has been called the hardest problem in mathematics, and now through a combination of human ingenuity and relentlessness, and the computational power of AI, the Riemann hypothesis may have finally been solved

articles.title: Our verdict on Dark Eden by Chris Beckett: ‘Holy cow. Chapter 44!’
articles.summary:
The New Scientist Book Club read Chris Beckett’s Dark Eden in November

Since starting the New Scientist Book Club in May 2023, I have aimed to vary our books as much as possible, moving between science fiction and popular science, older classics and the hottest new titles. Occasionally, though, I’m afraid I let the power go to my head and just choose one of my own personal favourites. That’s what I did in November, with Chris Beckett’s novel Dark Eden, a book I’ve loved ever since it won the Arthur C. Clarke award in 2013.

Set on the planet Eden, a sunless world that drifts alone far outside the Milky Way, this follows the descendants of two astronauts who were marooned there over a century earlier. Now numbering 532 people, they tell each other stories of the world their ancestors came from, and struggle to survive on this dark, cold planet as they await the return of “one of those sky-boats with lights on them”. I think it is all wildly imaginative and original and exciting. So it was with some trepidation that I awaited the verdict of my fellow book club members on our Discord channel. I really wanted everyone else to love it, too!

Free newsletter

Sign up to Book Club

Sign up to newsletter

It started well. “I managed not to stay up all night reading, but the temptation was definitely there – I am hooked,” wrote Dee55. Les was similarly gripped. “Started it? I’ve only gone and finished it, haven’t I? It really got me in, and I found it a fascinating exploration of social anthropology and linguistics in a very small, isolated population. And the world-building was fascinating, too – very different flora and fauna.”

Advertisement

Several other members also cited the strength of the world-building in Dark Eden. I also love the lanternflowers and woollybucks of this planet, and was fascinated to learn, in an essay Chris wrote for book club members, that, when creating a world for a story, he doesn’t “usually seek to make the whole thing scientifically accurate, but I try to make it hang together in a way that feels coherent”. I think he definitely succeeds in that here.

In Dark Eden, I imagined how life might exist on a sunless planet

Dark Eden, the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, takes place on a rogue planet outside the Milky Way. Award-winning author Chris Beckett explains how he thought through the science behind this night world

There were some excellent debates about the language these people have developed – they double up on words for emphasis, for example (“big big”; “cold cold”), use bastardised forms of our words (“Landing Veekle”; “leckytrickity”), and talk about Starry Swirl – the Milky Way they can see in their skies, a wonderfully evocative image.

“I think Beckett has done something really clever here. He’s created a language that feels familiar enough to read naturally, but is sufficiently different to remind us that this is an entirely separate culture that has evolved in isolation,” wrote Maria. “I enjoyed some of the language. Tom’s dick and Harry’s for instance,” wrote Matthew – referring to an exclamation the characters use for emphasis. “It’s contagious… yesterday I found myself saying Wow, it’s hot hot!” added leasabp. Dee55 also admitted to adopting some Edenisms: “My favourite bit of the language is ‘newhairs’! I am already using this for teenagers, but only to myself at present.”

The story’s protagonist is John Redlantern, a young man who decides there must be more to life than waiting for rescue around the Circle of Stones that marks the original astronauts’ landing point on Eden, and tries to spark an exodus from the Family’s small valley to explore the wider planet. John definitely drew some mixed opinions from readers.

“Problem is, I don’t much like our ‘hero’, he’s not a very sympathetic character, more Sméagol than Bilbo,” wrote Matthew. I chatted to Chris in an interview for book club members, and he was certainly aware of this: “He’s an awkward cuss, John, isn’t he? He’s not a particularly nice person,” he told me – before embarking on an enlightening discussion about why he chose to write from various viewpoints, and how hard it was describing the world of Eden from the perspectives of people who have never been anywhere else. “The discipline of just writing it from within the story is if I’m trying to describe the world to readers, I can’t use metaphors and analogies that refer to anything that’s outside of Eden. And that was quite tricky to do.”

Book club member Laura Akers, like others, said she “definitely enjoyed the story more when I realized that John, despite his own intentions, is not intended to be our ‘hero’”.

Overall, I think the book club mostly really enjoyed Dark Eden – I particularly appreciated leasapb’s comment: “Holy cow. Chapter 44!!!”, as I think the ending is fabulous – but one issue that was raised by a few people was the amount the characters have sex with each other. Incestuous sex.

“Certainly one of the odd things I found was the casual attitude to sex,” wrote Alan_P. Maria agreed. “I found the casual attitude towards sex quite unsettling too, particularly because the characters often seem almost childlike in their behaviour and understanding of the world, yet discuss sex so matter-of-factly. I honestly couldn’t bring myself to think too much about the incest!” And while Barbara Howe “loved the worldbuilding, and the story of John’s breakaway family’s trek to find a better place”, she found the “constant and highly unerotic sex… offputting”.

But given that at least some members have gone on to read the sequels, I think this was largely a popular choice – and a welcome change from the Earthly dystopias which seem to be dominating the big new sci-fi novels out this autumn (I’m looking at you, Audrey Niffenegger and Emily St. John Mandel).

articles.title: Is The Time Traveler’s Wife the perfect audiobook to experience on shuffle?
articles.summary:
Josie Ford

Feedback is our weekly column of bizarre stories, implausible advertising claims, confusing instructions and more

Reader Jenny Ozanne writes to tell us of a horrific incident that befell her partner. He had bought Audrey Niffenegger’s novel The Time Traveler’s Wife as a CD audiobook, to listen to on long car journeys.

“After a while, he complained that the plot was completely impossible to follow,” writes Jenny. “It was only when I checked his player that I realized he had accidentally set the CD to ‘shuffle’. “

Advertisement

Jenny raises two points, which Feedback heartily endorses: “I’m still not sure what’s more impressive: the story’s ability to survive total chronological chaos, or the fact that he listened to three random chapters before suspecting anything was wrong.”

Feedback would suggest that The Time Traveler’s Wife might be the ideal novel to experience on shuffle, since the narrative is heavily non-linear. The main character hops uncontrollably back and forth through history. This led us to wonder: would any similarly chrono-displaced stories survive the experience of being played on shuffle, or even be improved by it?

We wondered, for instance, about David Mitchell’s Cloud Atlas. This has six stories set in different periods, including a future in which human clones are used as cheap labour, and a more distant future in which everything has gone a bit Mad Max. The stories are linked by characters in later timelines reading about the earlier ones, and by subtle coincidences. What would it be like on shuffle?

However, after careful reflection, we realised there is only one correct answer to this, and that is Shane Carruth’s 2004 film Primer, which tells the story of two tech bros who invent a time machine in their garage. At first, they use it to go back in time and make money on the stock exchange, only to become caught up in an escalating web of betrayal and deception as they endlessly rewrite their lives.

Primer is so overcomplicated, so mind-wreckingly confusing, that some poor soul once went so far as to draw a diagram trying to convey its timeline. Posted on Reddit by u/Clawz114, the diagram looks like a cross between a metro map and a flowchart of the inner workings of a chemical factory. It is therefore possible that playing the scenes in random order might actually cause the film to make more sense.

The scent of success

It’s that time of year when many of us are thinking, “Oh blimey, I need to buy everyone presents” and then having a meltdown when we can’t think of anything. The last refuge of the true gift scoundrel is, of course, the scented candle. This item might as well come with a note saying, “Sorry, I couldn’t think of anything”.

Readers looking to step up their scented candle game may wish to investigate JD + Kate Industries, which is run by a pair of humour writers with a sideline in themed scented candles. They have taken these tedious items to new and different places.

For instance, consider the Late Bronze Age Collapse scented candle, which “commemorates everyone’s favorite late 13th century [BC] widespread societal collapse”. Happily, it doesn’t smell of violence and decay, but rather of “burning cedar”, since “Lebanese cedar was a popular building material in the Late Bronze Age”.

Those with more contemporary tastes may wish to consider the AI scented candle, which has a little sculpture of a data centre on the top, “surrounded by a post-apocalyptic, bombed-out city”. What does it smell of, you ask? “Diesel generator exhaust fumes”.

Finally, those nostalgic for the headier days of space exploration might appreciate the Apollo 11 scented candle. Disappointingly, this doesn’t smell of moon dust, which, as we understand it, basically smells of burning because it reacts with oxygen on contact. Instead, its scent mimics “a certain powdered orange drink mix often associated with the space program, but that was not brought on Apollo 11. The astronauts brought a generic, grapefruit-flavored powdered drink mix instead, because they selfishly did not consider us and our desire to market candles.”

Feedback has no idea if these candles are any good, but we enjoyed JD + Kate’s website a lot.

By the letter

Let us foray once again into the wonderful world of scientific acronyms. First, two reader claims that, for reasons that will become obvious, we cannot verify.

Michael Berkson tells us: “As a solicitor my late wife was involved in development of insurance for doctors. The firm had to tell the client that they needed to choose a better name. Their original choice was Professional Indemnity Support Scheme.” Michael says the clients were open to replacing “scheme” with “service”, which helps not at all.

Likewise, Jim Taylor asserts that he was once confronted with a military programme intended to ensure that spare parts would always be available for key equipment. It was called the Contractor Repair Advanced Provisioning System.

Finally, a story we can confirm is true because we looked it up. Reader Geraldine Beare is an indexer, which is one of those jobs that we often forget about but would swiftly notice if it wasn’t done. “I am at present indexing a book on goats,” says Geraldine. Through this assignment she has learned the acronym “OMAGOD”, which she recommends saying “quickly, or perhaps in a vaguely Scottish accent”. It actually stands for ovine mouth and gum obscure disease.

Got a story for Feedback?

You can send stories to Feedback by email at feedback@newscientist.com. Please include your home address. This week’s and past Feedbacks can be seen on our website.
