articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte at ICC: A cheat sheet on understanding his case, trial
articles.summary:
On Monday, November 30, former president Rodrigo Duterte, 81, will become the first Filipino and Asian head of state to be tried over a crimes-against-humanity case at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands.

He was arrested by Philippine authorities in March 2025 and was turned over the tribunal’s jurisdiction immediately. Duterte has been detained at the Scheveningen Prison since then.

The former president will be on trial because in April, the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed all three charges against him.

Here’s a cheat sheet to easily understand Duterte’s case and his upcoming trial.

What is he being accused of?

Duterte is facing a three counts of crimes against humanity case of murder and attempted murder.

This is because of his war on drugs launched in 2016, and the killings of the Davao Death Squad. The case’s coverage is from November 1, 2011, to March 16, 2019 — years that the Philippines was part of the court and when Duterte served as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.

The counts are divided into these alleged crimes:

1st count: Murder in Davao City when Duterte was mayor

2nd count: Murder of high-value targets

3rd count: Murder and attempted murder during barangay-level drug war operations

Must Read

Inside story: Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC arrest

Who are his co-perpetrators?

In February, the prosecution named eight persons tagged as Duterte’s indirect co-perpetrators. They were former officials who have alleged direct and indirect participation in implementing the drug war that killed nearly 30,000, according to several human rights groups.

They are:

Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa

Former police chief Vicente Danao

The late former police chief Camilo Cascolan

Former police chief Oscar Albayalde

Senator Bong Go

Former National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) chief Dante Gierran

Former Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency chief Isidro Lapeña

Former justice secretary Vitaliano Aguirre II

Dela Rosa has a standing warrant of arrest, but remains at-large as of writing.

Must Read

ICC warrant details Bato dela Rosa’s role in drug war

What happens during the trial?

November 30 is the start of the actual trial.

The hearing will open with Duterte being asked if he understands the nature of his cases. He will likewise be asked to enter a plea — guilty or not guilty. This is similar to an arraignment in local cases.

Afterwards, the prosecution and the common legal representatives of the victims (CLRVs) will have their opening statements.

It will be up to the defense if they will deliver an opening statement too. The prosecution will then present their witnesses after the opening statements. This is expected to run for several months.

After the prosecution’s presentation, CLRVs won’t present evidence but rather submit observations. As in a regular trial, the defense will have the opportunity to present their case and evidence too, to rebut the prosecution’s allegations.

These hearings could last for years, depending on the pace. In the end, the judges will decide to either acquit or convict Duterte. A conviction will demand from the prosecution presenting evidence that is beyond reasonable doubt.

Must Read

Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial

Can the decision be appealed?

In the Philippines, only conviction is appealable. Some parties use other remedies, like a certiorari, in cases of acquittal. Certiorari is essentially an order to a lower court to present case records for review by a higher court.

But in the ICC, both the prosecution and the defense may appeal the judgment before the ICC appeals chamber. This means that either way, the judgment against Duterte may be brought to a higher chamber after the promulgation.

If convicted, what will Duterte’s sentence be?

Like in other cases, the ICC may impose prison time, a fine, or even forfeiture of property or assets.

The maximum jail time could be up to 30 years, but the ICC imposes life imprisonment in extreme cases. It has no death penalty.

If convicted, where will Duterte be detained?

The Scheveningen Prison is designed only for short-term detention. Once convicted, the ICC said Duterte will be transferred to a prison of a state designated by the Court.

This state will be determined based on the list of nations that are willing to accept convicted persons.

What happened to the jurisdiction challenge?

Duterte had repeatedly questioned the ICC’s jurisdiction over his case. Jurisdiction determines whether the court is the proper avenue and has the power to try his case.

Must Read

EXPLAINER: What you need to know about ICC’s jurisdiction over Duterte

With finality, the ICC appeals chamber denied Duterte’s challenge in April and cleared the way for the November 30 trial. This jurisdiction challenge was among the options left for Duterte to derail his ICC proceedings.

Had Duterte won the challenge, it would have stopped his case and he may have been able to return home. But he lost, so he will remain detained for the duration of his trial. – Rappler.com

articles.title: [Rear View] Sara Duterte’s farewell walk?
articles.summary:
Is it just me or is Vice President Sara Duterte doing the political version of a farewell walk? 

Pageant bekis know the ritual, the one where the reigning queen, before relinquishing her crown, takes a long, almost leisurely walk on the runway, all smiles, waving at the adoring crowd while sentimental music plays in the background. 

A pre-recorded speech plays alongside, where she takes stock of her reign, of her experiences and lessons learned, and ends with grateful thank yous to the organization and her fans. The camera follows her as she fades into the background. Behind the curtains, she no longer holds the spotlight, and she knows it.

Watch the Vice President these past days and you will see that walk.

A round of visits to Duterte strongholds, a profuse thanks to supporters for keeping her strong despite adversities, a year-end thanksgiving brunch with political personalities known for loyalty, but no heavyweights who signal leverage and clout.

This is not a declared presidential candidate showing off the breadth of her political coalition. This is more like one thanking the people who stood by her as she prepares her exit.

The whisper in political circles is that the 14 votes needed to convict are there. 

Until the votes are in, it remains a whisper, and who knows, the Vice President might pull off a surprise in the Q&A or the Marcos administration’s operators might trip at the runway. But the Duterte camp surely has heard the whisper, and its behavior says it believes the whisper.

A Christmas verdict?

The impeachment trial resumes on Tuesday, December 1, and if the schedule holds, the verdict could come before Congress adjourns for Christmas. The verdict will surely be the topic at every family reunion and Noche Buena, along with grumblings over how this administration has made this Christmas season the most miserable since the pandemic lockdown.

Her critics, of course, do not expect her to walk off a winner. The Vice President has long proven she is no Miss Congeniality and after November, certainly not Best in National Costume either. Her defense spent the month showing us how ill-fitting the costume of a public servant living a simple lifestyle is. 

The impeachment trial rests on a single article of unexplained wealth. The defense expressed confidence it could make a rebuttal on the prosecution’s forensic report showing alleged unexplained wealth and undeclared assets at P817.87 million. So far, it has failed to make a convincing one.

Why not take the stand?

After announcing, then dropping, 16 bank officials from the list of witnesses, a move that, had it proceeded, would have provided an opening to question her joint account with her father, detained former President Rodrigo Duterte, the defense brought in their anti-money-laundering expert. But the said expert attacked the methodology of a forensic report he admitted he had not read. He also conceded the other claims he made in open court were outside his expertise. 

A witness testifying on the banana chip company tied to the Vice President’s husband admitted that the company lacks the property, plant, equipment, and personnel needed to run a manufacturing business. Other witnesses tested the patience of senator-judges with their selective amnesia. Their testimonies only raised more questions and bolstered the case against the Vice President.

Must Read

Defense witness grilled over ‘useless’ testimony

And through all of this, the Vice President herself has not taken the stand. The public, says a recent survey, now wants to hear her testify. 

In 2012, then-chief justice Renato Corona took the stand at his impeachment trial. He was convicted anyway, but he showed up for his own Q&A. Sara Duterte has chosen to let her lawyers do the talking for her. That’s no way to keep the crown.

When the senator-judges hand in their scorecards, and if the whisper turn out to be true, it would be difficult, if not impossible, for the Vice President to wave and smile, or deliver a generous and sincere thank you for the memories. – Rappler.com

Joey Salgado is a former journalist, and a government and political communications practitioner. He served as spokesperson for former vice president Jejomar Binay.

articles.title: Sandiganbayan suspends Pasay judge over bribery case
articles.summary:
MANILA, Philippines – The anti-graft court Sandiganbayan has ordered the three-month preventive suspension of a Pasay City regional judge who is facing a direct bribery charge filed in August by the Office of the Ombudsman.

The Sandiganbayan’s 6th Division rejected Pasay Regional Trial Court Branch 108 Judge Albert Cansino’s opposition, citing Section 13 of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, which makes preventive suspension mandatory for public officials facing a valid charge under the law involving fraud against the government or public funds or property.

Cansino was charged together with court interpreter Mariejoy Lagman over the alleged solicitation and receipt, directly or indirectly, of P6 million from a litigant in a property dispute.

Must Read

Ombudsman Remulla: Corruption in judiciary also ‘severe’

The order was signed by associate justices Sarah Jane Fernandez, Kevin Narce Vivero and Lord Villanueva, and directed the Office of the Court Administrator to enforce the suspension.

The bribery case stemmed from the May 23, 2024 arrest of Lagman in an entrapment operation conducted by the National Bureau of Investigation. The operation followed an anonymous complaint sent to the Judicial Integrity Board.

NBI agents found during the arrest a copy of a May 15, 2024 order signed by Cansino. A certified true copy of the order had been received by a representative of the defendants in the Pasay court property dispute.

The P6 million was allegedly sought as a “consideration for a favorable decision” in the civil case.

Cansino argued against the Sandiganbayan’s authority to suspend him, arguing that only the Supreme Court had the power to discipline and suspend judges.

He said the SC had already placed him under preventive suspension for 90 days in 2024 over the same allegations, extending the measure twice for a total of nine months.

Cansino said he resumed his judicial duties in February 2025 “without issue, interference, or untoward incident.”

But the Sandiganbayan rejected the argument, saying the SC’s suspension was imposed in an administrative proceeding, while the case before it was criminal in nature.

“This Court must, however, emphasize that administrative proceedings are separate and distinct from criminal proceedings, even if the said proceedings arose from the same facts and circumstances,” the anti-graft court said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: How China got access to Nvidia’s AI chips despite rules to stop them
articles.summary:
AI chips are a central battleground in the US-China technology race. To preserve its lead, in recent years Washington has imposed and revised rules to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors and chipmaking technology, while balancing national security concerns with trade considerations.

The drama around Nvidia, the top US exporter of AI chips to China, has thrust those rules into the spotlight.

Delving into the resulting regulations is a quagmire. Export control rules are often likened to the US tax code in their complexity and constant revision.

Here are some basics for understanding what’s legal, and what’s not, when it comes to China’s access to US AI chips:

When did the US start to restrict chips to China?

In October 2022, the US unveiled sweeping restrictions on advanced chips to China, marking the biggest shift in US policy toward exporting technology to China in decades.

A year later, it tightened the rules to capture more chips and stop chip designers such as Nvidia from selling products engineered to fall just below the performance thresholds of the earlier restrictions. It also expanded the restrictions to countries in the Middle East and restricted chips to overseas companies headquartered in China.

In January 2025, the Biden administration extended the restrictions globally, imposing a worldwide license requirement. But in May, days before it was set to take effect, the Trump administration announced it would not enforce that rule.

The Trump administration only formally rescinded and replaced the rule last week, leaving a gap that allowed data center capacity to proliferate in countries such as Singapore, where Chinese companies could rent computing power remotely to train and deploy AI models.

Did Megaspeed, the Singapore cloud company whose former executive allegedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, operate legally?

Must Read

At AI speed, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang finds exoneration

For over two years, authorities have been investigating whether Megaspeed diverted chips to China, which would be illegal. But companies in countries including Singapore were allowed to buy advanced AI chips for their data centers license-free until the US issued a new rule last week cutting off that practice.

Megaspeed likely won’t be getting any more chips. It was added to a US trade blacklist this week, along with its Thai and Malaysian subsidiaries, essentially blocking shipments. Nvidia also said it cut off sales to Megaspeed in June 2025.

Are Nvidia’s shipments of AI chips to China legal?

About a year ago, President Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, drawing criticism from experts who said the chips would help jumpstart China’s military modernization and erode the US lead in AI. The H200 chip is one of Nvidia’s more advanced chips, but not top-of-the-line.

Nvidia cannot simply ship the chips to Chinese companies that pay for them. Nvidia must apply for licenses from the US Department of Commerce, which has issued them since last spring on a case-by-case basis.

Last week, the House foreign affairs committee released licensing data showing the Trump administration approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026.

What does the new Trump administration rule do?

Last week, the Trump administration issued a new regulation, adding license requirements for five countries including Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, in an effort to crack down on chips being smuggled into China.

Prior to that, the chip-based license requirement generally applied to countries like Russia that raise national security concerns, along with companies headquartered in arms-embargoed countries. Now they also apply to Southeast Asian countries viewed as transshipment points with a high risk for illegal diversion to China.

The rule also clamped down on AI chip sales to non-US data centers that supply a high volume of computing power to Chinese-headquartered firms.

How big a problem is chip smuggling?

For years, Nvidia’s Huang has said there is no evidence of chip smuggling to China.

But that assertion, which experts already viewed skeptically, was further questioned in March when US prosecutors charged three people associated with California-based AI server maker Super Micro Computer SMCI.O, including its co-founder, in a scheme to divert about $2.5 billion of US technology into China, including AI servers packed with Nvidia AI chips.

Critics say Nvidia has tried to minimize a well-known risk. Huang once said Nvidia’s sophisticated Grace Blackwell AI chip platform weighed nearly 1.8 metric tons and could not fit into a pocket or backpack. But servers are not smuggled in backpacks. They are routed through third countries and intermediary companies.

Supporters say Nvidia may not have had verified evidence of diversion and that the company cannot keep tabs on all its products after they’re sold.

Can Nvidia track its chips to see where they end up?

Nvidia has built location verification technology that could indicate which country its chips are operating in, the company confirmed in December 2025. It has offered the feature as a software option for customers.

But the company has opposed proposed legislation that would require location verification and diversion reporting for advanced AI processors.

A measure known as the Chip Security Act is among several export control bills that gained new momentum in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, and may be included in the National Defense Authorization Act that Congress is expected to pass next month. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 76% of Australians struggling to tell apart real and AI content – new report
articles.summary:
Most Australians are using – or at least have tried out – generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini, among many others.

We can use them to search for information, answer questions, and generate text, images, sound and video. As generative AI becomes more sophisticated and ubiquitous, many people are no longer able to distinguish AI-generated content from authentic, human-made content.

Our new representative survey of 2,000 Australian adults conducted in August and September 2026 found 76% of Australians had recently encountered content they initially believed was real, only to later discover that it had been generated by AI.

Must Read

Lessons for the Philippines: AI content surge bypassed Brazil’s election rules — report

The challenge is not just that AI-generated content is becoming more realistic. It’s that many people are unsure whether they’re able to recognize it at all.

The synthetic trap

People with high levels of education who are interested in the technology and have high AI literacy are the most likely to report having mistaken AI content for real.

However, this doesn’t mean these groups are more exposed or susceptible to AI-generated content. Instead, the data suggests these people are better at recognizing when they’ve been misled.

In fact, people with low education and lower AI literacy are the most likely to say they don’t know whether they have mistaken AI content for real.

Therefore, many Australians may not recognize when they have encountered synthetic content. This presents a dilemma for users who are increasingly turning to AI tools to seek information.

Trust in AI is low

While AI use has grown rapidly, many are skeptical of the technology and concerned about how it might impact society. About half (51%) of Australian respondents said they use AI chatbots or tools at least weekly, and more than one quarter (28%) use them daily. Almost everyone (96%) is aware of at least one generative AI platform.

Despite widespread awareness and usage, trust in major AI tools remains very low. When asked “how much do you trust or distrust generative AI chatbots or tools?” only a minority said they trust ChatGPT (34%), Microsoft Copilot (24%), Google Gemini (24%) and Claude (17%).

Our survey also shows people are particularly distrustful of politicians and social media companies that use generative AI. More than half of Australians believe the use of AI by politicians and political parties will make society worse, with social media companies and news media viewed almost as negatively.

In contrast, the report reveals that people view scientists and healthcare professionals as the most trustworthy and benevolent users of AI, with around half saying their use of the technology will improve society.

How do people verify content?

Despite this high level of exposure to AI-generated content and low levels of trust, people rarely use proactive measures to identify or verify if content was AI-generated.

Must Read

Maria Ressa on AI overreliance: ‘Don’t outsource the nuances’

When people suspect AI-generated content, the majority simply take a closer look and examine the content carefully, relying on their intuition. Some check comments made by other online users. But few people look for disclosure statements or labels to identify whether it was made with AI, and even fewer turn to trusted sources of news.

Rather than engaging in lateral reading – leaving the content and checking independent sources – most people engage in vertical reading, which involves only looking within the source. They scrutinize the content itself and rely on their own judgment. This approach becomes less effective as AI-generated content becomes increasingly convincing.

Generally, younger people are more likely to check whether information is true, using a range of verification strategies. The exception is checking a trusted news source, which is more common among those aged 45 and over. Instead, young adults are far more likely to look at comments from other users than older age groups.

Additionally, AI literacy plays an important role in people’s verification strategies. Those with high AI literacy are much more likely to closely examine content than those with low understanding of the technology, suggesting that education about how AI works supports more active and critical evaluation of online information.

People want strong safeguards

Because of the low levels of trust in the technology, Australians say they want strong safeguards around it.

Most importantly, they want protections to ensure accuracy and reliable responses when they are using an AI platform.

They also want guardrails in place to prevent AI from generating illegal, dangerous or harmful content, and protections to reduce the presence of bias and ensure fairness and equity in the content it generates.

This points to the need for a multi-pronged response from the tech platforms and government.

First, digital platforms need clearer and more consistent labeling of AI-generated content. If people are expected to make informed decisions about what they’re seeing, they need transparent information about where that content comes from.

Second, the findings show people with higher levels of AI literacy are better equipped to recognize synthetic content and engage in more critical evaluation practices.

We need to educate all Australians with media and AI literacy. Education in schools is important, but adults need training too. We need a whole-of-society approach where adults can have access to education through local community or workplace initiatives.

Australia already lags behind other countries when it comes to media literacy education, and the rapid increase in AI only makes the need for a national approach more urgent. – via Reuters/Rappler.com

articles.title: [Vantage Point] The Marcos estate tax: A test of presidential statesmanship
articles.summary:
Ferdinand Marcos Jr. can help settle his father’s estate tax and show Filipinos that the law applies with equal force when the taxpayer is the President’s own family.

When President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. opened the 2025 tax campaign of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), he asked Filipinos to pay what they owe. That call for civic duty gained urgency on November 13, when he swore in Rolando Ligon Jr. as BIR commissioner. 

Ligon takes office facing a test that strikes at his bureau’s credibility: what has the government done to collect the unpaid estate tax of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.? While the duty to account and collect rests with the commissioner, the President can make that work far easier. 

By publicly assuring the BIR that it has his full backing to pursue every lawful remedy—even when the taxpayer is his own family—Marcos Jr. can turn a decades-old stalemate into an act of true statesmanship. 

Understanding what is at stake begins with the record. The starting figure is P23,293,607,638, per the assessment made by the BIR in July 1991 after a special audit found that no estate tax return had been filed. 

PCGG, BIR Letters Re Marcos Estate Tax by Nami Buan on Scribd

Because Philippine jurisprudence, as affirmed in Lorenzo v. Posadas, establishes that succession taxes accrue at death, the original assessment is governed by the tax laws in force when the elder Marcos died in 1989. 

The flat 6% estate tax rate introduced decades later under the TRAIN Law (Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion Act or Republic Act No. 10963) does not apply to that assessment. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] Estate tax amnesty: Essential compliance guide)

Instead, the tax code then in force imposed a graduated schedule peaking at 60% on any portion of a net estate exceeding P3 million, plus a P1,393,450 base tax on the first P3 million. 

Working backward from the P23.29 billion assessment—subtracting the base tax, dividing the remainder by 60%, and adding back the initial P3 million—implies a taxable net estate of roughly P38.82 billion if the assessment consisted entirely of basic tax. (READ: Facts and lies: the Marcoses’ unpaid estate tax)

While that arithmetic illustrates the assessment’s scale, reconstructing the actual tax base requires the audit schedules showing which assets were included, how they were valued, and what deductions were allowed. 

Public debate, however, has often centered on P203.819 billion. That figure stems from a 2021 calculation by retired Supreme Court senior associate justice Antonio Carpio, who took the P23.294 billion assessment and added a 25% surcharge of P5.823 billion, P139.762 billion in interest at 20% a year over 30 years, and P34.940 billion in interest on the surcharge. (READ: [ANALYSIS] The estate tax liability of the Marcos Estate)

The math explains how the headline number grew, yet its assumptions require an official accounting. The TRAIN Law changed how statutory interest is calculated starting January 1, 2018, and the Supreme Court has applied the transition from 20% to 12% in tax cases. The BIR should clarify which rates and periods govern this account, how each charge was computed, and what credits reduce the balance. 

What is beyond dispute is that the assessment itself is legally settled. Marcos personally challenged the collection measures decades ago, leading to the Supreme Court’s 1997 ruling in Marcos II v. Court of Appeals. 

The Court held that the assessment became final and unappealable after the heirs failed to protest it through proper channels, finding sufficient notice and timely levies under the three-year prescriptive period then applicable. 

LOOK: Supreme Court's Entry of Judgment which shows that GR 120880, where the High Court ordered Marcos heirs to pay P23 billion in estate tax, became final and executory on March 9, 1999. @rapplerdotcom pic.twitter.com/p9XbJxiIGZ

— Lian Buan (@lianbuan) March 30, 2022

Crucially, the justices ruled that the BIR could proceed against estate property without waiting for probate court approval. Though Marcos claimed in 2022 that his family could not argue its case while in Hawaii, the Court’s decision records that notices were served after his return to the Philippines—including papers for his mother delivered through his office at the House of Representatives. 

The coalition 1Sambayan is urging Ligon to act before December 2, marking five years since the BIR sent a written demand to the heirs—a notice confirmed by then-commissioner Caesar Dulay. 

Determining whether another demand letter is legally necessary to preserve the government’s claims requires reviewing the statute and the collection record. As the Supreme Court showed in Republic v. Hizon—where a collection suit was deemed time-barred even as the BIR was allowed to proceed against properties covered by timely warrants—deadlines matter. Ligon must swiftly establish which remedies remain live and act accordingly before any applicable window closes. (READ: [Ask the Tax Whiz] The new BIR chief’s 3 crosses: Will he dare audit the powerful?)

Just as importantly, the BIR owes the public a transparent accounting of past collection steps. Court records show that 11 Tacloban, Leyte, parcels went to auction in 1993. When no one bid, the properties were declared forfeited to the government. 

What became of those lands, and what value, if any, was credited against the tax? Subject to lawful disclosure limits, the bureau should lay out the full ledger: the original assessment, accrued charges, recoveries, and collectible balance. If any remedy has lapsed, it should explain when and why. After years of competing figures, Filipinos deserve a clear record they can examine. 

This moment gives Marcos a rare chance to show statesmanship. As an heir, he can help produce estate records, authorize disclosures where his consent can lawfully enable them, and work with the other heirs to settle what the BIR confirms is due. 

As President, he can give Ligon the space to reach and explain his own conclusions, even those inconvenient to the Marcos family. He can do both before December 2, while the bureau determines that date’s legal significance. 

Taking the high ground would give real substance to the President’s own appeals for tax compliance and hand revenue officers a powerful precedent the next time a well-connected taxpayer expects special treatment. 

Marcos has spent years asking Filipinos to judge his administration on its merits. Now, the choice is his. By using the authority of his office to protect the BIR’s independence in pursuing his father’s estate, he can show Filipinos that the law bends for no one. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Duran Duran guitarist and songwriter Andy Taylor dies at 65
articles.summary:
LOS ANGELES, USA – Andy Taylor, the guitarist and songwriter for pop-rock band Duran Duran and a Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee, died at age 65 on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates released on Wednesday, November 25.

Taylor, who co-wrote some of the group’s biggest hits, including “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “Rio,” and “Girls on Film,” died from metastatic prostate cancer. He was diagnosed in 2018.

The first section of the statement came from his family, while the second was from Duran Duran members Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor.

“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” Taylor’s wife, Tracy Wilson-Taylor, said on behalf of his family.

The members of the Grammy-winning band noted that Taylor brought a unique style to their sound.

“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story. From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music,” they said, adding that he faced his illness with courage, honesty and grace.

Born in 1961 in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, Taylor began learning guitar at age 11 and later dropped out of school to tour England and Europe with several bands. He moved to Birmingham and joined Duran Duran in 1980.

The group signed with EMI Records and released its debut album, “Duran Duran,” in 1981. While the record was successful in the United Kingdom, global fame followed with 1982’s “Rio.”

Taylor later launched a solo career, releasing his debut studio album, “Thunder,” in 1987.

The late musician has four children with Wilson-Taylor. – Rappler.com

articles.title: EXPLAINER: How scammers reach you, with or without your data
articles.summary:
Recent data breaches have exposed personal records across Philippine government agencies and private firms, making it more important than ever to stay alert to targeted scams.

The National Privacy Commission has advised the public to remain cautious about possible attempts at phishing, smishing, and other scams that may arise after the wave of cybersecurity incidents in the country.

Must Read

12 Christmas scams to watch out for

In its State of Scams Report, the Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA) found that 84% of Filipinos have encountered a scam this year. This is an increase from 77% in 2025. The survey, which had 1,160 Filipino adult respondents, was conducted from March 16 to April 13, 2026.

Knowing what a scam looks like is no longer enough, as scammers have upgraded their techniques to catch you. Here is how scammers reach you today.

Email messages

With your real name or account details, scammers can send convincing fake promotions, receipts, password-reset prompts, and even account-suspension warnings. 

Since emails allow you to enhance your text with styles, scammers can easily mimic official branding of government agencies, banks, and organizations to trick you into opening malicious attachments or clicking links.

SHAM PRIZE. A phishing email notifies the recipient that they have won free products from a hardware retailer. Rappler screenshot

Your email service can often detect whether a message is suspicious or not. But you must watch out for mismatched sender domains, unusual requests, or unexpected links and attachments.

Social media and messaging apps

As more telecommunication companies tighten SMS filters, scammers have migrated to Facebook, Instagram, Viber, Telegram, WhatsApp, and other social media platforms.

When they gain unauthorized access to your social media accounts, they target more victims by impersonating you and sending suspicious direct messages (DMs) or links to your contacts.

Some even casually ask how you are and proceed to offer you job opportunities or paid tasks.

FAKE JOB SCAMS. Individuals claiming ot be human resources (HR) staff of marketing agencies reach out on online messaging apps to offer virtual jobs or paid tasks. Rappler screenshots

Be mindful of engaging with messages not only from unknown contacts, but also from your loved ones. If you notice something suspicious, you may use your online messaging app’s report and block option.

Phone calls

Scammers do not only use unknown numbers to contact you. They can spoof their caller ID to imitate banks, digital wallets, government employees, and courier companies using Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP).

It allows users to make phone calls via an internet connection instead of an analog phone line, according to the Federal Communications Commission.

Fraudsters utilize VoIP to lure you into sharing sensitive information by telling you that you have unauthorized transactions or your account has been compromised. They cause panic and urgency, so they can access your account information.

Be cautious when answering phone calls from unknown numbers. Do not share sensitive account details or passwords, as banks and e-wallets will never ask for those details, and scammers can also spoof caller IDs.

Hang up and verify whether a phone number is associated with legitimate institutions by checking their official channels or by searching this list of hotlines and telemarketing SIM numbers published by local banks and e-wallets:

SMS and text messages

GASA also discovered that Filipinos mostly experience scams conducted through text messages this year.

Scammers used to deliver spam texts to you through an unknown phone number, which you can easily identify as suspicious.

DELIVERY FRAUD. A smishing text message from an international number informs the recipient that they have a pending delivery from PHLPost and includes a malicious website link. Rappler screenshot

But now they have found a workaround that does not require your phone number to reach you: International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) catchers. 

These are surveillance devices acting as fake cell towers that can intercept your mobile phone, access your device’s location, and manipulate message threads by sending spoofed messages to you. 

Such messages slip straight into your legitimate message threads because they are undetected by telco spam filters as they bypass cell towers.

BOGUS, NOT BONUS. Smishing messages from banks and a water service provider indicate that the recipient has expiring credit card points and a cash prize, which can be claimed by accessing the provided phishing links. Rappler screenshots

Cybersecurity advocacy group Scam Watch Pilipinas documented spoofed messages through IMSI catchers as early as 2024, according to an investigative report by The Philippine STAR.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas already released Memorandum No. M-2022-015 in 2022, prohibiting banks from sending clickable links through text, email, or messaging apps.

If you receive a text message with a link to your device, do not click it, since it may be a smishing scam. 

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security also advised turning off the 2G network connection of your device, if the option is available.

Websites

Unlike texts or calls that interrupt you, fake websites serve as the final trap.

Fraudsters draw you in through a link in a spoofed SMS, a phishing email, a social media DM, or a sponsored search or social media ad. The goal is for you to land on a bogus website that clones a banking portal, promo page, or online store.

Even scanning QR codes can lead you to malicious website links hidden as an image instead of text until the page loads. 

These fake websites often spoof banking portals that require you to enter your login credentials, card details, or one-time PINs.

Before clicking on any link, look closely at the web address for uncommon domains, misspelled or extra words, unfamiliar symbols, and numbers swapped for letters (e.g., 0 for O and 1 for l).

When scanning QR codes, check first if the printed image has signs of tampering. You may also read the link preview first before accessing the site after scanning.

Also ensure that you have activated the built-in anti-phishing or malware protection features of your browsers and have turned on multi-factor authentication for your digital accounts.

Scammers can spoof phone numbers, clone websites, or imitate cell towers. But they cannot get through a user who stops to verify first.

If you encounter any online scams, you may report them to the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center by dialing 1326. – Rappler.com

Must Read

Don’t let online scammers escape. Dial 1326 and report.

articles.title: FM Cho calls for bipartisan support for foreign policy ahead of departure
articles.summary: Foreign Minister Cho Hyun on Thursday called for bipartisan support for the government's foreign policy, as he made what could be his final appearance before a parliamentary committee ahead of his scheduled departure. Cho made the remarks during a plenary session of the National Assembly's foreign affairs and unification committee, as Lim Woong-soon, second deputy director of the National Security Office, has been nominated as his successor. "I feel greatly honored to have been able to contribute to the development of Korea's diplomacy as the first foreign minister of the (Lee Jae Myung) administration," Cho said. Noting the increasingly challenging international environment, Cho called on committee members to continue providing bipartisan support for the administration, particularly its summit diplomacy, which he said had recently been delivering significant results. Cho took office in July last year and has served as the country's top diplomat. Lim was scheduled to begin work at a designated office Thursday to prepare for his confirmation hearing, the date of which has yet to be set.

articles.title: Minister nominee says investigative independence must meet public expectations
articles.summary: Interior Minister nominee Han Jun-ho said Thursday that if appointed, he would address the issue of investigative agencies' independence in a way that meets public expectations. Han, a two-term lawmaker of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea, made the remarks to reporters as he arrived at an office in downtown Seoul to prepare for his parliamentary confirmation hearing. "The way powerful state institutions exercise their authority can lead to incidents like the Dec. 3, 2024, martial law declaration. Given that this administration was born out of such an experience, I will perform my duties in a manner that aligns with public expectations," Han said, when asked how he would ensure the independence of investigative agencies, including the police and the Serious Crime Investigation Agency, both of which are overseen by the ministry. "The interior ministry plays a role in allocating financial resources and is responsible for public order and safety. I pledge to approach my duties each day with the same care and dedication one would give to a newborn," he said. He then recounted a conversati

articles.title: Incheon airport becomes first Asian airport to win ACI innovation leader award
articles.summary: Incheon International Airport Corp. said Thursday it has won the best airport innovation leader award at the 2026 ACI World Airport Innovation Awards. It is the first time an Asian airport has won the award. The award was presented Wednesday (local time) at Airports Innovate 2026 in Barcelona, Spain. The annual conference brings together airports and industry companies from around the world to discuss future airport technologies. It is organized by the Airports Council International, a global trade association of airport operators, which has used the event since 2021 to recognize airports that lead innovation in the industry. The head of the corporation's new business division won the award for leading its Aviation AI Innovation Hub project from the initial concept to its business structure. The project will bring an artificial intelligence data center, a research and development center and a global business center together on unused land at Incheon International Airport, Korea's main international gateway, located west of Seoul. articles.title: Lee vows to ease financial burden on patients with rare diseases
articles.summary: President Lee Jae Myung on Thursday vowed to ease the financial burden on seriously ill patients and those with rare diseases, giving them greater hope of receiving treatment. Lee made the pledge in a post on his X account, citing a news report on the Cabinet's approval of a plan to reduce the health insurance copayment rate for seriously ill patients and those with rare or incurable diseases from the current 10 percent to 7 percent starting next month. "Around 370,000 people are expected to benefit (from the measure) which will reduce their annual costs by an average 220,000 won ($164.2) per person," he noted. "This would help ease concerns over treatment costs among patients with rare diseases and those who are seriously ill, giving them greater hope of receiving treatment," the president said. He said the government has been working on measures to ease the financial burden on patients and will continue efforts to further reduce their treatment costs.

articles.title: Police raid home of late LEET top scorer in cheating probe
articles.summary: Police on Thursday raided the home of the late top scorer on this year's law school entrance exam as part of a probe into his alleged cheating on the test. Investigators searched the home of Lee Jin-woo, a 32-year-old dental student who was found dead last week amid mounting suspicions about his possible use of artificial intelligence (AI) in getting a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET). Police also raided Younghoon High School in Seoul, where Lee's college entrance exam papers from last year have been stored. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency's financial crime unit launched the probe after receiving multiple complaints accusing Lee of cheating. Despite initial expectations they would close the case following Lee's death, the police have pressed ahead in the public interest, with the nation still grappling with the recent admission of AI-assisted cheating by the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam. The admission sent authorities scrambling to draw up and enforce anti-cheating measures during the annual college entrance exam last week.

articles.title: Lee's approval rating falls for 2nd straight time: poll
articles.summary: President Lee Jae Myung's approval rating fell for the second consecutive time to 43 percent, with negative assessments of his performance continuing to outnumber positive ones, a biweekly poll showed Thursday. In a survey of 1,000 adults nationwide conducted Monday through Wednesday, positive assessments of Lee's job performance fell 1 percentage point from two weeks earlier, according to the National Barometer Survey (NBS). Negative assessments also fell 2 percentage points to 45 percent, while 12 percent said they were undecided. Lee's approval rating has seen a downward trend from early this year in NBS polls, hovering below 70 percent from March to May before falling below 60 percent in June and remaining in the low-to-mid 40 percent range since September. When asked about the direction of state affairs, 42 percent said the Lee administration was heading in the right direction, while 46 percent said it was going in the wrong direction. articles.title: US military confirms inactivation of Apache helicopter squadron in S. Korea
articles.summary: The U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) confirmed Thursday that an Army aviation unit in South Korea has been inactivated, noting that the move does not change the United States' military force posture or commitment to the defense of the Asian ally. The inactivation of the 5th Air Cavalry Squadron, 17th Cavalry Regiment (5-17 ACS) at Camp Humphreys, a key U.S. base in Pyeongtaek, some 60 kilometers south of Seoul, came amid lingering speculation that the U.S. could consider a troop realignment to better address broader regional security challenges, including from China. "The inactivation of the 5-17 Air Cavalry Squadron is part of the U.S. Army's broader force structure and aviation transformation efforts to modernize capabilities and optimize formations for future operational requirements," the USFK said in response to a question from Yonhap News Agency. "This action does not change U.S. Forces Korea's mission, posture, or commitment to the defense of the Republic of Korea," it added, referring to South Korea by its official name. articles.title: Korea to ban ads on food, drugs, cosmetics featuring AI-generated experts
articles.summary: Korea will ban advertisements using experts generated by artificial intelligence (AI) to promote food, drugs and cosmetics starting this week, the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety said Thursday. The ministry said it has revised enforcement regulations of related laws, which will take effect sequentially starting Friday, the ministry said. Violators will be forced to suspend their businesses, or mandated to suspend advertising and sales activities. "We will protect the people from unfair advertisements abusing new technologies, while fostering an environment where customers can feel safe," an official from the drug ministry said.

articles.title: Kookmin University professor named among World's Top 2% Scientists for 6 straight years
articles.summary: Nam Ki-hyun, a professor at Kookmin University’s College of General Education, has been named to the 2026 World’s Top 2% Scientists list for the sixth consecutive year. The list, jointly released by Stanford University and global academic publisher Elsevier, identifies the top 2 percent of researchers in their respective fields based on a comprehensive analysis of citation metrics and other indicators of research impact drawn from Elsevier’s Scopus database. Nam ranked in the top 0.52 percent of researchers in the field of biochemistry and molecular biology when self-citations were excluded, and in the top 0.25 percent when they were included, the university said. “I am deeply honored to have been named among the World’s Top 2% Scientists for six consecutive years,” Nam said. “This achievement would not have been possible without the collaboration and dedication of the researchers in Korea and abroad with whom I have worked, and I would like to express my sincere gratitude to all of them." The university placed third among regional flagship national universities, behind Kyungpook National University and Pusan National University, which tied for 19th overall. articles.title: Sogang University expands AI collaboration with University of Toronto
articles.summary: Sogang University is expanding collaboration with the University of Toronto in education, research and talent development, with a focus on artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics. The two universities held a joint workshop on Oct. 28 at Sogang’s Seoul campus to share research findings and explore opportunities for joint research and talent development. The Sogang-University of Toronto Collaborative Workshop on AI for Intelligent and Physical Systems was organized by Sogang’s College of Computing and Anchor Project Group and supported by the Seoul Metropolitan Government. The workshop followed a memorandum of understanding signed by the two universities in January and aimed to translate the agreement into concrete educational and research initiatives. The partnership is part of Sogang’s efforts to realize its vision of becoming an “AI-Driven University.” Sogang President Sim Jong-hyeok expressed hope that the partnership would lead to expanded joint education and research. “Through these efforts, Sogang University will play a key role in helping Seoul emerge as a global hub fo

articles.title: PM vows to protect teachers from false accusations of child abuse
articles.summary: The government will take steps to protect teachers from false accusations of child abuse to help them concentrate on educating children without worrying about such malicious complaints, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said Thursday. The concept of emotional abuse will be defined more specifically to distinguish it from legitimate teaching, while unnecessary investigations into legitimate educational acts will be minimized, Han said during a government policy coordination meeting. "Protecting students from child abuse is more important than anything else. But at the same time, an educational environment should be guaranteed where legitimate educational activities are not discouraged and teachers can focus on guiding students according to their principles," she said. The government will also have schools and regional education offices take responsibility for responding to malicious complaints directed at individual educators so as to better protect teachers' rights, Han said. articles.title: Unionized rail workers launch work-to-rule campaign; service disruptions likely
articles.summary: Unionized workers of Korea Railroad Corp. (KORAIL) launched a work-to-rule action Thursday, making disruptions to train services nationwide likely. Under the action, which began at 9 a.m. and is set to last through Dec. 4, the workers plan to strictly adhere to safety and other regulations, such as not driving trains faster to make up for lost time, refusing to work overtime and responding to passenger complaints in line with manuals, according to the Korean Railway Workers' Union. Through the campaign, the union is demanding improvements to the employee promotion system, extra allowances and additional personnel. It has threatened to launch an indefinite general strike on Dec. 10, if the needs are not addressed. Disruptions could occur on various services operated by KORAIL, including the KTX and SR high-speed trains, the ITX-Saemaul trains and parts of the subway network in the capital area. articles.title: Supreme Court confirms ex-President Yoon's acquittal in perjury case
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Thursday confirmed former President Yoon Suk Yeol's acquittal on charges that he perjured himself during the martial law trial of former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo. Yoon was indicted on charges of making false claims during Han's trial in November last year that he had planned to call a Cabinet meeting for his martial law declaration on Dec. 3, 2024, even before Han proposed such a session. Special counsel Cho Eun-suk's team viewed the testimony as false, arguing that Yoon had initially called in six Cabinet members without planning a formal session but later summoned additional members at Han's suggestion to meet the quorum that would legitimatize his martial law declaration. An appellate court in September upheld a lower court's acquittal of Yoon, ruling that the unusual circumstances of the Cabinet meeting alone are not enough to find Yoon guilty. The Supreme Court did not find issues with the appellate ruling, noting that a conviction requires evidence strong enough to substantiate the charges as true. articles.title: Building a community for Black creatives in Seoul
articles.summary: When Marie Noel moved to Korea in 2024, the plan was simple: find a way to continue her filmmaking career as a writer and actor. Her profession had given her opportunities to travel across Austria, Germany and the U.K. In all these places she went, she found herself in spaces where representation and access were not always guaranteed. As soon as she began reconnecting with filmmaking in Korea, she was confronted with a similar reality about visibility and representation. Identifying and connecting Black creatives specifically required time and deliberate effort. The reality was further compounded by the fact that Black creatives were living and working across Korea and pursuing their own artistic interests, yet many were doing so independently, oblivious of each other, in the same industry. It was this revelation that sparked her to establish Black Seoul Creatives, a community connecting Black creatives and members of the Black diaspora across Korea. articles.title: 'Hope' wins top Blue Dragon award; Sul, Jeon take acting honors for 'Possible Love'
articles.summary: Director Na Hong-jin's sci-fi thriller "Hope" won best picture at the 47th Blue Dragon Film Awards on Wednesday, while Lee Chang-dong's "Possible Love" emerged as the night's biggest winner with four awards, including both top acting honors. "Hope," which competed at this year's Cannes Film Festival, entered the ceremony at KBS Hall in Seoul with 10 nominations. In addition to best picture, it also won awards for cinematography and lighting. Accepting the best picture trophy, Na drew laughter from the audience by joking that he should have won the award at Cannes. "They should have given me this at Cannes. Why here instead?" he said. Na then credited the cast and crew, describing the experience of making the film as one of the happiest and most memorable times of his life. Lee's "Possible Love," which won the Grand Jury Prize at this year's Venice International Film Festival, dominated the acting categories. articles.title: Sindh High Court restores dissolution of marriage provision in Christian divorce law
articles.summary:
KARACHI: The Sindh High Court on Wednesday revived a provision of the Divorce Act of 1869 that had been omitted in 1981, enabling Christian couples in the province to approach courts for dissolution of marriage on ordinary grounds.

A two-judge constitutional bench headed by Justice Yousuf Ali Sayeed ruled that the omission of such provision was inconsistent with various provisions of the Constitution.

Former military dictator Ziaul Haq had omitted Section 7 of the Divorce Act through an ordinance in July 1981, leaving Christian citizens with no ground to divorce their spouses except on charges of adultery.

Section 7 of Divorce Act 1869 was omitted by Gen Zia in 1981 through an ordinance; LHC had revived the provision in 2017 only in Punjab

An NGO, said to be providing free legal representation to marginalised persons including religious minorities, along with two Christian citizens, had petitioned the SHC in 2023 and pleaded to declare the impugned omission unconstitutional and without any legal effect, and to direct the district and family courts of Sindh to disregard it.

The petitioners argued that the impugned omission had frozen the law in its 19th-century form, compelling a spouse to remain bound for life in a marriage that had irretrievably broken down unless he or she could prove adultery, with conversion to another faith or a false accusation of adultery remaining the only practical means of exit.

They also contended that such action had violated fundamental rights, including the right to liberty and dignity, and amounted to discrimination against Christian citizens in comparison with citizens of other faiths, as well as against Christian women in comparison with Christian men.

The federal and provincial law officers could not controvert the submissions advanced by the counsel for the petitioners as to the effect of the impugned omission, and instead fell back on Article 270A to argue that the ordinance was protected thereunder and that fresh legislation on the subject remained under consideration in both the federal and provincial domains.

The Archbishop of Karachi strongly opposed the petition and contended that it was not maintainable, as the petitioners lacked locus standi to institute proceedings on behalf of the Christian community, and that any reform must be preceded by meaningful consultation with all Christian denominations and representative bodies.

On his behalf, it was also argued that the Roman Catholic Church regarded marriage as a holy sacrament governed by Canon Law, and that any reform which directly or indirectly interfered with sacramental doctrine or ecclesiastical jurisdiction would offend Article 20.

The bench noted in its judgement that, apparently, the divorce law had recognised cruelty and desertion for two years or more as conduct sufficiently grave to warrant a decree of judicial separation, but not on their own as grounds for dissolution of the marriage. It said a spouse who establishes such conduct may live apart from the other under the sanction of a decree, but the bond itself subsists, with the consequence that neither party is free to marry again.

“For a husband, dissolution is available only upon proof of adultery. For a wife, it is available only upon proof of adultery coupled with an aggravating circumstance, or of conversion coupled with a further marriage, or of rape, sodomy or bestiality. The disparity between the grounds available to each spouse is evident on the face of the provision,” it added.

Referring to the decision of the LHC, the bench observed that it was a lucidly reasoned judgement where the vires of the impugned omission was examined on the touchstone of constitutional guarantees of dignity, equality and freedom of religion with great sensitivity.

After the 18th Amendment, it noted that the issues of marriage and divorce came within the residual legislative competence of provinces and by virtue of Article 270AA(6), every law with respect to a matter in the omitted list that was in force immediately before commencement of the amendment continued to remain in force until altered, repealed or amended by the competent authority.

“The Act, in the form in which the impugned omission left it, is therefore an existing law that continues to operate in this province, the competent authority to alter it now being the Provincial Assembly of Sindh, which has not done so,” the bench remarked.

“Equally, a husband and wife who have lived apart for many years and who both desire to bring their marriage to an end have no lawful means of doing so, unless one of them is prepared to accuse the other of adultery. We are unable to conceive of a more intrusive restriction on personal liberty than one that obliges an individual to remain bound in a relationship from which all substance has departed, with no prospect of release, save on terms that the individual cannot or will not meet,” it added.

While concurring with the conclusion reached by the LHC in its judgement, the SHC said, “The impugned omission is inconsistent with Articles 9, 14, 20 and 25(2) of the Constitution and is, by virtue of Article 8(1), void to the extent of such inconsistency.”

Published in Dawn, November 26th, 2026

articles.title: Anthropic chief denies wanting humans to 'surrender' free will to AI
articles.summary:
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei on Wednesday denied wanting humanity to give up its free will to AI, calling it “absurd” to attribute the idea to him as rival tech leaders push back.

“No, I do not believe that we should ‘surrender human free will’ to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do,” Amodei wrote in a lengthy post on X, a week after Anthropic’s record-setting stock market debut.

“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he added.

Fears that AI tools could slip out of human control have haunted Silicon Valley since a string of incidents this summer, including the hacking of Hugging Face by autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI.

“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” an Anthropic safety lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote in September.

Amodei took aim, without naming names, at “some AI CEOs” who repeat slogans like “AI should be just a tool” but then are not “actually doing anything different in their products.”

On Sunday, Meta’s Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang wrote on X that “we should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said earlier this month that if the tradeoff for curing cancer is “you are going to lose all agency and control and voice in the future,” that is “a terrible sales pitch.” Amodei’s post was in response to an article by US outlet Axios on AI debate, though he did not address his previous remarks on the topic.

In February, Amodei told The New York Times that in “life-critical, safety-critical cases, we really want to turn it over” to AI.

And in late 2024, he predicted that AI systems “will be the leaders, and they’ll be ordering humans or other AI systems around.” On Wednesday, he acknowledged that “we may want limits” on recursive self-improvement, or RSI, in which AI models can autonomously create new versions of itself, and that “we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously,” without saying where the line should be drawn.

Yet in its IPO filing, Anthropic said that “each new version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next,” and that Claude wrote over 90 per cent of the contributions to its codebase in September.

Elon Musk, who has long predicted that superintelligent AI would leave humans “like pet Labradors,” reposted Amodei’s statement with a one-word comment: “interesting.”

articles.title: Curtains on COP31
articles.summary:
THE 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) took place in the backdrop of geopolitical fragmentation, a rising cost-of-living crisis, tightening of national and international budgets and the imminent threat of a 1.5ºC overshoot.

Despite high stakes, the talks — instead of propelling the agenda forward — highlighted significant gaps in international cooperation and revealed critical areas where progress was stalled, resulting in an underwhelming outcome.

At its core, COP31 faced a leadership vacuum, leaving parties to navigate the negotiations with limited political direction. Turkiye’s presidency for hosting and Australia’s presidency of negotiations were unable to shepherd political compromises for the highest possible ambition. The result was a watered-down draft cover decision with the lowest common denominator that failed to secure consensus and was therefore not adopted.

The lack of ambition was visible across all critical workstreams. The negotiations failed to get a tangible commitment from major emitting countries to ratchet up their 2030 greenhouse gas emission reduction targets in line with the Paris Agreement.

COP31 reaffirmed that multilateralism must endure as the backbone of climate action.

Many nations maintained vague promises without concrete policies or mechanisms to accelerate carbon cuts. This failure underscores the persistent divide between developed and developing countries over responsibility and capacity. Financial pledges for climate adaptation and loss and damage remained grossly insufficient, especially for vulnerable countries grappling with the worst climate impacts.

COP31 did not substantially increase the promised climate finance commitment, nor did it establish clearer mechanisms for operationalising this support. This shortfall deepened the trust deficit between richer and poorer nations and hampered purposeful progress. COP31 made little headway in solidifying a comprehensive loss and damage framework that would provide timely financial assistance to countries suffering from climate-induced disasters.

Despite long-standing calls for compensatory mechanisms, negotiations were bogged down in political disagreements, reflecting the complexities and sensitivities surrounding liability and responsibility.

Although adaptation is a critical pillar of climate action, COP31 showcased a yawning gap between rhetoric and reality. Concrete and enforceable commitments for adaptation planning, funding, and technology transfers failed to materialise.

Perhaps the most glaring omission at COP31 was the absence of decisive action on phasing out fossil fuels. Despite growing scientific consensus on the need to rapidly transition to renewable energy, the conference sidestepped a clear, actionable roadmap away from fossil fuel dependency, highlighting the influence of entrenched economic interests.

While these shortcomings are disappointing, they offer a valuable opportunity for reflection and reform. The failure at COP31 should not be viewed as the collapse of the global climate effort but as an urgent signal that the status quo in multilateral climate negotiations is insufficient to meet the scale and immediacy of the crisis.

This moment calls for re-energising international cooperation, urging countries to bridge their divergent interests and work with renewed transparency and solidarity. It also brings to light that the current voluntary pledging model needs firmer accountability mechanisms for enforcing compliance and incentivising larger, more actionable and ambitious commitments.

The inability to get an overarching political consensus also demonstrates that countries are no longer willing to go along without assurance of financial, technical and policy support needed to adapt and recover. The setbacks also highlight the need to examine new approaches that include civil society, indigenous voices and private-sector leadership for fresh perspectives and urgency into a traditionally slow-moving process.

The weak outcome at COP31 should not cause despair but create a renewed sense of purpose. Sometimes a failure in negotiations is less damaging than weak agreements (like previous COPs) that create a false sense of security. COP31 has forced a reset and serves as a crucial pivot point for rejecting unfair agreements and harnessing the moment to strengthen the spirit of the Paris Agreement, keeping its promise alive and escalating its ambition. The failure of COP31 is in fact a triumph of COP21.

COP31 may have faltered but it reaffirmed the essential truth that multilateralism must endure as the backbone of climate action. The diplomatic disagreements at COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009 resulted in the milestone triumph of COP21 in 2015 in Paris. The failure of COP31 can serve the same turning-point purpose for future COPs and multilateralism.

The writer is a climate policy analyst.
aisha@csccc.org.pk

Published in Dawn, November 26th, 2026

articles.title: Choking the provinces
articles.summary:
LET’S be very clear about one thing: this business of cutting the provinces up into “administrative units” has nothing to do with good or bad governance. It is mainly about recentralising control over the state’s resources.

A paper written by three eminent Pakistani academics in 2005 made a related point that is worth revisiting in the present debate. The authors were Ali Cheema, Asim Ijaz Khwaja and Adnan Qadir and the document was published in 2005 as a working paper for Harvard’s Kennedy School of Government. They took a longer view of all attempts to bring in local governments in the country’s history, and came to the following conclusion: “local government empowerment has always been combined with centralisation of political power in the hands of the non-representative centre. The centralisation of political power has undermined representative institutions not only at the level of the centre but also at the level of the provinces.”

Their analysis is especially relevant all over again, as the same gambit to centralise power is being rolled out for the fourth time in our history. They noted that in all such experiments in the past, “[o]ur interpretation is that these reforms have been used as a means for a non-representative centre to gain legitimacy by by-passing the political agents at the provincial and national levels”.

Today almost 30pc of the federal deficit is being financed by provincial resources, and the demand from the centre for more is continuing to grow.

The seventh NFC award agreed to in 2009 and made effective in July 2010 reversed the centralisation of powers and resources that the federal authorities had grown accustomed to over the decades. It was the first time in Pakistan’s history that powers and, more importantly, resources, flowed down from the federal government towards lower tiers of government in such large quantities. And almost immediately, from its very first year of operation, a thrust emerged from the federal authorities to try and undo this.

It began slowly at first. Then in the middle of the decade it achieved its first written form. Here is a brief timeline of how small, subtle changes in how fiscal resources are measured and counted turned into a full-blown programme for reversing the flow of these resources to the provincial governments.

In FY2011, the first year after the seventh NFC award, the federal government “successfully pressed” the provincial governments to run a surplus and not spend all the money being devolved down to them. Then the next year they asked for these surpluses again, but with no Fund programme in force, the provincial governments did not comply.

This changed in 2013 when the IMF made it a prior action for provinces to post a surplus, and provincial deposits with the State Bank leapt from Rs42 billion in June 2013 to Rs257bn by March 2014. This was ratified in the Council of Common Interests, and provincial finance secretaries agreed to continue the practice into 2015. By June 2015 the IMF programme called for written agreement from the provinces to raise their surpluses, as a prior action and a few months later, in September, provincial spending was capped at 6.5 per cent of GDP.

By June 2016, as the programme was winding up with only a few months left in it, the government set up the Fiscal Coordination Committee to ensure that centre and provinces coordinate their spending and surpluses. The very next year, as the Fund programme ran out, provincial governments ramped up their spending, running a deficit of Rs163bn in FY17.

In July 2019 another IMF programme was signed, after replacing finance ministers. This one again made it a prior action to get provinces to run surpluses, and raised the surplus targets from one to 2.7pc of GDP. That agreement was renewed in the two years that followed, and provincial surpluses leapt from Rs77bn in FY20 to Rs314bn in FY21 and Rs351bn in FY22. That was the most troubled programme of Pakistan’s history, with more false starts than any other programme Pakistan had ever signed.

The blowout came in 2024. As part of the bailout in July 2023, the provinces now had to agree not only to post a surplus, but also submit spending plans. Provincial deposits were already netted against government borrowing in the IMF’s targets for the budget deficit and SBP’s net domestic assets, thereby helping the federal government meet its targets under the Fund programme. Most importantly, the targets for provincial surpluses agreed to in that programme rose to Rs1.2 trillion in the first year, rising to Rs1.9tn by FY27.

So in 2011 the provinces left unspent 13.5pc of what they received as a transfer under the NFC award. This figure fell as soon as the Fund programme lapsed, then rose again every time Pakistan entered a Fund programme. Today it stands at 19pc, skyrocketing in the last three years.

Today almost 30pc of the federal deficit is being financed by provincial resources, and the demand from the centre for more is continuing to grow.

In May 2025, for example, provinces were required to put surplus cash into T-bills. Their holdings of federal government debt rose from Rs19bn in June 2025 to Rs1.8tn as of October 2026, though this figure fluctuates a lot with maturities every few months. And then in June 2026, under Article 164 grants, the provinces were made to hand over Rs1.0tn to the federal authorities, or about 12.66pc of each province’s NFC share.

What began as a plea to restrain spending in 2011 slowly grew into a codified demand to run a surplus. Then the targets for these surpluses were raised. Then came requirements to buy government debt paper followed by a reverse flow from province to centre as a “grant” under Article 164. And now they want to dismantle the whole set-up altogether, in the name of governance. The irony here is that it is the governance failures of the federal authorities themselves that have fuelled their hunger for resources from the provincial authorities.

The writer is a business and economy journalist.

articles.title: Red lines
articles.summary:
INTERIOR Minister Mohsin Naqvi is right to say that freedom of expression cannot be a licence to promote terrorism, hate speech, incitement to violence or child sexual exploitation.

No responsible media outlet or citizen would argue otherwise. And few would object to curbing such content on social media. Those who spread such material should expect to answer for it under the law. But drawing red lines is only half the job. The state must also show that it respects them. This is where its record raises questions.

There are visible red lines against hate and violence. But there are also invisible ones that journalists and citizens encounter every day when they question powerful quarters or report matters considered inconvenient. Journalists have been picked up, threatened and intimidated for publishing stories that upset those in power.

Media organisations have faced pressure over their editorial choices. Reporters often find themselves working out what they can safely publish and which subjects are best avoided. This has created a vacuum that social media is rapidly filling. So when Mr Naqvi tells journalists they are free to report, and that citizens are free to ask questions, it rings hollow.

Terms such as “anti-state activity”, “misinformation” and “hate speech” are elastic. And when officials interpret them without checks, they become tools for silencing critics. Having a law or a regulator does not make its use legitimate. Enforcement agencies should operate within defined legal limits, give valid and legitimate reasons for their decisions, act in proportion to the harm and be answerable to the courts. The rules should apply equally to everyone, whatever their politics or standing. Otherwise a measure meant to protect citizens ends up policing public debate. The minister’s assurance that dissent, including criticism of the state, will be heard is welcome. But assurances count for little while media organisations and journalists are still being intimidated.

The state must guarantee complete press freedom, subject only to clearly defined constitutional and legal restrictions. A sensible first step would be to bring journalists and their representative bodies, media owners, civil society and relevant state institutions together to agree on what responsible expression means in practice. Such consultations should produce a clear commitment to protect journalists, safeguard editorial independence and prevent the misuse of regulatory powers.

Freedom of expression carries responsibilities. But those responsibilities cannot be imposed on the media alone. The state must also accept its own obligations and allow uncomfortable questions to be asked. Rules against violence and hatred are fair enough. Unwritten and invisible ones against independent journalism are not.

articles.title: Govt raises Rs689bn via treasury bills
articles.summary:
KARACHI: The government raised much less than the amount maturing at Thursday’s treasury bills auction, sticking to its strategy of cutting short-term debt despite strong demand from banks.

The government raised Rs689.5 billion against a target of Rs750bn and maturities of Rs1,317bn. Total bids amounted to Rs2.77 trillion, of which Rs173.6bn was accepted through the auction and Rs515.9bn through non-competitive bids.

Cut-off yields were mix­ed. The yield on one-month bills fell by 19 basis points to 11.69 per cent, while the yield on six-month bills rose by 10bps to 12.29pc and that on 12-month bills rose by 11bps to 12.52pc. The 12-month return exceeded the 12pc policy rate by 52bps.

The three-month bill attracted the highest bids, at Rs902.8bn, against whi­ch the government raised Rs69bn. Its rate remained unchanged at 11.99pc.

Bids for the six-month tenor were the lowest, at Rs483.9bn, with only Rs1bn accepted.

For one-month bills, bids totalled Rs627.5bn, with Rs25bn accepted. For 12-month bills, bids totalled Rs756bn, with Rs78.5bn accepted.

Financial experts said the bidding pattern showed ample liquidity with banks, while the government appeared less interested in short-term borrowing.

The long-term PIBs remain the government’s priority, with outstanding stock now double that of short-term T-bills.

The financial sector believes there is room for another 50bps increase in the policy rate, citing double-digit average inflation over the past four months. The State Bank expects inflation to fall to 5-7pc by the end of FY27.
