A mining dispute in a town of a few thousand people tucked away in the remote roof of the Sahara has become entangled with an arms corridor sustaining one of the world’s deadliest wars

The Tibesti mountains run through northern Chad into southern Libya, and are home to the Tubu people (MEE)

Off

Deep inside the Tibesti mountains of northern Chad, in the central Sahara, the town of Miski sits surrounded by a succession of never-ending wadis. 

A couple of families live at the top of each of these valleys and in August, when the rainy season comes, the wadis become a river that washes through the mountains. When the rains go, the valleys become green and camels feed on them.

A remote volcanic range characterised by rugged, bare rock, rivers of lava and volcanoes that climb to 3,000 metres, the Tibesti, which runs through northern Chad across the border into southern Libya, is sometimes called the roof of the Sahara. 

These mountains are home to the Tubu, an indigenous community whose territory also includes a part of southern Libya, northern Niger and northwestern Sudan.

And the valleys that surround the town of Miski contain vast deposits of a precious metal that throughout human history has been prized almost above anything else: gold. 

The mountains, too, are filled with antimony, a toxic heavy metal that is putting the ecosystem of this indigenous community at severe risk and is also exported in great quantities. 

For decades, the gold that sits in this remote place has been one of the drivers of armed conflict between the Tubu and the Libyan, then Chadian states. 

Now, the Tubu find themselves caught up in a web of warfare and illicit trade that stretches out from Chad into Libya, Sudan and over the sea to the United Arab Emirates, from where arms and supplies are flown to proxy armies, militias and paramilitaries. 

On 14 October, armed clashes broke out in Miski.

The day after fighting began, the Chadian army’s general staff accused Miski’s self-defence committee - a local armed group descended from the Tubu institution of village guardianship - of breaking a peace agreement struck between them and the army last year by attacking the National Brigade for the Control of Mining Activities.

The army gave the Tubu group an ultimatum: lay down your arms at once or be treated as rebels. In response, the committee accused the brigade of firing first and of opening new mining fronts in grazing lands, in violation of the Bardai peace accord signed last year.

The gold ends up in Dubai…'yet we do not have a single clinic in Miski or a single paved road in the whole of the Tibesti' 

- Tubu commander

One Tubu commander in Miski told Middle East Eye that last year Chad had exported over $1bn worth of gold and more than 15,000 tonnes of antimony, all sourced from the Tibesti mountains.

Almost all this gold ends up in the UAE, in the gold market of Dubai.

“And yet we do not have a single clinic in Miski or a single paved road in the whole of the Tibesti,” the commander said. “We won’t let this continue.”

Since the armed clashes broke out in October, the Chadian army has moved considerable numbers of troops and armoured vehicles into the Tibesti.  

The situation on the ground, according to one Chadian army officer who spoke to MEE, is difficult for government troops. “We are fighting the mines and the mountains in Miski,” he said.

This fighting has not stopped: scores of people have died in the clashes and the Chadian army has conducted multiple drone strikes across the mountain range.

Weapons corridor

Miski’s uprising appears, on the surface, to be a local fight over gold - and in a large part, it is. 

But it is unfolding inside a region that has become one of the most consequential, least scrutinised arms corridors in Africa: a route that, according to United Nations investigators and extensive reporting from Middle East Eye, has carried weapons, fuel and fighters from the UAE through Libya and Chad to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan. 

How the UAE continued supporting Sudan's RSF through Haftar and Libya

Read More »

These weapons are part of a network of arms and mercenaries that spans swathes of north and central Africa, utilised not just in Sudan but by organised criminal groups and armed entities across the Sahel.   

Between October 2024 and the end of 2025, according to a UN Panel of Experts report, heavy cargo aircraft made 458 flights between military airports in the UAE or the Emirati base at Bosaso in the breakaway Somali region of Puntland and eastern Libya.  

Some 239 of these landed at Kufra, a town about 300km from the Sudan border that was transformed, in the months before the RSF took el-Fasher in October 2025, into a fortified logistics hub complete with new hangars and scheduled flights. 

Separately, as reported by MEE and confirmed by UN experts, the UAE was using Amdjarass, in eastern Chad, to land cargo planes.

Senior Egyptian army sources told MEE earlier this year that the Emiratis have a military operations room inside Amdjarass airport to coordinate with the RSF.

Just over 100km from the border with Darfur, the vast western region of Sudan controlled by the RSF, Amdjarass is a Zaghawa-dominated town that is the home region of Chad’s president, Mahamat Idriss Deby, and the site of a lavish state infrastructure programme that residents of Tibesti, 1,300km away and without a single paved road or a functioning hospital between them, have started to openly resent.

Abu Dhabi continues to deny supplying the Rapid Support Forces.

Haftar’s expanding footprint

In November 2025, Chad and the UAE-backed Haftar family’s Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), de facto commanded by Khalifa Haftar’s son Saddam, formed a joint border force covering roughly 1,050km of shared frontier.

The Haftars are not just in control of eastern Libya: leaked details of US adviser Massad Boulos’s plan to unify Libya propose Saddam Haftar as president of a government that would continue to be led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah. 

Chad’s government has two reasons to want this partnership, and they reinforce each other. 

One is logistical: Chad and Haftar can cement their relationship in the eastern Libyan corridor that carries Emirati arms to the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan. 

The other is that a joint border force hems in the Tubu, who have supplied the armed resistance to Mahamat Deby’s government and to Haftar’s forces alike. 

Jalel Harchaoui, an analyst focusing on Libya and political economy, told Middle East Eye that when the deal was initially struck, the Tubu were not part of the thinking.

The only connection in the remote area - Starlink (MEE)

“It was to ensure better security along the route between Chad and Libya, especially with the passage via Ma’tan as-Sarra in Libya down through Chad to Amdjarass and then on to Darfur,” he said.

This “security problem” included armed groups attacking the convoys headed to Darfur to supply the RSF, Harchaoui said. There was also the need to build further cooperation between Emirati allies who were not natural bedfellows.

“Saddam Haftar and Mahamat Deby don’t get along, so there was a need to please the UAE by doing a joint force. And the agreement was never that the joint force would be pushed to the west, it was really to cover the northeastern corner of Chad,” Harchaoui said.

That changed earlier this year, when Saddam Haftar “ran into trouble” with armed Tubu groups like the Southern Liberation Operations Room (Slor), which is led by Mohamed Wardougou, a Libyan Tubu, and often hides out in northern Niger.

Haftar asked Chad to move forces to the west, arguing correctly, according to Harchaoui, “that Wardougou’s activism served as a shot in the arm for the anti-Deby Chadian group Front for Change and Concord in Chad (Fact) in northern Niger”.

History of revolt

This move played into the Tubu’s long record of rising up against the central governments of Chad, going back to the country’s independence from France in 1960. 

Their most recent armed revolt, in April 2021, culminated in the death on the front line of President Idriss Deby Itno, who had decided at the age of 68 to command his forces in person. His son Mahamat succeeded him.

In Libya too, the Tubu rose against Muammar Gaddafi, and after his fall in 2011, they held sway over vast stretches of southern Libya until 2021, when Haftar’s forces pushed into the areas they had controlled. The containment effort carries a human cost well beyond Tibesti. 

In Libya, Tubu communities describe a steady tightening around their citizenship, with human rights researchers long having flagged discriminatory practices such as treating the Tubu as second-class citizens and stopping them from obtaining passports and IDs. 

'We do not want to be part of a bigger game… We just want peace and justice and foremost, transparency in mining and the development of our region'

- Tubu defence committee member

On 14 October, the same day gunfire broke out in Miski, Libya’s attorney general in Tripoli said he was prepared to strip the 28,000 families registered at Murzuq, in the Fezzan region of southwest Libya, of their Libyan nationality, citing alleged forgery. 

Because the overwhelming majority of Libya’s Tubu are registered through that one civil registry, the announcement reads as an existential threat: if carried through, most of Libya’s Tubu would become stateless.

On the border between Libya and Niger, Wardougou’s Slor group has fought a running battle with Haftar’s forces, using northern Niger as a rear base. The Slor’s declared aim is to remove Haftar’s men from southern Libya.

In July, photographs circulated online showing Chadian soldiers at Libya’s Wigh airbase, near the Nigerien border - evidence, the group’s leadership says, that Chad is fighting on Haftar’s behalf. 

On 20 October, the LAAF arrested a former Chadian minister and senior opposition figure, Hassan Soukaya, as he tried to cross from Libya into Niger, and handed him to the Chadian army.

Days later, Niger’s government publicly accused the Chadian military, with alleged French support, of carrying out a drone strike on 24 October near the Salvador Pass that killed two civilians. The attack was reportedly meant to target Slor positions in Libya, but hit Nigerien territory by accident.

The UAE-Israel desert axis

On 19 October, Israel’s second-ever ambassador to Chad landed in N’Djamena to present her credentials to Deby.

Since taking power after his father’s death in 2021, Deby has made a point of binding Chad ever closer to the UAE and Israel: diplomatic relations with Israel were restored in 2022, and the first Israeli ambassador in more than half a century - since Chad broke off ties in 1972 - was received shortly afterwards. Despite this, in November 2023, Chad recalled its ambassador from Israel, citing “the unprecedented tide of deadly violence” inside Gaza.  

Chadian alignment with the UAE is not only military. As previously reported by MEE, the Emiratis offered Deby “more than a billion dollars” to “flip Chad towards supporting the RSF” after the war in Sudan began, according to former CIA analyst Cameron Hudson.

Senior UAE and regional officials referred to ICC over role in Sudan atrocities

Read More »

That figure now looks like loose change. In May 2025, in Abu Dhabi, Chad unveiled Chad Connexion 2030, a $30bn national development strategy to remake the infrastructure of a landlocked country from the ground up.

The UAE was, by a wide margin, its most important bilateral underwriter, securing $20.5bn in total backing and signing 18 contracts of its own worth over $6.2bn. 

Among the headline projects: an 800-km Etihad rail line to Cameroon’s port of Douala, a 50 MWp solar plant by Global South Utilities, industrial zones, Abu Dhabi Ports logistics hubs, and critical-mineral exploration permits. 

The partnership has tightened Chad’s dependence on the UAE and has become, in effect, the economic lifeline of Deby’s administration. To the west, Chad is already at odds with its neighbour Niger, which has drawn closer to Algeria.

In late October, Algeria deployed troops to Niger, the first time it had done this outside its borders since 1973. The move came days after Niger’s military government survived a coup attempt on 28 August.

Algeria’s move into Niger, according to the retired Algerian diplomat Amar Belani, is designed to counter what he described as “a destabilisation strategy actively involving the United Arab Emirates, Morocco, Israel and certain French proxies.”

The current geopolitical shifts, Belani went on, together with all they entail by way of rivalry and intervention by foreign actors, mean that “new tools, such as a show of presence including at the military level, are no longer a taboo and will be utilised to draw and reinforce Algeria’s red lines.”

Borderlands unrest

What is forming, in other words, is not one war but two rival blocs assembling around unrest in the desert borderlands. 

Rape, ransom and execution: The road out of Sudan's el-Fasher

Read More »

On one side: the Sudanese Armed Forces (which receives backing from Egypt and Turkey), Niger, Algeria, and the Tubu in Libya and Chad. On the other: the RSF, the Haftars, the UAE, Ethiopia and the Chadian state, with the French leaning towards this camp.

And the local fights and the larger one are no longer separate. A mining dispute in a town of a few thousand people tucked away deep in the remote mountains of Chad has become entangled with an arms corridor sustaining one of the world’s deadliest wars, with a succession contest inside Libya’s eastern military establishment, and a Sahelian realignment redrawing alliances from Algiers to Khartoum. 

“We do not want to be part of a bigger game,” one member of the Tubu defence committee in Miski told MEE. “We just want peace and justice and foremost, transparency in mining and the development of our region.”

But whether it remains a local counter-insurgency or becomes the spark for something larger will depend less on what happens in the mountains of Tibesti than on decisions being made in Abu Dhabi, Benghazi and Paris.

Sahel

Oscar Rickett

Miski, Chad

articles.title: Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes
articles.summary:
Houthis say they attacked Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery in retaliation for deadly strikes

Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 15:56

Yemeni movement says the refinery attack was in retaliation to Saudi strikes, including one that killed at least 26 people earlier this week

This satellite image shows a large smoke cloud billowing over Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery on 25 November 2026 (Planet Labs PBC/Handout via Reuters)

Off

Yemen's Houthi movement claimed responsibility for an attack on Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery, Ras Tanura, on Wednesday, describing it as retaliation for repeated Saudi strikes that have killed scores of civilians.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a post on X that the refinery attack caused fires and came in retaliation for the "brutal Saudi aggression against our country, including its targeting of passenger buses and citizens' trucks in the Al-Maqatirah district of Lahij, as well as other crimes in the capital, Sanaa, and the governorates."

The attack in the district of Lahij earlier this week killed at least 26 people.

In a follow-up post on X, Saree responded to Saudi threats to retaliate against Yemen's civilian Hodeidah port, which Saudi Arabia has already bombed, by warning that all "enemy Saudi ports along the Red Sea coast will be targets".

"We warn employees, workers and those near these ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away, and we call on all shipping companies to remove their ships from those ports immediately," the post added.

Ansar Allah, known as the Houthis, which controls the capital Sanaa and much of north and western Yemen, has been firing missiles at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen's frozen civil war reignited in July in a spillover from the Israeli-US war on Iran.

Riyadh broke the ceasefire, which also included Saudi Arabia, when it bombed Sanaa's international airport on 13 July.

Since then, the Saudi military has struggled to contain the Houthis and their ability to counter Saudi-backed forces in Yemen.

The ongoing attacks are wreaking havoc on the Saudi economy, oil infrastructure and the country's international image.

Airlines have cancelled international flights from the Saudi capital, Riyadh, while previous attacks on the country’s oil infrastructure have disrupted oil supplies.

The attacks have also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football's AFC Asian Cup and the flagship Future Investment Initiative conference.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Saudis said that air defences had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in the country's Eastern Province. They did not deny that the attack had struck the oil refinery there.

Who are Yemen's Houthis and what do they want?

Read More »

Satellite images reviewed by Reuters showed large swathes of thick black smoke around the refinery, covering an area spanning around 600 square kilometres.

The Houthis have previously targeted Ras Tanura, which has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, during the conflict.

The refinery forms part of a strategic complex on the kingdom's Gulf coast facing Iran, through which the country exported most of its oil before the Israel-US war on Iran started on 28 February.

Since then, Saudi Arabia has had to send some of its oil through Yanbu on the west coast along the Red Sea, which receives oil via the East-West pipeline and has also faced attacks.

Separately, Houthi spokesman Saree had also said the group had attacked Riyadh's financial district in three phases.

Saudi civil defence said a strike on Tuesday wounded 11 people at a tower in Riyadh’s financial district. The tallest building in the capital, the tower houses the headquarters of the Public Investment Fund, the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the tower in less than a week.

The first, on 19 November, damaged the building but caused no injuries. Saudi civil defence posted an image on Tuesday of the landmark tower showing some damage about halfway up the facade, similar to the impact of last week's attack.

articles.title: Jeremy Corbyn and Rashida Tlaib join politicians and legal groups condemning Ulm 5 prosecution
articles.summary:
Jeremy Corbyn and Rashida Tlaib join politicians and legal groups condemning Ulm 5 prosecution

Submitted by
Katherine Hearst
on
Wed, 11/25/2026 - 13:02

Two letters signed by 26 politicians and 31 legal groups demand the 'immediate release' of defendants in Germany

The 'Ulm Five' from left to right: Daniel Tatlow-Devally, Zo Hailu, Crow Tricks, Vi Kovarbasic and Leandra Rollo (supplied)

Off

Jeremy Corbyn and Rashida Tlaib are among dozens of politicians and legal organisations raising alarm over the prosecution and treatment of pro-Palestine activists in Germany.

Two letters issued on Wednesday, signed by 26 politicians and 31 legal groups from across the globe, condemned the treatment of five activists who have been held in pretrial detention for over 14 months.

Daniel Tatlow-Devally, Zo Hailu, Crow Tricks, Vi Kovarbasic and Leandra Rollo, who are from Germany, Spain, Ireland and the UK, were arrested on 8 September following an alleged break-in at the premises of Israeli arms firm Elbit Systems in the southwestern German city of Ulm.

Known as the “Ulm Five”, the group is accused of damaging the building's glass facade and smashing office equipment, including computers, screens and telephones.

In addition to charges of trespass and damage to property, the five are accused of "membership of a criminal organisation", namely Palestine Action Germany, under Section 129 of the German penal code.

The legislation is typically used to target organised crime networks and carries a potential sentence of up to five years in prison.

All the defendants have been held in prolonged pretrial detention, where they report facing restrictive conditions.

Under Section 129, suspects can be held for up to six months before trial, though lawyers say this period has now been significantly extended.

In their letter, the elected officials - including members of the German Bundestag, the European Parliament, the US Congress, the Irish Parliament and other legislatures across Europe and the Americas - called for the activists’ “immediate release”.

They further warned that the implications of their prosecution and treatment extend beyond the five defendants, forming “part of an international effort to discipline opposition to war and to place the interests of arms manufacturers above the rights of peoples and the obligations of international law”.

'Politically inconvenient facts'

Meanwhile, a separate letter signed by 33 legal groups - including the Center for Constitutional Rights, the Punjab Bar Council, European Democratic Lawyers, the American Association of Jurists, the Irish Council for Civil Liberties, the German Association of Democratic Lawyers - warned that the conduct of the trial could constitute a breach of German and international law.

In particular, the letter raises concerns about the courtroom’s security arrangements, which it said obstruct confidential communication between the defendants and their lawyers and could undermine the presumption of justice.

MEE previously reported that the trial, which began on 27 April, is taking place at a high security courtroom in the notorious Stammheim complex.

The defence team has repeatedly protested their clients’ treatment during proceedings, where the defendants are handcuffed and seated behind a glass barrier, preventing confidential communication with their lawyers.

The legal groups also challenged the court’s rejection of multiple applications by defence lawyers to hear expert witnesses. 

MEE previously reported that the court refused to hear weapons expert Dr Shir Hever and international law expert Isabel Feichtner, who were presented by the defence team to give evidence regarding Elbit Systems’ role in Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Germany’s obligations under international law.

The organisations further rejected the use of Section 129 against the defendants, insisting that “the prosecution of specific acts of property damage must not be conflated with the criminalisation of a political protest movement”.

"A criminal trial must establish the relevant facts impartially," they urged. "It must not exclude politically inconvenient facts merely because they concern the conduct of a powerful arms manufacturer or the actions of a state in an ongoing armed conflict".

Rutte believes Trump is putting Putin to the test
articles.summary:
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has defended US President Donald Trump's approach to Vladimir Putin, saying Trump is putting the Kremlin leader to the test.

Source: German news agency dpa, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Speaking ahead of a Wednesday meeting with Trump at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida, Rutte stated that Trump is putting Putin to the test, including during their talks in Shenzhen last week.

Rutte noted that Trump is asking: "Is he willing to come to the negotiating table? Is he willing to really engage in talks?"

The NATO secretary general emphasised that this pressure must be kept up.

"I think it is working, and we have to keep that going," he added.

Background:

On 19 November, ahead of the trilateral meeting in China, Trump entered the hall in Shenzhen accompanied by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. As he entered, Trump smiled, pointed at Putin and said: "Who is that? He's my friend." Trump then shook Putin's hand.

At the same press conference, Trump stated that the Kremlin leader had assured him that he wants to end the war with Ukraine through diplomacy. He also said that Putin is "having a hard time right now" because of the war he started against Ukraine.

articles.title: "Vicious circle": Ukraine says situation around Starshield remains unresolved
articles.summary:
Denys Sienik, Chargé d'Affaires of Ukraine to the United States, has stated that the situation surrounding restrictions on the operation of the Starshield system remains unresolved.

Source: Sienik on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda

Details: The Ukrainian diplomat noted that the longer the issue goes unresolved, the higher the chance it will slowly drop off the radar of officials authorised to fix it.

"The Starshield restrictions in Ukraine have created a vicious circle: neither of the key stakeholders has been able to clarify who made the decision to impose these limitations," Sienik noted.

According to him, Ukraine cannot treat a disruption to a vital system like Starshield as just another passing incident and forget about it.

"This issue must remain on the agenda until it is fully resolved," the diplomat stressed.

Sienik emphasised that the abrupt limitations, introduced over a week ago with no advance notice, have put Ukrainian civilians at further risk.

"Every day these limitations remain in place creates real risks and potentially devastating consequences for people on the ground," Sienik added.

Russia is continuing to ramp up its drone manufacturing and sends thousands of UAVs against Ukraine each week, he emphasised.

"At a time when the scale and intensity of these attacks are growing, any disruption to a capability that helps protect Ukrainian lives is a matter of the utmost urgency. We simply cannot afford to let this issue fade away," the diplomat concluded.

Background:

On 12 November, Zelenskyy said that the Ukrainian military had been experiencing significant disruptions to Starshield for several days.

He later said SpaceX told the Ukrainian Defence Ministry that it has not imposed any restrictions on Starshield operations and that the problem is technical in nature.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump claimed he had not heard about restrictions on Starlink operations in Ukraine.

On 23 November, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that disruptions to the Starlink and Starshield satellite systems in Ukraine require a clear explanation.

articles.title: Russians' tactics remain unchanged: they strike power lines and substations, we repair them – Zelenskyy
articles.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated on 25 November that Russia's tactics in striking energy infrastructure remain unchanged: to complicate the transmission of electricity from generation facilities.

Source: President Zelenskyy's evening address

Quote: "Wherever Russian strikes have occurred, repair crews and energy companies are currently working. The most difficult situation right now is in Dnipro, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast and Zaporizhzhia. The necessary equipment and resources for restoration are available everywhere, and that is very important.

Repairs have to be interrupted due to the threat of more and more strikes, but our people often do simply impossible, incredible things and work as needed to restore electricity to everyone.

The Russians' tactics are unchanged: they are striking power lines, grids and substations specifically to complicate the transmission of electricity from generation facilities. We are repairing them. And we will respond to Russia for every strike – and we will respond appropriately."

Details: The head of state also thanked the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, who struck a Russian military airfield with drones.

Quote: "The very one from which their aircraft take off to destroy lives in Ukraine. We are currently confirming the exact damage the Russians sustained this time. We will continue delivering our responses to them. Russian aircraft, Russian warships and vessels transporting Russian weapons are our completely legitimate targets."

articles.title: Hungarian PM Magyar says Zelenskyy gave him gift honouring his great-grandfather
articles.summary:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has revealed details of a gift presented to him by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during his visit to Zakarpattia.

Source: Péter Magyar on Facebook, as reported by European Pravda

Details: The Hungarian prime minister recalled that he has repeatedly spoken about his great-grandfather Lajos Erőss, who worked during the Second World War as chief secretary of the village of Rosvyhovo, now the suburbs of Mukachevo.

In memory of this, the Ukrainian president presented Magyar with an August 1942 issue of the now-defunct Zakarpattia weekly newspaper Az Őslakó, which published a notice announcing the hiring of the Hungarian prime minister's great-grandfather.

Magyar called the gift a "true family heirloom".

He wrote that it goes without saying how much such a personal gift means in terms of protocol.

In turn, Magyar presented Zelenskyy with a painting of Mukachevo Castle by Attila Kopriva, an artist of Hungarian descent from Zakarpattia, as well as a book by Kyiv-based artist, restorer and researcher Árpád István Magyar titled Hungarians in Kyiv: Chapters from the History of Hungarian-Ukrainian Relations from the 9th Century to the Present Day.

Background:

On 24 November, Magyar made his first visit to Ukraine as Hungary's prime minister and met President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Zakarpattia.

There, the Hungarian prime minister announced an aid package for Zakarpattia Oblast, which included medical equipment, generators and vehicles.

According to Magyar, Ukraine has pledged to speed up the process and implement these rights by the end of June 2027 – six months earlier than envisaged in the European Commission's roadmaps.

articles.title: Value of frozen Russian assets in Switzerland rises to over US$10bn
articles.summary:
The value of Russian assets frozen in Switzerland has risen to CHF 8.5 billion (US$10.2 billion).

Source: Bloomberg

Details: This figure represents a 15% increase compared with April 2025, when it stood at CHF 7.4 billion (US$8.9 billion). The rise is due to more assets being frozen and an increase in the value of some gold reserves.

According to Daniel Aeby, Head of Sanctions at Switzerland's State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), the total volume of Central Bank of Russia assets fell by 9% to CHF 6.8 billion (US$8.2 billion) compared with 18 months earlier. These funds were not unfrozen, but the assets were held in a basket of currencies that depreciated.

Aeby also said SECO had received more than 870 reports of suspected sanctions evasion, compared with 600 such cases a year and a half ago.

In early November, Switzerland joined the EU's 21st package of sanctions against Russia and Belarus.

Background: Switzerland joined the EU's restrictive measures against Russia following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. This step marked a softening of Switzerland's traditional policy of neutrality.

articles.title: Ukraine and Hungary to hold first meeting of minority rights commission in early 2027
articles.summary:
Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration, and Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán will co-chair a Ukrainian-Hungarian commission on the rights of national minorities in Ukraine, with its first meeting planned for early 2027.

Source: European Pravda, citing a post by Anita Orbán on X (Twitter)

Details: The Hungarian-Ukrainian intergovernmental commission will work on the issue of national minority rights in Ukraine, regarding which Hungary has a number of demands.

Quote: "The relaunch of the Commission will provide an important opportunity to address outstanding bilateral issues and explore new areas of cooperation. I look forward to our joint work and to building a mutually beneficial partnership between Hungary and Ukraine based on respect and trust."

Details: The relaunch of the commission became possible after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar discussed a 10-point plan on national minority rights to be implemented by Ukraine.

During a visit to Zakarpattia on 24 November, Péter Magyar said he hopes to continue providing humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, but he does not support the inclusion of funding for Ukraine in the European Union's seven-year budget.

articles.title: Ukraine shoots down Russian jet-powered Geran drone with combat laser for first time – video
articles.summary:
A Russian jet-powered Geran-type drone has been shot down with a combat laser in Ukraine for the first time.

Source: Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, a radio technology expert and adviser to the president of Ukraine

Details: According to Beskrestnov, the drone was hit by a Blysk laser air defence system developed by the Ukrainian company Carmine Sky. The system was being used to protect a critical infrastructure facility. Beskrestnov said this is the first confirmed downing of a jet-powered Geran by a combat laser.

Quote: "Several companies in Ukraine are working on developing lasers for air defence. Laser technologies are very complex and expensive, so it is gratifying when someone has good news. At the moment it is too early to talk about mass-producing lasers. Trials are underway, and lasers are protecting critical infrastructure facilities during these trials."

Details: According to Beskrestnov, anti-drone laser systems are being developed within a private air defence project and the Brave1 defence tech cluster, among other initiatives.

Background:

Ukraine's General Staff recently reported that during October 2026, Ukraine's defence forces downed or jammed 4,859 of the 6,473 Shahed-type strike drones that Russia used to attack Ukraine.

The Ukrainian company SpaceRay has developed the SpaceRay SA handheld tracking and targeting system for mobile air defence fire groups, which uses laser designation to engage targets.

articles.title: Head of Zelenskyy's office says prisoner swap could take place in late November or early December
articles.summary:
Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, has said that a prisoner exchange between Ukraine and Russia could take place in late November or early December.

Source: Budanov at the Dialogue for Unity event, as reported by Novyny Live

Details: Budanov said the planned exchange could involve more than 1,000 people. He noted that preparations are already underway and the process is being coordinated with the Russian side.

"These are some more or less realistic dates when the first prisoners of war should be brought back," he said.

Budanov explained that it will not be possible to bring back that number of people in a single exchange.

"We will carry this out, but in several stages – that is, several hundred people at a time, in several stages. It is unlikely that this can be done in one day," he said.

Ukraine is also working on options for humanitarian missions to evacuate civilians from temporarily occupied territories. Budanov added that he is personally overseeing this effort. For now, the plans concern the occupied parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts.

Background:

Following a meeting with US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on 12 November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that the "largest-ever" prisoner exchange with Russia would take place.

Zelenskyy did not specify the number of prisoners involved, but he had previously said that the possibility of a 1,000-for-1,000 or 1,500-for-1,500 exchange had been discussed.

On 17 November, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would pass on its proposals for the prisoner swap to the US, following an agreement reached in Abu Dhabi during a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, the US and Russia.

On 19 November, Zelenskyy expressed hope that Ukraine would receive lists of Russian prisoners of war for an exchange within the coming weeks.

On 25 November, Dmytro Usov, Secretary of the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, visited a camp where Russian prisoners of war are held and said Ukraine is ready to carry out the next exchange.

Parts of the city of Dnipro and four districts of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast have been left without electricity following another Russian attack on energy infrastructure.

Quote: "Main power grids have been damaged. Parts of Dnipro and the Dnipro, Pavlohrad, Synelnykove and Samar districts have been left without power."

Details: DTEK promised that energy workers will begin restoration work as soon as the security situation allows. Electricity will first be restored to critical infrastructure facilities.

Background:

Russian forces repeatedly damaged the region's energy infrastructure, cutting off electricity to people whose supply had just been restored following a widespread outage.

In Poltava Oblast, a Russian UAV struck an energy facility, injuring three people.

A Russian attack on Mykolaiv Oblast has cut off electricity to 85 settlements in the Mykolaiv district.

A Russian attack has left some consumers in two districts of Odesa without electricity.

On the morning of 25 November, power outages were recorded in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa and Kharkiv oblasts following Russian attacks. The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant switched to diesel generator power.

A thermal power plant belonging to DTEK has ceased electricity generation following a massive Russian attack that significantly damaged its equipment.

articles.title: Ukrainian border guards repel Russian mechanised assault in northern Kharkiv Oblast – video

When the occupiers' armoured group moved forward, it was met by the coordinated efforts of our strike drone operators, artillery personnel and infantry."

https://www.youtube.com/embed/Sai54Ff9NYQ?feature=oembed

articles.title: Poland says NATO refuses to shoot down drones over Ukraine due to "numerous complications"
articles.summary:
Poland has said that NATO did not support a proposal to shoot down drones over Ukraine, as this would entail "numerous complications".

Source: European Pravda, citing Polish radio station RMF24

Details: Polish Deputy Minister of National Defence Cezary Tomczyk noted that discussions on countering Russian targets over Ukrainian territory have been ongoing for several months. However, the Alliance does not support such a proposal.

Tomczyk said NATO does not back the idea in any way, noting that it would create numerous complications.

According to him, previous talks concluded with a decision that such a procedure is "impossible".

Implementing such a decision would require Ukraine's consent, including providing warnings and granting allies access to Ukrainian airspace. However, a unanimous decision by all NATO members would be crucial.

Background:

Bloomberg reported that Poland has appealed to its allies to consider the possibility of bringing down Russian missiles over Ukraine when they are heading towards NATO territory.

The request came after three Russian missiles violated Polish airspace during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine.

The Polish government plans to introduce a no-fly zone in the east of the country at the end of this year or the beginning of next year.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces thwart Russian assault south of Dobropillia – video
articles.summary:
Ukrainian forces have successfully thwarted a Russian assault involving two armoured vehicles and an infantry group south of Dobropillia in Donetsk Oblast.

Source: statement by the 25th Sicheslav Airborne Brigade

Quote: "On the southern outskirts of the settlement of Dobropillia, Sicheslav paratroopers of the 7th Air Assault Corps, together with adjacent units, thwarted an assault by the occupiers.

Taking advantage of difficult weather conditions, the enemy attempted to attack our positions with a force of 11 soldiers supported by two armoured vehicles. The adversary failed to break through the forward line of defence.

The enemy was confident that in such weather conditions with strong winds, no drones could be in the air. They were mistaken."

https://www.facebook.com/plugins/video.php?height=314&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.facebook.com%2Freel%2F1110291945160372%2F&show_text=false&width=560&t=0

Details: The brigade reported that the movement of the Russian column was detected in advance by a patrol crew of FPV drones, which delivered the initial strike.

Quote: "The occupiers regrouped into the other armoured vehicle and attempted to continue advancing towards Dobropillia, but the vehicle hit a minefield. The surviving infantry dispersed into the nearest tree line."

Background: On 20 October, Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Ukrainian President's Office, said that the city of Dobropillia in Donetsk Oblast remains under Ukrainian control, but a Russian general has deliberately misled Russian leader Vladimir Putin by claiming it has been captured.

articles.title: Six injured, including child, in Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia – photos
articles.summary:
Six people, including a child, have been injured in a Russian attack on a residential area and the grounds of a motor transport company in Zaporizhzhia's Kosmichnyi district.

Source: Mykhailo Semikin, acting head of Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration, on Telegram

Update: Semikin initially reported one person injured, but later added that another five people had been injured.

The aftermath of the Russian attack
Photo: Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration

Quote: "Another five people, including a child, have been injured in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia's Kosmichnyi district."

The aftermath of the Russian attack
Photo: Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration

Details: Semikin said the Russians damaged around 10 houses, a warehouse building and cars. A fire broke out on the premises of a motor transport company. All those injured are receiving medical assistance.

Background: Six people were injured and residential buildings and cars were damaged in a Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia on the morning of 25 November.

Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Self-proclaimed Belarusian president denies that he knew Russian forces would advance on Kyiv from Belarus in 2022
articles.summary:
Self-proclaimed Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko has claimed he did not know in 2022 that Russian forces would launch an offensive on Kyiv from Belarusian territory.

Source: Lukashenko in an interview with the French magazine Le Point, a video of which was cited by Belarusian media outlet BelTA

Details: The journalist asked why he acted as an ally to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin in 2022 and provided Belarusian territory as a staging ground for Russian troops. Lukashenko responded that this was "entirely inaccurate phrasing".

He then produced a map of Belarus and began claiming that he was unaware of Russia's plans.

Quote: "We were no staging ground for an attack on Ukraine. Look, I even brought a map of the country. There were military exercises between Belarus and Russia in the Brest and Homiel oblasts – scheduled drills in 2022. The Americans were already shouting that a war might start and warning Ukraine that troops were massing there. I, for instance, did not believe that could happen.

The Russians began withdrawing their troops back to Russia by rail [along the border with Ukraine – ed.]. Then these troops [which had already been concentrated in the Homiel Oblast – ed.] for some reason turned towards Kyiv and decided to withdraw via Kyiv. I say that jokingly. There are no grievances against me. I have absolutely nothing to do with this war.

I did not know about the start of the war, and the Russian General Staff did not inform me of it."

Details: Meanwhile, Lukashenko expressed bewilderment as to why he should have stopped the Russians.

Quote: "Why should I have stopped the Russians and fought for Ukraine? Ukraine was already in a state of war with Belarus."

Background:

In 2022, Lukashenko claimed in Moscow that "Ukraine was preparing to attack the joint forces of the Russian Federation and the Republic of Belarus on Belarussian territory".

He also asserted that an attack on Belarus was allegedly being prepared from four directions.

During the interview, Lukashenko offered to act as a "security guarantor" for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and fly to Moscow together.

In response, Zelenskyy invited Lukashenko and Putin to Kyiv.

articles.title: Three injured in Russian drone strike on energy facility in Poltava Oblast
articles.summary:
A Russian drone has struck an energy facility in Poltava Oblast, injuring three people.

Source: Vitalii Diakivnych, Head of Poltava Oblast Military Administration

Quote: "An enemy drone strike on an energy facility has been recorded in the Poltava district. Early reports indicate that one person has been injured."

Details: Diakivnych later reported that the number of people injured had risen to three.

Local news outlet Poltavshchyna reported that at 14:54, unofficial monitoring channels had warned of a Russian drone threat to Poltava, Shcherbany and Suprunivka, and also reported that air defence systems were operating.

An explosion was heard shortly afterwards in Poltava, as confirmed by Kateryna Yamshchykova, Secretary of Poltava City Council.

The media outlet adds that overnight, a Russian drone also struck the grounds of an industrial facility in the Poltava district, causing a fire.

Background:

A Russian attack on Mykolaiv Oblast has cut off electricity to 85 settlements in the Mykolaiv district.

A Russian attack has left some consumers in two districts of Odesa without electricity.

On the morning of 25 November, power outages were recorded in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Odesa and Kharkiv oblasts following Russian attacks. The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant switched to diesel generator power.

A thermal power plant belonging to DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, has ceased electricity generation following a massive Russian attack that significantly damaged its equipment.

articles.title: Poland plans to establish a no-fly zone near its border with Ukraine
articles.summary:
The Polish government is planning to introduce a no-fly zone in the east of the country along its border with Ukraine at the end of this year or the beginning of next year.

Source: European Pravda, citing Polish media outlet Interia Wydarzenia

Quote from Polish Deputy Minister of National Defence Cezary Tomczyk: "A no-fly zone is needed in the east of the country, extending a dozen to several dozen kilometres from the border. We want the relevant decree to enter into force at the end of December or the beginning of January."

Details: Interia Wydarzenia reported that this decision is linked to recent incidents involving Russian missiles and a drone violating Polish airspace.

Tomczyk noted that at present, protecting NATO's eastern flank is a "very important issue".

Quote: "All the programmes we are implementing – whether it is the East Shield project or protecting Polish airspace with fighter jets – are a guarantee of our security."

Details: The deputy minister also recalled that two months ago, Poland changed its response procedures for aerial targets in its airspace.

Quote: "In practice, in peacetime across NATO, visual identification is required to bring down a foreign assets or means of air attack. In pre-war conditions, in critical circumstances – which is precisely what we are living in now – this has lost its meaning, so Polish pilots, at the request of the Operational Commander, General Nowak, switched to so-called positive identification."

Details: In practice, this means that a pilot must "gather a set of indicators" and, on that basis, carry out identification before destroying the target.

Background:

Three Russian missiles violated Polish airspace during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine on 20 November.

Debris from Kh-101 cruise missiles was found in three locations: Nowy Lipowiec (Lublin Voivodeship), Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz in Podkarpackie (Subcarpathian) Voivodeship.

Following this, the Russian ambassador in Warsaw "received a very sharp diplomatic note" from Poland's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. However, he dismissed the Polish ministry's accusations as groundless and a manifestation of "Russophobia".

Additionally, overnight on 23-24 November, a drone flew into Poland's airspace.

Bloomberg reported that Poland has appealed to its allies to consider the possibility of bringing down Russian missiles over Ukraine when they are heading towards NATO territory.

articles.title: Russian drone damages Dovzhenko Film Studio hostel in Kyiv – video, photos
articles.summary:
A Russian attack on Kyiv damaged the hostel and accommodation building of the National Oleksandr Dovzhenko Film Studio overnight on 24-25 November.

Source: Dovzhenko Film Studio

Details: A Russian drone crashed near the building. The blast wave shattered all the windows from the ground to the eighth floor. None of the residents were injured.

Dovzhenko Film Studio noted that the building is home to veterans, former studio employees and cultural figures. Staff are currently documenting the damage and working to assist the residents using their own resources.

https://www.facebook.com/plugins/post.php?href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.facebook.com%2Fdovzhenkofilmstudios%2Fposts%2Fpfbid0hr6dxSYKwvFVDMyx4aFHjdJqw3DZpXzpAJj7P86dx9cfRXJQQ2jubXbWXVoWa12wl&show_text=true&width=500

Background:

Since the beginning of 2026, the film studio has repeatedly sustained damage as a result of Russian attacks.

In particular, on 2 and 15 June, missile strikes damaged 18 studio buildings, including historic soundstages, an office building, the film archive and utility networks.

The studio suffered its greatest losses during the 15 June attack, when a Russian missile destroyed the costume department. It housed one of the largest collections of film costuming in Ukraine. Some of the unique costumes survived because they were on loan to museums and exhibitions at the time of the strike.

In July, emergency repair work began at the film studio. However, on 7 October, it was damaged once again by Russian attacks – missile debris damaged the roofs of the sixth and seventh soundstages, sparking a fire.

articles.title: "She was the guardian of her family": woman injured in Russian strike on central Kryvyi Rih dies in hospital
articles.summary:
Svitlana Kuropiatnik, who was injured in a Russian attack on central Kryvyi Rih on 20 November, has died in hospital. Doctors fought to save her life for five days but were unable to save her.

Source: Oleksandr Vilkul, Head of Kryvyi Rih Defence Council

Details: The 57-year-old Svitlana sustained multiple injuries during the Russian ballistic missile attack on Kryvyi Rih. Her injuries proved fatal.

Svitlana Popova, the deceased woman's close friend, told Suspilne Dnipro that Svitlana was celebrating a friend's birthday at a venue in the city centre on 20 November. At the time of the attack, Svitlana was standing by the restaurant's entrance and was thrown back by the blast wave.

"Svitlana was about to return to the dining area when the strike happened. Other guests were injured too. Svitlana was among the most seriously injured: she lost consciousness and had a head injury. She underwent surgery that very night.

Yesterday [24 November – ed.], my daughter and I visited Svitlana. We thought she could hear us. Svitlana moved her hand and her leg a little, as if she wanted to say something. Sadly, she never regained consciousness. Her heart stopped this morning," her close friend said.

She added that Svitlana was a kind-hearted and sincere person who was always ready to help.

"She was the guardian of her family; she had inherited that from her mother. Her family was the most important thing [to her]. [Svitlana] adored flowers, loved to spend time at her summer house, cook and have guests over," Svitlana Popova recalled.

Svitlana is survived by her husband Vitalii, to whom she had been married for more than 30 years, her daughter Yuliia, her son Vladyslav and two granddaughters.

Svitlana Kuropiatnik's funeral will take place in Kryvyi Rih on 26 November.

Background:

On 20 November, Russia attacked the city centre with ballistic missiles. During the rescue operation, three more jet-powered Shahed drones struck medics and rescue workers.

A female paramedic and a seven-year-old boy were killed, and another 47 people were injured, including six children.

Vilkul has reported that 15 people, including one child, are currently treated in hospital. Three of them are in a serious condition and are receiving the necessary medical care.

articles.title: Recent sinking of Russian vessels abroad shows the Russia-Ukraine war has officially gone global
articles.summary:
Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world. Ukrainian forces disabled a Russian cargo vessel off the coast of Finland, and sunk a Russian corvette, the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters.

These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies.

The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A stagnant battlefront, increased Russian aerial attacks and a recalcitrant American president have increased the burdens on Ukraine’s government and its people.

Russia hasn’t had a good year either. More than 400,000 Russians have been killed in the war — and potentially as many as 700,000.

For Ukraine to have any chance of winning, it must increase the pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it.

The international dimension

Since its outset, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has had an international dimension. Ukraine’s allies, both prior to and after Russia’s full-fledged invasion in 2022, rushed supplies to Ukraine in its moment of need.

Providing aid to Ukraine has continued for the past four years, despite disruptions caused by United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in the negotiation process.

The supplies provided by Ukraine’s allies are critical to its success. While the fighting is conducted by the Ukrainian people and Ukraine has increased domestic arms production, outside supplies are crucial in a number of areas — notably, air defence.

Equally important is the economic aid Ukraine’s allies have and continue to provide the country. Given the size differential between Russia and Ukraine and how hard the war has hit the Ukrainian economy, economic aid allows Ukraine to provide basic services to its citizens.

Initially, Russia did not court outside support to the same extent as Ukraine, as it believed it would achieve a rapid victory over its adversary. Once the reality of the conflict became clear, Russia turned to the international community for support.

That support has taken many forms. Iran and North Korea have been among Russia’s top supporters, providing drones and soldiers.

Other countries, most notably China, have provided an economic lifeline to Russia, allowing it access to their markets in an effort to stave off the worst impacts of the economic sanctions Ukraine’s allies have imposed on the Russians.

Countries in Central Asia and the Middle East have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials.

Targeting support

In a conflict that is increasingly defined by attrition, it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of industrialized warfare and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own.

Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has reached an equilibrium. In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting.

For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict.

The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent.

Ukraine has focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws. The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that the West has flouted international norms for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South.

Russia has put forward several narratives to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine.

Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains in Africa and earning support among far-right European parties.

Narrative campaigns, however, typically unfold over a long time frame. As both Ukraine and Russia seek immediate ways to boost morale and undermine their adversary, direct military operations abroad have become all the more significant.

Read more:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s removal of two top defence officials highlights the role of morale in long wars

Attacking the secure ‘rear’

In military terms, the rear is the area furthest from the enemy and ideally secure from military threat. For both Ukraine and Russia, this area has been other countries.

While Russia and Ukraine cannot attack the assets of other countries directly, they can and do engage in espionage against other countries.

For Russia, these efforts have focused on destabilizing Europe using drones and other assets via attacks that that are easily deniable. Russia also seeks to create pressure through violating European air space. The more Russia destabilizes Europe, Ukraine’s primary ally, the better its chances in the conflict.

For Ukraine, Russia’s aspirations to be a so-called Great Power mean its network is global — so Ukrainian special operation forces and intelligence agencies strike at Russian assets abroad where possible. These range from attacks in nearby areas, like the Baltics, to Africa and beyond.

Read more:
Putin wanted to make Russia great again. Instead, Ukraine is the new rising power in Europe

While news agencies view this development as widening the conflict, and the United Nations may wish to prevent the conflict from going global, the reality is it’s been a global conflict since before 2022.

The strikes in Libya and the Baltic, and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediate acknowledgement of Ukraine’s role, is just making it public.

James Horncastle does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Climate diplomacy is stuck – these three big changes would get it moving again
articles.summary:
The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, held in Antalya, Turkey, was being branded “possibly the worst Cop in history” even before its sorry conclusion.

I was there, and the conference was badly managed from start to finish: initial traffic jams and queues sapped energy and goodwill, while the final plenary was one embarrassment after another, with the summit president sniping at the UN’s climate chief (to audible gasps from delegates), and the closing “Antalya pact” being comprehensively rejected.

This sad outcome was not merely the fault of the conference’s Turkish-Australian presidency, however. The bigger issue is that climate diplomacy is stuck – and has been for several years. Structural changes are required, three in particular.

1. Climate finance is not an optional extra

First, climate finance – money provided to developing countries to help them tackle climate change – has to be increased, in particular public, grant-based finance from developed states.

This may seem an odd place to start for those weaned on the mainstream western media, where most accounts of Cop31’s failure focused on the stand off over fossil fuels. But climate finance is not an optional extra under the Paris agreement: it is the glue that holds the entire arrangement together. Ensuring adequate finance flows is one of the agreement’s three main stated aims (alongside limiting global temperature rises and supporting adaptation). And these flows are meant to progressively increase in line with mitigation ambitions and adaptation needs.

But in recent years they have not. At Cop29 in Baku, an ambitious new finance goal was planned. But instead, the conference saw a pushed-through decision that failed to offer the “progression beyond previous efforts” required by Paris and drew widespread condemnation from developing states. Nigeria termed the deal “an insult” to the UN Climate Convention.

Actual country pledges and disbursements have been falling short too. This year has seen a 70% drop in total developed country finance pledges. Meanwhile, the UK is cutting its development assistance to 0.3% of gross national income, while halving its climate finance.

The consequences have been profound. By no coincidence, within a year of the finance debacle in Baku the other side of the global climate bargain had unravelled too. The 2025 round of national mitigation plans were barely more ambitious than their previous iterations, mostly late, and collectively non-compliant with the goals of the Paris agreement.

For many developing countries, inadequate climate finance was one of the biggest frustrations at Cop31.
Rehman Asad / Shutterstock

Cop31 continued this pattern. On the conference’s eve, EU Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra declared the prospects for additional climate finance “dead in the water”. New developed world pledges for the Adaptation Fund, which helps countries prepare for and cope with the effects of climate change, totalled just US$50 million, less than half the cost of a single F-35 fighter jet.

The predictable result was deadlock on most key negotiation tracks. Indeed, for many developing countries, as well as NGOs, it was above all this climate finance issue – and not the question of whether “fossil fuels” should be named or not – that most underpinned their rejection of the Antalya pact.

The lesson should be clear: to unblock future climate summits, vastly improved finance offerings will be needed from developed countries. And that means that money will have to be diverted from elsewhere, including from the US$2.9 trillion being spent globally on militaries and war.

2. Climate coalitions need to become alliances

More money will not be enough though. Sharper political strategies are also needed, ones that are appropriate to a geopolitically fractured world and to tackling fossil fuel interests.

Cop30 in Belém, Brazil, brought a big step forward on this, with its recognition that “coalitions of the willing” are needed to overcome the UN’s consensus rules. Right now, these rules effectively give fossil fuel-dependent countries a veto on meaningful action. This led to a new process explicitly focused on “transitioning away from fossil fuels”, which began with a 57-country summit in Santa Marta, Colombia, in early 2026.

The risk, though, is that such coalitions just become new talking shops, and lack teeth. The “national roadmaps” that countries in the Santa Marta coalition are producing seem to illustrate this: the first wave of published roadmaps contains not a single new major policy commitment.

But other coalitions show us what might be possible. On the greenhouse gas methane (the focus of my current research), a powerful network of international partnerships, NGOs, funders and regulatory initiatives has transformed policy and practice over the last five years.

And building on the EU’s world-leading methane regulation, this coalition is now constructing a global marketplace that rewards cleaner producers with preferential market access, in order to help drive down methane emissions.

To really work, however, both this and other such coalitions will need commitment, regulation and enforcement. Voluntary initiatives will not be enough. And over time, such ad hoc “climate clubs” will need to transform into something much firmer – binding, treaty-based climate alliances.

3. Public pressure and protest matter

Last, it should be stressed that progress in international climate politics is not the responsibility of diplomats alone. Whatever they achieve, or do not, always reflects diverse lobbying and social pressures.

And sadly, on this front there has been a sharp regression. Since a peak in 2020, mass climate activism has largely died out. Media coverage of climate change has declined worldwide. And, spurred on by the Trump administration and war, fossil fuel interests are ascendant.

These things will only be changed through education, mobilisation and a widespread taking to the streets.

As Tasneem Essop, executive director of the NGO Climate Action Network, put it during an early Cop31 press conference: “We cannot give up on multilateralism … But if we can’t win back home, we cannot expect to win things in this space.”

Jan Selby receives funding from the European Research Council. He is a member of the Green Party of England and Wales.

articles.title: The efficiency paradox: why greener AI means more waste
articles.summary:
Data centres are getting bigger and more abundant, not necessarily more efficient. cflaten/Shutterstock

AI is increasingly being promoted as a solution to climate change. It can help companies use less fuel, reduce waste and make production more efficient.

For example, AI can help delivery companies plan more efficient routes, reducing the fuel they use and the emissions they produce. Similar savings could be made across other industries and transport networks, potentially reducing the overall environmental impact. But greater efficiency can also encourage more consumption.

AI is being promoted as a climate solution and as a driver of competitiveness, productivity and economic growth. The World Trade Organization estimates that the widespread adoption of AI could increase global trade by around 40% by 2040. This is generally presented as a benefit.

But there is an obvious contradiction here. If AI makes firms more efficient and profitable, it encourages further investment and expansion. Successful firms do not use productivity gains to produce less, but to expand and to make greater profits.

When these dynamics are generalised across the economy, the result is more production, transportation, resource extraction, consumption and ultimately more environmental destruction.

This is capitalism’s efficiency paradox, known as the Jevons paradox. According to William Stanley Jevons, a 19th-century English economist, any increase in resource efficiency generates an increase in long-term resource consumption, rather than a decrease.

Read more:
DeepSeek claims to have cured AI’s environmental headache. The Jevons paradox suggests it might make things worse

New technologies can help businesses produce more goods using less energy, materials and labour. But by making production cheaper and faster, they can also encourage businesses to make and sell more, increasing the total amount of resources that people use.

Industrial efficiency gains have been a defining feature of capitalism since the Industrial Revolution. Steam-powered textile mills and coal mines in the late 18th century, the Bessemer steel process (making steel by blowing air through molten iron) in the 19th century, and Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th all dramatically increased efficiency.

The industrial revolution has evolved as efficiency improved, from the development of coal mines in the 18th century to Henry Ford’s car assembly line in the 20th century.
Parilov/Shutterstock

Yet none of these efficiency gains reduced society’s overall consumption of resources. Rather, they underpinned successive waves of industrial expansion, fossil-fuel use and environmental degradation.

AI is no different.

My research shows how digital technologies provide a historical example of this dynamic.

For decades, improvements in computers, telecommunications and data storage have allowed companies to spread different stages of production across several countries. They can now use real-time digital networks to share information and coordinate manufacturing and trade around the world.

These technologies have made possible today’s highly integrated global supply chains, allowing firms to source components from thousands of suppliers and move goods across continents with extraordinary speed and precision.

The environmental consequences are immense.

Digital technologies have helped companies produce and sell more goods around the world. This has increased the demand for raw materials, pollution from transport and damage to the natural environment. International trade in goods is now linked to around 30% of threats to the world’s species

Rather than reversing these trends, AI is deepening them. It is making supply chains faster, more responsive and more geographically extensive. From a business perspective, this is progress. Environmentally, it accelerates ecological breakdown.

Cleaner technology, more fossil fuels

The same contradiction can be seen in the energy sector. Much discussion of AI and green technology assumes that cleaner technologies replace dirtier ones. Yet, as the historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz shows, new energy systems tend to accumulate on top of rather than substitute for each other.

Wood, coal, oil, gas and renewables have largely been added to one another rather than replacing one another. Green technologies are making fossil-fuel industries more efficient, rather than replacing them.

Many of the technologies being promoted as climate solutions, including AI, are actually accelerating the extraction of fossil fuels that is driving climate change.

In Guyana, since commercial oil production began in 2019, the country has become one of the world’s fastest-growing producers of oil, with targets to produce 1.3 million barrels per day by 2027. AI-enabled drilling and “geosteering” – the real-time adjustment of a well’s path to keep it within oil-bearing rock – are increasing the rate of oil extraction.

So, can a technology designed to increase productivity, competitiveness and growth solve a crisis rooted in relentless profit-oriented expansion of production and consumption on a finite planet? Until that question is confronted, greener AI is likely to make ecological destruction more efficient rather than bring it to an end.

Benjamin Selwyn works for the University of Sussex.

articles.title: Nicotine-free vaping may still harm blood vessels – small MRI study
articles.summary:
Alones/Shutterstock.com

A nicotine-free vape sounds like a safer choice. Yet new research found that just one session of vaping, with no nicotine in it, can affect how blood vessels work.

The study, which was presented at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America, identified changes in blood flow and oxygen levels following just one episode of vaping, regardless of whether the e-cigarette contained nicotine. The findings raise an important question. Have we been focusing too much on nicotine and not enough on what else we are inhaling?

E-cigarettes, commonly known as vapes, are battery-powered devices that heat a liquid to produce an aerosol vapour. Unlike conventional cigarettes, they do not burn tobacco, meaning users are exposed to fewer harmful chemicals.

The cloud that people inhale and exhale, however, is not simply water vapour. Most vaping liquids contain a mixture of propylene glycol, vegetable glycerine and flavouring chemicals. Although some of these ingredients are used in food production, eating a substance is not the same as inhaling it.

When heated, these liquids can produce potentially harmful chemicals, including formaldehyde and acrolein. Research has also identified tiny particles of metals, including nickel, chromium and lead, in vaping aerosols. Some originate from the metal coil used to heat the liquid. Simply removing the nicotine does not remove these substances.

What happens in blood vessels?

Blood vessels are more than a network of pipes transporting blood around the body. They are living structures that constantly adjust to the changing demands of our organs.

The inner lining of our blood vessels, known as the endothelium, produces a chemical called nitric oxide. This allows blood vessels to relax and widen, increasing blood flow when our tissues need more oxygen.

When we exercise, for example, blood vessels widen to deliver more oxygen to our working muscles. When this process becomes impaired, it is known as endothelial dysfunction, which is a very early feature of cardiovascular disease.

In the latest study, researchers recruited 41 otherwise healthy adults, aged between 20 and 50, who had smoked, vaped or used both products daily for more than a year. A further 17 people who had never smoked or vaped acted as a comparison (control) group.

Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), researchers examined participants before and after three separate activities: smoking a cigarette, vaping with nicotine and vaping without nicotine. They measured several aspects of cardiovascular health, including how effectively blood vessels responded to changing oxygen demands and the stiffness of the aorta, the largest artery in the body.

Following all three activities, researchers found a reduction in the amount of oxygen remaining in blood returning from the leg. This could suggest that vaping temporarily interferes with the ability to transfer oxygen in the lungs into the bloodstream, although changes in blood flow and oxygen use by tissues could also explain the findings.

Surprisingly, vaping affected more of the measurements investigated than smoking did. This does not mean that vaping is more harmful than smoking. But it does challenge the assumption that nicotine-free vaping is harmless.

Vape liquids contain propylene glycol, vegetable glycerine and flavouring chemicals.
Rawpixel/Shutterstock.com

These findings chime with earlier research. In a study published in 2019, 31 healthy non-smokers were exposed to nicotine-free vaping aerosol. After a single session, the ability of an artery in the leg to widen in response to increased blood flow was reduced by 34%.

A 2022 study also found that regular e-cigarette users and cigarette smokers had poorer blood vessel function than non-users.

More recently, research published in 2025 found that smoking and vaping can affect how well the blood vessels supplying the heart regulate blood flow. This means the vessels may be less able to increase the blood supply to the heart when it needs more oxygen, such as during exercise.

One possible explanation is oxidative stress, which occurs when the body produces more reactive molecules than it can get rid of. These molecules can reduce levels of nitric oxide and cause inflammation, which can damage blood vessels and contribute to heart disease.

However, not all studies agree. A clinical trial published in 2018 found changes in blood vessel function following vaping with nicotine, but not without it. Differences in vaping devices, ingredients and research methods may partly explain these conflicting findings.

The latest study involved relatively few people and looked only at short-term effects. It is still unclear whether repeated exposure causes lasting harm or increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

It is important not to overlook the benefits of vaping for people trying to stop smoking.

A large, well-conducted review found that nicotine-containing e-cigarettes were more effective at helping people quit smoking than nicotine replacement products such as patches and gum.

The NHS advises that vaping is less harmful than smoking but is not risk-free.

Nicotine-free vaping may remove the addictive ingredient, but it does not remove all the potential health risks. Being nicotine-free is not the same as being harm-free. And that is a distinction that should not be overlooked.

David C. Gaze does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Black Friday: consumer behaviour expert on what’s really behind our need to chase bargains
articles.summary:
vetre/Shutterstock

Black Friday is a highly successful US export. The retail strategy designed to kickstart festive shopping has become a global phenomenon.

But are the hype and the pressure (and the occasional fight over electrical hardware) worth it? After all, most products on offer during Black Friday are available at the same price (or even less) at other times of the year.

So why do so many people still join in? Here are some of the marketing tricks and psychological drivers that help to explain the appeal of Black Friday.

Marketing push

Offers that exist for a limited time period are among the oldest retail marketing tricks in the book. And there is plenty of research which shows that they reliably increase a shopper’s intention to buy.

If we think a deal will disappear after Black Friday, the fear of missing out on a bargain can push us towards buying that air fryer or scented candle. Or we might buy it to avoid the potential feelings of regret that may come if we don’t.

Price tags also have a big effect. Psychologists have shown that when making value judgments, the first number we see disproportionately shapes how we evaluate subsequent numbers.

So when a price tag reads: “"Was £100! Now £60!”, the £100 figure is the one we latch on to. This makes £60 feel like a £40 saving rather than a £60 expense, even if the item was never really worth £100 in the first place.

Consumer pull

While many people will be aware of these kinds of retail marketing tricks, they will still willingly participate in Black Friday. This may be partly due to its timing, but also to the psychological rewards that shopping could offer.

In the northern hemisphere at least, Black Friday coincides with the “winter blues”, potentially offering a source of excitement as the days get colder and darker. We may also shop to improve our mood with a little “retail therapy”.

One explanation for the effectiveness of retail therapy is that negative emotions often come from situations we cannot change. Making choices about what we want and then buying those things might help us to restore a feeling of personal control.

Another reason is that buying generally might bring more positive than negative emotions. But studies have also shown that the temporary uplift from purchasing does not last as long as we often think it will.

Landing a bargain can also make us feel good about ourselves. Being a “smart shopper” has been linked to a personal sense of achievement and pride when we secure a good deal. Buying things at a (genuine) discount can also demonstrate competence and good financial management to others.
