But that is not the only social appeal of Black Friday. Even the most independently minded consumer can be influenced by what other people do. And engaging in an activity at the same time as others, even among strangers, can temporarily enhance feelings of social connection.

What are we really buying?

Despite the thrill of a bargain, or joining in with a commercial social event, what feels rewarding in the moment may not necessarily contribute to our longer-term wellbeing.

Research in consumption has shown that spending money on things that fit our personality or that help us with personal goals might be a good idea. For example, an extrovert or someone looking to develop new connections will probably benefit more from spending money on social activities than buying a discounted item.

Read more:
Eight ways to resist spending too much on Black Friday bargains

But why we buy is as important as what we buy. In a recent study, my colleagues and I found that spending money in response to social pressure, to gain status or to seek others’ approval was linked to low wellbeing. So even experiences do not always bring more happiness.

Our expectations can also mislead us. In another study I worked on, my colleagues and I found that people thought that buying new clothes would make them feel better about themselves than buying second-hand clothes. But it turned out that buying old and new clothes had pretty much the same effect.

Stuff for sale.
Elena Rostunova/Shutterstock

More broadly, research shows that focusing on economic gains and consumption brings a lower sense of wellbeing and is detrimental to our personal relationships.

In contrast, choosing to live more simply or buying less is consistently linked with greater wellbeing. People who become less focused on material goals tend to become happier over time.

So perhaps Black Friday should not simply be about how much money we are saving or how much temporary joy our purchases might bring us. Maybe it’s a time to reflect on what we gain from spending more money on more stuff, and whether there might be more sustainable and lasting alternatives.

Olaya Moldes Andrés had received funding from the British Academy and the Academy of Marketing.

articles.title: GTA 6: four surprising ways playing video games could benefit your health
articles.summary:
Playing video games can offer opportunities to socialise, relieve stress and develop cognitive skills. Miljan Zivkovic/Shutterstock

After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, with fans around the world celebrating the latest instalment of one of gaming’s most successful franchises.

The excitement surrounding its release has also brought renewed attention to a familiar debate: what effect does playing video games have on us?

Gaming has long been associated with concerns about addiction and social isolation. But depending on what we play and how we engage with it, gaming can offer benefits for our cognitive abilities, social lives and physical and mental wellbeing.

1. Developing cognitive skills

Playing an action game such as Grand Theft Auto can be mentally demanding. Navigating a busy virtual city while driving, monitoring your surroundings and responding to unexpected events requires considerable attention and an ability to process information quickly.

A 2022 study of 163 adults compared regular action video game players, whose preferred games included Grand Theft Auto and Assassin’s Creed, with people who rarely or never played video games.

The gamers performed better on tests of mental rotation, the ability to imagine how an object would look if turned in a different direction. They were also more accurate at keeping track of multiple moving objects.

However, the researchers could not establish whether gaming had developed these abilities or whether people with stronger spatial and attentional skills were naturally drawn to action games.

A review of experimental studies found that playing action games could improve our ability to focus on relevant information while ignoring distractions, as well as our understanding of spatial relationships. These skills are useful in everyday activities such as navigating unfamiliar places.

However, researchers continue to debate how far the skills developed through gaming translate into broader improvements in our thinking and learning.

2. Building social connections

Despite the perception that gaming is an isolating activity, many modern games are designed around interaction with other people. Online multiplayer games allow players to communicate, collaborate and maintain friendships across geographical distances.

A study of 2,213 gamers and 287 non-gamers in Germany found that social gamers were generally as well connected as non-gamers, and that spending more time playing socially increased the likelihood of forming friendships online. These connections became particularly valuable during the COVID pandemic, when people had fewer opportunities to meet in person.

Some games also encourage players to work together towards a shared goal. In massively multiplayer online games, where large numbers of people play in the same virtual world, team members may need to plan their approach and share information.

For instance, research into team communication in the game World of Tanks found that higher-ranked teams tended to communicate more before battles, although this does not establish that gaming improves teamwork outside the game.

Of course, online gaming communities can expose players to harassment or abusive behaviour. The social experience depends on the game, its community and the people involved.

3. Promoting wellbeing and relieving stress

Gaming can be something to look forward to after a long day at work, offering a chance to relax and put everyday responsibilities aside.

Completing a difficult level or overcoming an obstacle can also satisfy our psychological need for competence: the feeling that we are capable of achieving something. Even an unsuccessful attempt gives players an opportunity to adjust their approach and try again.

Games often described as “cosy” are particularly appealing to people who prefer a slower pace, achievable goals and a relaxed atmosphere. My personal favourite is the Animal Crossing series, in which players live alongside animal characters and take on tasks such as gardening and crafting.

In interviews with 27 families, researchers found that Animal Crossing: New Horizons helped some parents and children cope with pandemic-related stress. The National Videogame Museum’s Animal Crossing Diaries collects players’ experiences of the game during the pandemic.

Some games are designed specifically for health or education rather than entertainment alone. Known as “serious games”, they can be used as part of mental health interventions. A review of therapeutic games for young people found promising effects on anxiety and depression, although more rigorous research is needed.

4. Encouraging physical activity

Not all gaming involves sitting still. “Exergames” incorporate physical movement into play, through activities such as dancing or sports simulations.

These games can make exercise more appealing to people who find conventional workouts less engaging. Research on virtual-reality exercise suggests that adding game elements can increase enjoyment during high-intensity interval training.

My favourite example of a game that encourages physical activity is Pokémon Go. It encourages players to walk around their neighbourhoods to collect digital creatures and visit locations, using augmented reality to add virtual objects to a view of the real world.

A study using fitness trackers found that the most engaged Pokémon Go players increased their activity by an average of nearly 1,500 steps a day over a month. Whether that increase lasts in the longer term is less clear.

Finding the right balance

None of these benefits is guaranteed. Gaming can become harmful when it interferes with sleep, work, education or relationships.

The World Health Organization recognises gaming disorder as a condition involving impaired control over gaming and continued play despite significant negative consequences. Simply spending a lot of time playing does not amount to a diagnosis.

Read more:
From novels to GTA 6: the long history of fears about addictive entertainment

Why people play also matters. A review of research linked playing primarily to escape distressing experiences with problematic gaming, although those studies could not establish cause and effect.

Meanwhile, a large Oxford study found little evidence that the amount of time spent playing, on its own, substantially affected wellbeing.

While it is too early to establish the specific cognitive benefits of playing Grand Theft Auto 6, research into similar games suggests that navigating its virtual world could have some benefits.

Rather than judging all video games as good or bad, it is more useful to consider what people get from the games they enjoy and how gaming fits into the rest of their lives.

George Farmer does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s drug targets tau protein in promising clinical trial
articles.summary:
pikselstock/Shutterstock.com

An experimental Alzheimer’s drug that reduces the production of a protein called tau has slowed the decline in memory and thinking skills by up to 54% in a clinical trial.

The drug, called diranersen, works differently from approved Alzheimer’s treatments. These focus on clearing amyloid, one of two proteins that build up abnormally in the brain. Diranersen targets the other protein – tau.

Amyloid forms sticky plaques between brain cells, while tau clumps together inside them, forming tangled structures. Both proteins damage brain cells, disrupting the signals they use to communicate and the processes that keep them alive.

Tau has an important job in a healthy brain. It helps stabilise tiny structures called microtubules, which act like railway tracks, transporting nutrients and other materials around brain cells.

In Alzheimer’s, tau changes structure, detaches from these tracks and clumps together inside brain cells, forming tangles. These tangles interfere with the cell’s internal transport system, contributing to its eventual death. The amount of tau accumulating in the brain is closely linked to how quickly people’s thinking skills decline.

Two drugs, lecanemab and donanemab, have been approved by most regulators (including in the US, Europe and the UK) for treating people with early-stage Alzheimer’s, although they are not available on the NHS.

Both help to remove amyloid plaques from the brain and modestly slow the decline in memory and thinking skills. Neither targets tau, and both can cause significant side-effects, including brain bleeds.

Tau tangles explained.

Researchers have found it harder to develop drugs that target tau. Several experimental treatments have used antibodies designed to recognise and destroy abnormal tau. However, these drugs have struggled to improve patients’ symptoms. The problem is that tau builds up inside brain cells, where antibodies find it difficult to reach.

Diranersen takes a different approach. Instead of trying to remove tangles that have already formed, it reduces how much tau brain cells produce in the first place.

The trial

The drug was tested in a phase 2 clinical trial, involving 416 people with early Alzheimer’s disease. Phase 2 is the stage when researchers investigate whether a drug appears to work and which dose is most effective.

The most promising results – which are yet to be peer-reviewed – came from the group given the lowest dose (60mg twice a year as an injection in the spine). After 96 weeks, 60 people taking this lower dose had 38% less decline compared with 115 participants originally assigned to placebo on a scale measuring memory, thinking skills and ability to carry out everyday activities.

On a separate test of cognitive performance, their decline was 54% slower. A third measure, assessing everyday activities, showed 30% less decline.

Most side-effects were mild. The most common were pain and headaches linked to the spinal injections, and short spells of confusion that typically cleared up within a week. The researchers found no new safety problems over the two years of follow-up.

Diranersen is a gene-silencing drug. It belongs to a class of medicines called antisense oligonucleotides, which are designed to switch off specific genetic instructions.

The drug attaches to messenger RNA – the molecule that carries the instructions for making tau – and causes it to break down. Without these instructions, brain cells make less of the protein.

Reducing tau raises an important question: could lowering a protein that brain cells need to function also cause harm? Studies in mice have suggested that substantially reducing tau does not significantly disrupt these processes, and the trial found no serious short-term side-effects. But nobody knows whether lowering tau in people is safe over many years.

How strong is the evidence?

There are important reasons to be cautious about the two-year results. They come from an extension of the original trial in which participants and researchers knew who was receiving the drug. After a year and a half, participants who had initially received a placebo were switched to diranersen. This meant researchers could no longer compare the drug with a placebo group over the full two years.

The original 18-month trial also failed to meet its main objective, which was to show that different doses produced a clear difference in clinical decline. Although some other measures showed improvements, missing this main target makes it harder to know how much confidence to place in the longer-term findings.

What is needed next is a much larger phase 3 trial, comparing the drug with a placebo in many more people. Regulators would want to see the results of such a trial before considering it for approval.

For years, Alzheimer’s research has concentrated on amyloid. Targeting tau offers another possible way to tackle the disease. Combining drugs that act on both proteins might eventually prove more effective than either approach alone. But both possibilities still need to be tested in larger trials.

Rahul Sidhu does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Creatine is popular with bodybuilders – could it help older adults stay independent?
articles.summary:
Creatine may give older adults a small extra gain in strength when combined with resistance training. Chay_Tee/Shutterstock

Climbing stairs or getting out of a chair can become harder with age, partly because muscle mass and strength tend to decline.

Resistance training, such as lifting weights or exercising with resistance bands, can help maintain muscle strength in later life. Research suggests that creatine, a supplement more commonly associated with bodybuilders and athletes, may help older adults gain a little more strength from this type of exercise. Whether that makes everyday tasks easier or helps people stay independent for longer is less clear.

Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that the body makes from amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. It’s also found in foods such as meat and fish. Most of the body’s creatine is stored in muscle, where it helps replenish the energy needed for short bursts of intense activity, such as lifting weights.

Taking creatine increases the amount available in muscles. That may let people complete a few more repetitions before their muscles tire. Over time, that extra work could help explain some of the gains in strength.

Muscle strength in later life

A 2026 review of 11 randomised trials found that adults aged 60 and over who added creatine to a resistance training programme gained slightly more strength than those who did the training without creatine. The review found no clear improvement in muscle mass or in how well people performed physical tasks.

Participants were generally healthy and were 67 on average, so the findings tell us less about people in their 80s and beyond. It’s also unclear whether the same benefits apply to people with sarcopenia, a condition in which low muscle strength is accompanied by reduced muscle mass or quality.

An earlier review found that people who took creatine gained about 1.3kg more lean tissue, on average, than those who took a placebo while following the same training programme. Measures of lean tissue include water. Creatine can make muscles hold more water, especially in the first few days, so it’s difficult to tell how much of that increase was new muscle.

When people take creatine without doing resistance training, some small studies suggest their muscles take longer to tire. The evidence for gains in strength is clearer for people who also train.

Everyday movement and falls

One way researchers test whether strength gains carry over into daily life is with the sit-to-stand test, also known as the chair-rise test. Researchers count how many times someone can stand up in 30 seconds or time how long it takes them to stand up five times, usually without using their arms for support.

A 2026 review pooled results from five trials of the chair-rise test. Middle-aged and older adults who added creatine to their training performed better than those who trained and took a placebo. The evidence for walking and balance was limited and inconsistent.

In the sit-to-stand test, researchers assess leg strength by asking people to rise from a chair repeatedly.
agusyonok/Shutterstock

In a two-year trial involving 237 postmenopausal women, whose average age was 59, both groups were asked to do resistance training and walk regularly. On average, the women taking creatine walked 80 metres about 1.5 seconds faster than they had at the start of the trial, while the placebo group’s time barely changed. There was no clear difference in reported falls through the end of the third year. The trial was designed to study bone health, so it gives limited information about whether creatine affects the risk of falling.

Research involving frailer older adults is also limited. In two trials involving people who were frail or at risk of frailty, participants got stronger with resistance training. Adding creatine produced no clear extra benefit. There is still too little evidence to say whether creatine helps older people avoid falls or remain independent for longer.

The brain also uses creatine to help maintain its energy supply. This has led researchers to investigate whether taking creatine might help preserve memory in later life.

A review focused on older adults found just two studies that tested supplements. They reached different conclusions. The other studies estimated how much creatine people got from food, so they could only identify links between intake and performance on cognitive tests. There is too little evidence to say whether taking creatine can slow cognitive decline or prevent dementia.

What to know about taking creatine

Creatine monohydrate is the most widely studied form. Some trials have used 3 to 5g a day, while others have used higher doses. The amount that might improve everyday physical function is still uncertain.

Creatine is generally well tolerated at the doses studied. Some people report stomach discomfort, and the extra water in muscle can lead to weight gain. Studies in people with healthy kidneys have generally found no evidence of reduced kidney function. There is less evidence on safety for people with kidney disease.

Creatine can raise blood levels of creatinine, a natural waste product, which is produced when the body breaks down creatine. Because blood tests use creatinine to estimate how well the kidneys are working, taking the supplement can make those results harder to interpret. Research on interactions with prescription medicines is limited. If you have kidney disease or take several prescription medicines, check with a GP or pharmacist before starting.

For older adults who want to stay strong, regular strength exercises are the place to start. NHS guidance for adults aged 65 and over recommends exercise to build strength and improve balance and flexibility on at least two days a week. For people who already do resistance training, creatine may offer a small extra gain in muscle strength.

Alexandra Cremona receives funding from the University of Limerick, Ireland.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s controversial return to Nvidia poses the question – what’s the point of a board?
articles.summary:
Patrick T. Fallon/Getty

It’s hard to think of Nvidia without picturing Jensen Huang. Rarely seen without his signature black leather jacket, Huang has led chipmaker Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, turning it into a central player in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

Earlier this month, Huang resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of Nvidia’s board, in the wake of a bombshell scandal involving affairs and alleged corporate espionage.

Days later, the board linked his departure to “personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”. It said it did “not intend to reinstate” him.

This week, however, it voted unanimously to bring him back, following a remarkable intervention by US President Donald Trump.

Many analysts have already weighed in on why the US government intervened. But there’s a deeper, more fundamental question here about corporate power.

If a chief executive is seen as too valuable to lose, can a company’s board still hold them to account? If it can’t, what exactly is the board for?

Read more:
Trump had 4 reasons to ‘convince’ Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang. Here’s why it matters globally

The ‘key person risk’

Sometimes, the “hero” leader of a company can become its biggest vulnerability. In corporate governance, this is called “key person risk”. It is the danger a company comes to depend so heavily on one person that losing them would do serious damage.

This problem often grows out of success. A founder who builds a business and shapes its culture becomes its public face. Staff, customers and investors start to see the person and the company as one.

Think of Steve Jobs, co-founder and longtime chief executive of Apple, or even the fictional media magnate Logan Roy in the TV series Succession.

Nvidia itself recognised this risk before Huang’s brief removal. Its 2026 annual report warned the company was “highly dependent on the services” of its longstanding executive team, and that failing “to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions” could hinder its success in the long term.

Despite this, when Huang left, no permanent successor was ready. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, stepped in temporarily while the board searched for a replacement.

Who’s watching the boss?

So, what is a board actually for? Shareholders can’t supervise the managers in a large company like Nvidia; instead, they elect a board of directors to do it for them. While the board isn’t involved in daily operations of the company, it approves big decisions, watches the chief executive and, if needed, replaces them.

It’s designed to solve something economists call the “principal-agent problem”. A company’s managers (the agents) may put their own interests ahead of the owners’ (the principals).

That’s why independence matters. Independent directors don’t work for the company and have no close financial or personal ties to its management. Filling a board with the chief executive’s employees (such as other senior executives) and friends is like letting students mark their own exams.

Nvidia’s U-turn shows how fragile independence can be. A committee of independent directors is still investigating claims that Huang was targeted by China’s top spy agency.

Huang is also due to answer questions from US lawmakers behind closed doors on December 1. The board brought him back before either had finished.

The board acknowledged that its decision to rehire Huang was heavily influenced by the US government. It said it was “confident” Huang posed “no national security risk”, based on “input from senior US government levels”.

We have seen other boards cave under pressure before. In November 2023, OpenAI’s board fired its chief executive, Sam Altman. Within days, nearly all of its 770 staff threatened to quit. Altman returned, and the board that sacked him was replaced.

Independent of whom?

On paper, there are strong safeguards to protect board independence. For example, the Nasdaq stock exchange, where Nvidia is listed, requires most directors to be independent. The committees that check a company’s accounts and set executive pay must be fully independent.

But these rules fall short in three ways.

First, the board itself gets to decide who counts as “independent”.

In 2024, a US court found several Tesla directors who approved Elon Musk’s pay deal were too close to him to be independent. A higher court later restored the deal on other grounds.

Second, directors get much of their information from the very executive team they are meant to be keeping in check.

And third, a board without its own independent leader often struggles to push back against a chief executive. Nvidia only appointed its first-ever board chair on the day Huang resigned.

Why no one should be irreplaceable

“Key person” risk can’t be removed, but it can be managed.

Boards can train a credible successor, appoint an independent chair before a crisis hits, and finish investigations before deciding. They should also explain their reasoning in public.

An independent board that isn’t able to fire and replace a chief executive is just a cheer squad – not the umpire it’s supposed to be.

This matters well beyond Silicon Valley. Many retirement funds around the world own shares in Nvidia. For the sake of protecting millions of people’s long-term savings, retirement funds and others representing shareholders should be advocating for better governance than we’ve seen at Nvidia so far.

Anish Purkayastha does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar
articles.summary:
By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide.

The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted.

Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights.

Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya.

The repatriation conundrum

It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya.

Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government.

Gen. Min Aung Hlaing is seen at the IX Moscow conference on international security in Moscow in June 2021.
(AP Photo/Alexander Zemlianichenko)

Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament. This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility.

The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army.

The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region, where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state.

The enforcement deficit

The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided.

But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law.

Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it.

The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs.

How the ruling might help the Rohingya

The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs.

Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance.

Read more:
Thousands are feared dead in Myanmar’s quake. Trump’s USAID cuts will cause even more unnecessary deaths

Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps.

More attention could also result in stronger political pressure, not just on Myanmar but also on its regional partners. Malaysia, for example, began deporting refugees back to Myanmar in September 2026.

Since the government continues to deny access to international agencies for the refugees, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, it could not be verified whether these returns were voluntary, as Malaysia claimed.

It’s unlikely the Rohingya, who make up the majority of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia, are returning of their own free will. International pressure could force Malaysia to stop the deportations and avoid causing further harm to its already vulnerable Rohingya refugee community.

Not ‘illegal immigrants’

Finally, the most immediate benefit of the ruling is that, for the first time, there is a formal recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct people. The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine.

The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice.

San Beauchemin is a member of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

articles.title: Mother tongue language rights don’t implement themselves: Lessons from Nepal’s classrooms
articles.summary:
In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.

“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English.

Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue.

A country of 124 mother tongues

Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world, though the state has not always acknowledged it. The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues.

Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages. Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population.

I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity. The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities.

In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language, a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali.

For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue.

Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011. Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk.

Rights on paper

On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues.

In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown, policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support.

In a 2026 study from Tanahun, one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.”

Grade 1 students at Shree Sahara Bal Primary School in Pokhara, Nepal, in June 2013.
(Photo by Jim Holmes for AusAID), CC BY

The evidence for local languages

A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams.

Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English, according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale.

In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.”

Obstacles to implementation

A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents, points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.”

Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained.

Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget, well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education.

Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them.

From paper to practice

As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.”

Children should begin school in the language they understand best, with Nepali and English introduced gradually, building on that foundation. Making this work requires sustained funding, teachers trained to teach in children’s languages, and materials that reflect their lives and communities.

Some municipalities have introduced local-language education programs, while Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre has developed curricula for elementary education in more than 20 mother tongues.

Language policy can sound technical, but at heart it is about whether a child’s first experience of school is a welcoming one. In Renuka Dahal’s classroom in Rautahat, where children now teach their teacher, the message is simple: their languages belong in school, and so do they.

Mark Turin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC).

articles.title: Flu and other winter viruses can hit older adults harder – here’s what you need to know
articles.summary:
Flu and other respiratory infections can be more serious in older adults, especially those with long-term heart or lung conditions. fizkes/Shutterstock

“Put a coat on or you’ll catch a cold.” It is a familiar warning, but it leaves out the most important character in the story, the virus.

Colds are caused by viruses, so cold air alone cannot give you one. In winter, though, viruses can spread more easily indoors, and cold, dry air may make some of the body’s early defences less effective.

For older people, there is a further concern. Infections such as flu and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a common virus that can cause a runny nose or a cough, are more likely to lead to serious illness in this age group.

In colder weather, people often spend more time together indoors with the windows shut. In rooms where little fresh air comes in, tiny particles carrying viruses can build up in the air, making it easier for an infection to pass from one person to another.

If you’re unwell with a respiratory infection, put off visiting anyone at higher risk until you feel better. When you do get together indoors, open a window for a few minutes to help clear the air.

Some of the body’s first defences are inside the nose and airways, the passages that carry air to the lungs. Mucus, the sticky fluid that coats these passages, traps particles, including viruses, and tiny, hair-like structures sweep the mucus along so the body can get rid of it. These hair-like structures act like a tiny conveyor belt, helping clear viruses before they can establish an infection. A 2024 review of research on indoor air found that dry conditions can slow this process.

If a virus does infect a cell, another defence comes into play. Infected cells can send out chemical signals that warn neighbouring cells and help them protect themselves. This can limit how far the virus spreads.

A 2024 study found that some cold viruses multiplied more easily in cells from the nose when they were kept at lower temperatures. The cells also produced a weaker early immune response to the virus. But the study was done in laboratory conditions, so it doesn’t tell us whether being out in the cold makes someone more likely to catch a cold.

Serious illness in older people

The immune system, which helps the body fight infections, changes with age. Some of its cells become less effective, and the body can make fewer of the protective proteins called antibodies that help stop a virus from infecting cells. At the same time, the body’s reaction to infection can become harder to regulate. If it goes on too long, it can damage the tissues it is trying to protect.

Long-term heart or lung conditions can make an infection harder to cope with. Cold air can also narrow the airways, making breathing harder, and cold weather can raise blood pressure, putting extra strain on the heart. Flu can lead to pneumonia or make an existing heart or lung condition worse.

Vaccines give the immune system a head start by helping it recognise a virus and respond more quickly. Vaccines against flu, COVID and RSV can reduce the risk of serious illness.

Because flu viruses change and protection fades, the NHS offers a flu vaccine every year to people aged 65 and over and others at higher risk. In England, eligibility for COVID vaccination and RSV vaccination depends on factors such as age and health.

Most colds get better on their own. If you are 65 or over and have flu symptoms, the NHS advises asking your GP surgery for an urgent appointment or contacting NHS 111.

If you are in a group at highest risk of serious illness from COVID and develop symptoms, take a rapid COVID test as soon as possible, even if the symptoms are mild. If the test is positive, contact your GP surgery, NHS 111 or your hospital specialist promptly. Medicines for COVID need to be started early.

When checking on an older relative or neighbour, pay attention to whether they seem like their usual self. Older people can have flu without a high temperature. In someone who is already frail, going off their food or behaving differently can be a sign of illness.

New confusion or unusual drowsiness can be signs of serious illness. If someone is more short of breath than usual, seek urgent advice from their GP surgery or NHS 111. If they become suddenly confused, are difficult to wake or are struggling to breathe, call 999 immediately.

Fran Ludwig does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Climate summits need radical reform – here’s how to transform global negotiations
articles.summary:
DENIS ESAULOV 1987/Shutterstock

The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy
expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.

Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Ending unanimity

Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.

The Cop climate negotiation process hinges on all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties.
metamorworks/Shutterstock

It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend).

It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration (issued by Colombia’s
then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business.

Coalition of the willing

Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?”

This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks.

Read more:
What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains

Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results.

As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute.

The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero).

We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats.

Francesco Grillo is Director of the think tank Vision.

articles.title: Jensen Huang, Nvidia and the risks that come with ‘boomerang bosses’
articles.summary:
Jensen Huang’s swift return as boss of Nvidia surprised – and pleased – many people. Donald Trump was happy about it, as were many who invest in the future of AI.

There are plenty of high-profile business leaders who have returned to a company after stepping down, with good results. Michael Dell did it at Dell computers, Steve Jobs did it at Apple and Sam Altman did it at OpenAI.

But there are also many cases where a returning CEO has actually harmed the performance of the firm. So will Jensen Huang prove to be a successful or a harmful “boomerang boss”?

As its co-founder and CEO, Huang was behind Nvidia’s extraordinary success. But the company also had one crucial weakness – its dependency on Huang.

The idea of “key person risk” is the vulnerability from depending heavily on one person whose absence could severely disrupt how a business works. This aspect of Nvidia was dramatically exposed when it was revealed in late October that Huang had had an extra-marital affair with an executive with alleged links to Chinese government secret services.

After another affair with an employee came to light a few days later, swiftly followed by claims about another, Huang stepped down. This led to a massive drop in the firm’s share price, which triggered wider falls in technology-focused markets around the world. Huang’s affairs had become a matter of global economic stability but also geopolitical importance, amid debates about how his departure might affect America’s narrow lead over China in the AI race.

The financial markets clearly approve of the Nvidia board’s announcement that Huang will step back into his role as CEO. The share price has shot back up, helping to lift many companies in the sector. But research on boomerang CEOs paints a more nuanced picture.

Often these bosses are invited to return on the basis that they had been successful in the past so are likely to be successful in the future. However, one study of over 6,000 CEOs found that boomerang bosses tend to perform significantly worse than others.

The main reason was that they often revert back to their old strategic playbook when the rest of the world has moved on. This means they are using outdated ideas.

Yet the dataset for this study included many founders who returned years after they had left. Huang was only out of the Nvidia saddle for 11 days, so his strategic playbook is likely to be as up to date as ever. A more recent working paper looking at boomerang CEOs who had only been away for a short time found that the firms in question showed improved operating performance, investment and growth.

However, other research suggests boomerang CEOs tend to receive slighly higher performance evaluations than other new hires mainly because they have a better understanding of the hidden social structure of the organisation and how to navigate it. Another study found that they tended to perform on average about the same as other managers, but were also more likely to leave.

Nvidia ups and downs.
Saulo Ferreira Angelo/Shutterstock

Back for good?

Beyond the world of business there are cases of boomerang leaders in politics and sport. In politics, returning leaders – including Winston Churchill, Silvio Berlusconi and Donald Trump – are a persistent but relatively minor feature of many political systems.

In the world of sport there are a of cases of coaches being fired and then returning to Premier League football teams. One piece of analysis found that of 11 Premier League coaches who returned, only three saw their results improve.

Read more:
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is getting his CEO job back, but history shows companies perform better when corporate boards take executive misbehavior seriously

Perhaps this all suggests that Huang’s return to Nvidia may not be a cause for immediate performance concerns. His strategic knowledge and networks are still very valuable.

What is likely to be a longer term worry is issues of reputation and governance at the world’s most important chip-maker. Addressing these is likely to require revisiting the structure and oversight practices of the company – which the new old boss may or may not feel like doing.

Andre Spicer does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Norovirus is spreading – how to recognise the symptoms and what to do
articles.summary:
Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com

Described as the “Ferrari of the virus world” for the way it races from person to person, norovirus is once again on the move as we head into winter.

Reports from the UK Health Security Agency have highlighted that cases of norovirus – commonly known as the “winter vomiting bug” – have increased by more than 35% in England over the past two weeks, compared with the previous fortnight.

While that sounds alarming, this is still within expected levels for the season. Overall case numbers are about 5% above what’s typical for this time of year. Cases have fallen in Scotland, but Wales has seen a rise.

Norovirus symptoms include sudden-onset nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, sometimes accompanied by fever, stomach pain, body aches and headaches.

Most healthy adults recover within one to three days. However, those with weakened immune systems, older adults and young children face a higher risk of severe symptoms. When this happens, people can be ill for much longer and may need hospital treatment if they become dehydrated.

Norovirus is highly contagious, with some studies suggesting that as few as ten virus particles can cause an infection. It spreads from person to person when tiny amounts of virus from infected faeces or vomit get on to food, hands or surfaces and are then transferred to the mouth.

Close contact between people can also spread the virus. This may help explain why cases peak in winter, when people spend more time together indoors. However, you can catch it at any time of the year.

The virus is also particularly resilient; it can survive on hard kitchen surfaces such as stainless steel and ceramic for up to two weeks, and it takes temperatures of around 60°C to kill it.

There are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for norovirus. It evolves quickly to escape our immune systems, and has proved notoriously difficult to grow in the lab, which has hampered research efforts. That said, recent breakthroughs in growing norovirus using lab-grown human gut cells may make it easier to develop treatments in future.

How to protect yourself and your household

While alcohol-based hand sanitisers can be effective against other viruses, such as the ones that cause COVID and flu, they don’t work well against norovirus. Instead, the best way to protect yourself is by washing your hands often with soap and hot water, ideally for 15 seconds or more. This is particularly important before or after preparing food, and after going to the toilet.

Norovirus is also frequently spread through contaminated food. Fresh produce such as fruit and vegetables may pick up the virus during harvesting, packaging or handling, so wash these thoroughly before use. Shellfish such as oysters can also be contaminated with concentrated norovirus from the water they live in, so ensure these are thoroughly cooked, rather than steamed or eaten raw.

If someone in your household has norovirus, cleaning surfaces regularly with bleach-based products can help prevent the virus from spreading.

Using a dummy called Vomiting Larry, researchers found that norovirus-containing droplets can spread around ten feet (three metres) when someone vomits. So, it’s important to immediately clean areas that have been contaminated by vomit or faeces.

Vomiting Larry in action.

Frequent cleaning of heavily used surfaces such as door handles, light switches, taps, toilet seats and flush handles, ideally while wearing disposable gloves, can help reduce the chances of the virus spreading.

Washing soiled clothes or bedding separately from other laundry, at a temperature of 60°C or above at the longest cycle time possible, can also help kill the virus on soft surfaces.

If you are unlucky enough to get norovirus yourself, the only solution is to allow the virus to run its short, but deeply unpleasant, course.

Replacing lost fluids is essential, so drink plenty of water, tea or electrolyte drinks, or use oral rehydration sachets. If you feel able to eat, stick to plain foods that are easy to digest, such as toast, rice, pasta or soup, and avoid fatty or salty foods that may make your symptoms worse.

As norovirus is highly contagious, ensure that you stay at home and rest as much as possible. Keep your distance from other people in your household where you can, and avoid preparing food for others while you’re unwell and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.

Even after full recovery, infectious virus can still be shed in poo for up to two weeks, so continuing to frequently clean bathroom areas can help prevent further transmission.

With cases rising as winter sets in, the Ferrari of viruses may be doing the rounds for a while yet. A few simple habits could save you, and others, a very unpleasant few days.

Charlotte Lewis receives funding from the UK Medical Research Council.

articles.title: Swimming spots won’t get official bathing water status if they’re tricky to clean under England’s new rules
articles.summary:
Church Cliff beach, Lyme Regis, Dorset. Sarah2/Shutterstock

If a beach or riverside spot in England is popular with swimmers, anyone can apply for it to be given official bathing status. Official status means that the water will be tested and monitored regularly, and given a rating from “excellent” to “poor”.

Now, though, popular swimming spots can be refused official bathing water status in England if government agencies judge that meeting minimum water quality standards will be too difficult or disproportionately expensive.

Until recently, official bathing status was granted to a place being used by large numbers of swimmers – the water did not have to be clean before designation. A site could be granted official bathing status while being classified as “poor”, with recommendations to avoid swimming there. Bathing status designation and water quality classification were separate.

But official status requires regular Environment Agency testing for bacteria that indicate faecal contamination, with up to 20 samples taken during the bathing season, from May to September. Further requirements include information for swimmers and duties to investigate and address pollution.

England’s new rules, in force since May 2026, have added a check before official designation. Can water realistically be improved to at least “sufficient” status without disproportionate expense? A polluted site can still be designated if it passes that assessment, but designation must be refused if ministers accept that improvement is not feasible or is considered too expensive.

If status is refused by the Environment Agency (with final decisions being made by Defra, the government’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs), who will tackle the water pollution and keep swimmers informed?

Designation driving improvement

Church Cliff beach in Lyme Regis, Dorset, was first designated as a bathing water in 1988. Its water was classified as “poor” in 2015. Routine testing for bacteria in water stopped when the beach lost its official status in 2016 due to so few people swimming there.

But some people did continue to swim at Church Cliff beach. For two years, campaigners fought to restore its designation as an official bathing spot and secure action on pollution. The town council supported the public call for redesignation and subsequent water quality monitoring. People were still swimming at this beach and when designation returned in 2024, testing for bacteria resumed and pollution information signs followed. But the water had not been cleaned up in the interim and this site was classified as “poor” again that year.

Designation could help drive the work needed to help clean up water pollution. After redesignation of Church Cliff beach, the Environment Agency drew up a plan in 2025 to reduce sewage discharges, fix leaking pipes and tackle farm pollution. Utility company South West Water committed to sewage upgrades, while the town council worked with the Environment Agency to set up a group to oversee improvements.

For new applications, this process will not be possible if it is judged that improving water quality is not feasible or would be disproportionately expensive.

The government argues that limited resources should go where they can deliver results. It also wants to avoid giving swimmers false reassurance about places that cannot meet minimum standards. Yet Defra’s original 2024 consultation on reforming bathing water regulations acknowledged that refusing designation could discourage investment at polluted sites. Whether that happens will depend on how decisions are made and what follows.

These decisions depend on understanding pollution sources. At East Looe in Cornwall, the bathing water was rated “poor” in 2015. After heavy rain, the River Looe can carry runoff from farmland and sewage from overflowing sewers miles downstream to the beach.

Different sources call for different measures. Upstream in Liskeard, South West Water built two underground tanks to store wastewater during storms and reduce sewage spills into Looe Bay. This was part of a bathing water scheme completed in spring 2015. Cornwall Wildlife Trust offered farmers grants for better roofing and drainage to keep farm waste out of streams during heavy rain. In 2019, East Looe’s bathing water earned its first “good” rating, which it still held in 2025.

East Looe, Cornwall.
BijM/Shutterstock

The new rules under scrutiny

The new bathing water status application process includes water quality checks before designation and, where necessary, an assessment of whether improvements are feasible. But the published guidance does not specify how thoroughly each pollution source will be investigated.

The watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection welcomed the reforms. It has also called for clear reasons and public involvement.

Defra’s guidance on bathing water applications says decisions will be explained. Details of the feasibility assessment will follow. It remains unclear whether the method will follow the watchdog’s advice on calculating cleanup costs.

The environmental campaign charity Surfers Against Sewage is challenging the rules in court. Surfers Against Sewage argues that the new rules undermine the protections that designation is meant to provide. The High Court granted permission for the challenge to proceed in October 2026, with a hearing scheduled for February 2027.

Any refusal should explain which pollution sources were investigated, why cleanup was judged infeasible or too expensive, and what could allow reconsideration. It should clarify which monitoring will continue and who will inform swimmers. This would help people make informed choices and communities track whether pollution is being tackled.

For swimmers and river users, the consequences go far beyond a place on an official list. Without clear warnings, people may unknowingly enter polluted water and develop infections. These can cause diarrhoea and vomiting and, in severe cases, life-threatening complications such as kidney failure. Refusal should never mean abandoning efforts to improve water quality.

Karolina Krupska is the founder of the Water Science Foundation.

articles.title: Pimple-popping videos can be disgusting – and strangely satisfying
articles.summary:
Pimple-popping videos leave some viewers squirming and others waiting eagerly for the next squeeze. Lena May/Shutterstock

Some people relax by watching someone squeeze pus from a stranger’s face. I’m one of them. I have favourite accounts, strong opinions about technique and very little patience for a video that ends before the pore has been properly cleared.

I tend to watch with the sound off and the speed doubled, slowing things down if a particularly promising spot needs closer attention. My hairdresser discovered this interest when she caught sight of my phone. She was considerably less enthusiastic.

But why does something that makes one person recoil keep another watching? And are people like me less easily disgusted in the first place?

In the latest episode of Strange Health, The Conversation’s podcast about unusual health and wellness trends, I explore pimple popping with my co-host Dan Baumgardt, a practising GP and lecturer at the University of Bristol.

Our guest is Albert Wabnegger, a scientist at the University of Graz in Austria who specialises in the psychology of disgust. He doesn’t particularly enjoy pimple-popping videos himself, but has spent rather more time studying them than most non-fans would volunteer for.

Measuring the pleasure of a popped pimple

Wabnegger and his colleagues developed a questionnaire to measure how much people enjoy popping their own spots or watching someone else’s being squeezed. He takes me through it during the episode. I rapidly develop concerns that the scale doesn’t go high enough.

For a study involving 80 women, the researchers showed enthusiasts and non-enthusiasts pimple-popping videos inside a brain scanner. For comparison, they showed water spraying from fountains and steam cleaners removing dirt from cars and stone floors.

Fans of pimple-popping videos reported more pleasure and less disgust while watching, although they still felt some disgust. On a separate questionnaire, the two groups gave similar ratings when asked how disgusting they found situations that might expose them to germs. Fans did report fewer difficulties managing feelings of disgust. The scans also revealed differences in activity in a brain region involved in motivation and reward.

Wabnegger explains why that needs careful interpretation. Brain activity cannot tell researchers precisely what somebody feels, and these findings don’t demonstrate a dopamine rush.

Enjoying disgust from a safe distance

One possible explanation involves the safety of the screen. Watching a pimple being squeezed puts you close enough to see everything without any chance of its contents reaching you.

Wabnegger compares this with enjoying a horror film: an uncomfortable experience can become entertaining when the viewer feels safe.

His later research has also linked pimple-popping enjoyment with morbid curiosity, an interest in disturbing or threatening subjects. That association offers a possible clue to the appeal, rather than establishing why any individual watches.

Some viewers say the videos help them relax. Wabnegger wants to investigate what prompts people to seek them out and how they feel afterwards. Whether watching helps people sleep remains untested.

Listen to the episode for the science behind this divisive viewing habit, and my increasingly unsubtle attempts to secure a place in his next experiment.

Have you spotted a bizarre health trend you’d like us to investigate? Email strangehealth@theconversation.com. The stranger the question, the better.

Strange Health is hosted by Katie Edwards and Dan Baumgardt. The executive producer is Gemma Ware, with editing and mixing by Anouk Millet. Artwork by Alice Mason.

Listen to Strange Health on your preferred podcast app, download it via our RSS feed or find out how else to listen here.

The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Brain lesions: what causes them and when they need follow-up
articles.summary:
Brain scans can help doctors identify lesions, which are areas of damaged or abnormal tissue. Gorodenkoff/Shutterstock

You open your brain scan report and see the word “lesion”. It’s a worrying word to come across while waiting to speak to your doctor.

In a report, it means there’s an area in or around the brain that looks abnormal on the scan. That could be anything from an area of tissue damaged by a stroke to a pocket of fluid that’s been there for years.

What happens next depends on what the radiologist thinks they’re looking at.

Take a stroke. If a clot blocks an artery supplying the brain, the tissue downstream is starved of oxygen. Brain cells can die, leaving an area of damage that doctors call an infarct. Even a tiny stroke in an area that controls movement can leave someone with lasting weakness. If your face suddenly droops on one side or you develop arm weakness or trouble speaking, call 999 straight away, even if the symptoms pass.

A lesion can also form through inflammation. In multiple sclerosis (MS), the immune system attacks myelin, the protective coating around nerve fibres. Damage to that coating makes it harder for messages to travel along the nerves. The damaged areas can show up on MRI scans in the brain or spinal cord. Doctors look at where those areas are and what pattern they form, because several other conditions can produce spots on an MRI.

Sometimes the lesion is a growth. A meningioma is a tumour that starts in the protective layers of tissue around the brain. Most meningiomas are non-cancerous and grow slowly. They can go unnoticed for years and turn up on a scan that’s being carried out for another reason. Even a non-cancerous tumour can cause symptoms if it presses on the brain.

What the scan can tell you about a lesion

If you’ve ever looked at a set of MRI images, you might have noticed that the fluid around the brain can look bright in one picture and dark in another. Think of how an Instagram filter makes some details stand out. The MRI scanner does something similar by changing how it captures the image.

Radiologists call these different settings “sequences”. One can turn down the signal from the fluid so that patches of abnormal tissue next to it stand out. Another is sensitive to the movement of water within tissue and can help pick up a recent stroke.

Comparing brain scans taken at different times can help doctors see whether a lesion has changed.
PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Sometimes the radiologist will go looking for an older scan. If the same area looked exactly the same several years ago, that gives them information a single scan can’t. If there’s no earlier scan to compare it with, a repeat scan may help show whether the lesion is changing over time.

When a brain lesion needs follow-up

Some findings on a scan can be left alone. An arachnoid cyst is a pocket of fluid in one of the membranes around the brain. On a scan, it typically has a clear outline, and the fluid inside looks the same as the fluid that normally surrounds the brain. In adults, a small cyst with these features often needs no further scans if it causes no symptoms and is in a place where it’s unlikely to block the flow of fluid.

For some lesions, a repeat scan helps doctors see whether they’re growing. If a meningioma is found by chance and is causing no symptoms, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence suggests a repeat scan after a year. If the tumour looks the same, clinicians can consider ending follow-up or scanning again five years after it was first found.

If the scan shows a brain abscess, a pocket of pus in the brain caused by an infection, the next step is urgent treatment in hospital.

If you’re reading your own report, look for the summary, often headed “impression” or “conclusion”. That’s where the radiologist usually gives their best explanation of what they’ve seen and may suggest a next step. When you speak to the clinician who arranged the scan, ask what they think caused the lesion and whether you need to do anything about it. If they recommend another scan, ask what they’ll be looking for.
