articles.title: Brain lesions: what causes them and when they need follow-up
articles.summary:
Brain scans can help doctors identify lesions, which are areas of damaged or abnormal tissue. Gorodenkoff/Shutterstock

You open your brain scan report and see the word “lesion”. It’s a worrying word to come across while waiting to speak to your doctor.

In a report, it means there’s an area in or around the brain that looks abnormal on the scan. That could be anything from an area of tissue damaged by a stroke to a pocket of fluid that’s been there for years.

What happens next depends on what the radiologist thinks they’re looking at.

Take a stroke. If a clot blocks an artery supplying the brain, the tissue downstream is starved of oxygen. Brain cells can die, leaving an area of damage that doctors call an infarct. Even a tiny stroke in an area that controls movement can leave someone with lasting weakness. If your face suddenly droops on one side or you develop arm weakness or trouble speaking, call 999 straight away, even if the symptoms pass.

A lesion can also form through inflammation. In multiple sclerosis (MS), the immune system attacks myelin, the protective coating around nerve fibres. Damage to that coating makes it harder for messages to travel along the nerves. The damaged areas can show up on MRI scans in the brain or spinal cord. Doctors look at where those areas are and what pattern they form, because several other conditions can produce spots on an MRI.

Sometimes the lesion is a growth. A meningioma is a tumour that starts in the protective layers of tissue around the brain. Most meningiomas are non-cancerous and grow slowly. They can go unnoticed for years and turn up on a scan that’s being carried out for another reason. Even a non-cancerous tumour can cause symptoms if it presses on the brain.

What the scan can tell you about a lesion

If you’ve ever looked at a set of MRI images, you might have noticed that the fluid around the brain can look bright in one picture and dark in another. Think of how an Instagram filter makes some details stand out. The MRI scanner does something similar by changing how it captures the image.

Radiologists call these different settings “sequences”. One can turn down the signal from the fluid so that patches of abnormal tissue next to it stand out. Another is sensitive to the movement of water within tissue and can help pick up a recent stroke.

Comparing brain scans taken at different times can help doctors see whether a lesion has changed.
PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Sometimes the radiologist will go looking for an older scan. If the same area looked exactly the same several years ago, that gives them information a single scan can’t. If there’s no earlier scan to compare it with, a repeat scan may help show whether the lesion is changing over time.

When a brain lesion needs follow-up

Some findings on a scan can be left alone. An arachnoid cyst is a pocket of fluid in one of the membranes around the brain. On a scan, it typically has a clear outline, and the fluid inside looks the same as the fluid that normally surrounds the brain. In adults, a small cyst with these features often needs no further scans if it causes no symptoms and is in a place where it’s unlikely to block the flow of fluid.

For some lesions, a repeat scan helps doctors see whether they’re growing. If a meningioma is found by chance and is causing no symptoms, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence suggests a repeat scan after a year. If the tumour looks the same, clinicians can consider ending follow-up or scanning again five years after it was first found.

If the scan shows a brain abscess, a pocket of pus in the brain caused by an infection, the next step is urgent treatment in hospital.

If you’re reading your own report, look for the summary, often headed “impression” or “conclusion”. That’s where the radiologist usually gives their best explanation of what they’ve seen and may suggest a next step. When you speak to the clinician who arranged the scan, ask what they think caused the lesion and whether you need to do anything about it. If they recommend another scan, ask what they’ll be looking for.

articles.title: From novels to GTA 6: the long history of fears about addictive entertainment
articles.summary:
The release of Grand Theft Auto VI has renewed concerns about excessive gaming, but spending hours immersed in a video game does not necessarily indicate addiction. SolidMaks/Shutterstock

The release of Grand Theft Auto VI, arguably the most anticipated video game in history, has prompted warnings about excessive gaming. Addiction specialists have urged players to recognise when gaming begins to interfere with their lives, while experts have raised concerns about its potential effects on younger players. These warnings reflect broader concerns about gaming addiction, rather than evidence that GTA VI itself is particularly addictive.

There are genuine health concerns behind these fears. The World Health Organization recognises gaming disorder as a condition wherein someone loses control over their gaming, prioritising it to the extent that there are serious consequences.

Taking a sneaky sick day for a marathon gaming session when a new game launches isn’t the issue. Gaming disorder is far more serious. It involves significant disruption to someone’s personal life, relationships, education or work.

Gaming disorder is a recognised health condition, and researchers have investigated how common it is. But the broader fear that people might become so absorbed in fictional worlds that they neglect everyday life predates video games. Similar concerns were once directed at other forms of entertainment, including novels.

Fiction fixation

As novels became increasingly popular during the eighteenth century, they attracted the same criticism that video games receive today. In Germany, commentators coined the term “Lesesucht”, meaning “reading addiction” or “reading mania”, to describe what they saw as an unhealthy obsession with books.

In England, critics worried that people would spend too much time reading novels and struggle to distinguish fiction from reality. Young women were considered particularly vulnerable, with fears that romantic stories might corrupt their morals or encourage unrealistic expectations about what they might expect from life.

Prominent writers joined the debate. In his autobiography Biographia Literaria, the poet and critic Samuel Taylor Coleridge criticised readers of popular fiction for losing themselves in daydreams rather than thinking critically about what they read. Jane Austen, meanwhile, defended novels as a serious form of literature in Northanger Abbey.

The fears continued as new forms of entertainment emerged. During the 19th century, cheap adventure and crime stories known as penny dreadfuls in Britain and dime novels in America were blamed for encouraging juvenile crime.

In 1954, following growing concerns about the influence of horror and crime comics on children, the American comics industry established the Comics Code Authority, which imposed restrictions on what publishers could show.

Later, critics accused television of turning audiences into passive viewers and taking time away from more worthwhile activities, including reading. More recently, streaming services and binge-watching have revived concerns about spending too much time absorbed in entertainment.

Although the form of entertainment changes, the underlying fear remains familiar: that popular stories can have a harmful influence on the people who enjoy them.

Novels and video games share an important attraction. Both can transport us into fictional worlds, allowing us to escape everyday life, explore unfamiliar experiences and become emotionally involved in stories.

Moral panics

Many historical fears about popular entertainment reflected the social attitudes and prejudices of their time. But fiction can influence how people see themselves and the world around them. It can shape expectations, encourage dissatisfaction with everyday life or offer an escape from problems that people would rather avoid.

Video games can be particularly absorbing because they allow players to take an active part in fictional worlds. Instead of simply following a story, players can explore, make decisions and influence what happens.

Some games also encourage people to keep playing by regularly introducing new challenges, rewards and items to collect. In Grand Theft Auto Online, the online version of GTA V, new vehicles and weapons were continually released, giving players reasons to return and avoid missing out.

This approach can also encourage spending. Players can use real money to purchase in-game currency, which can then be spent on virtual items. Such features have helped make the franchise enormously profitable, with GTA V and its online component reportedly generating an estimated US$10 billion in revenue since the game’s release in 2013.

These commercial strategies raise important questions about how games are designed to keep people playing and spending money. For those already struggling to control their gaming, systems that offer frequent rewards and encourage repeated play may be particularly concerning.

However, gaming disorder affects a relatively small minority of people. A review of research from 17 countries estimated that around 2% of the general population experiences gaming disorder, although estimates varied considerably between studies.

Spending a lot of time playing video games does not, by itself, mean someone has an addiction. What matters is whether they have lost control over their gaming and whether it is causing serious problems in their everyday life.

Gaming can provide an escape from difficult circumstances, just as books, television and other forms of entertainment can. The reasons someone plays, and the effects gaming has on their life, are therefore more revealing than the number of hours they spend doing it.

So, if you or someone you know is currently spending a lot of time in Vice City, you probably needn’t worry. We shouldn’t judge someone’s gaming habits simply by counting the hours they play, any more than we would judge their reading habits by counting the pages they finish.

Someone pretending to have a cold to get a day off work for a new game’s release may simply be enjoying a rare occasion. But if they repeatedly miss work, neglect relationships or struggle to stop playing despite serious consequences, there may be cause for concern.

articles.title: Nearly half of autistic girls are persistently absent from secondary school – new research
articles.summary:
Ben Molyneux/Shutterstock

Children not attending school has become a growing national concern in England. Government policy has increasingly focused on improving attendance, while parents can face fines for unauthorised absences.

However, behind this wider attendance problem is a striking disparity. Our recently published research shows that between 2021 and 2023, nearly half (44%) of autistic girls attending mainstream secondary schools in England were persistently absent, meaning they miss 10% or more of school.

This high level of absence is not seen equally across all pupils. In 2022-23, 31% of autistic boys in mainstream secondary schools were persistently absent, compared with around 25% of girls and 20% of boys with no identified special educational need. Although absence has increased significantly across all groups since the pandemic, autistic girls stand out as being particularly likely to miss significant amounts of school.

Before the pandemic, around 25% of autistic girls in secondary schools were persistently absent. By 2021-22, this had risen to 44% and remained at a similar level in 2022-23. Although absence increased for all pupils over this period, the gap between autistic girls and autistic boys widened considerably – absence in boys rose from 18% to 31%.

Importantly, there are signs that difficulties with attendance may begin much earlier in a child’s life following the pandemic. In 2022-23, 28% of autistic girls in primary school were persistently absent, compared with 26.5% of autistic boys. Before the pandemic, in 2018-19, 16.6% of primary-aged autistic girls and 15% of autistic boys were persistently absent.

Although the difference between autistic girls and boys is much smaller in primary school than in secondary school, these findings suggest that we need to start paying closer attention to attendance difficulties earlier.

Finding the data

Despite the scale of these differences, it has been difficult to tease out using publicly available school attendance data. Government figures have routinely grouped children with different types of special educational need together, masking the scale of the attendance problem for autistic girls within the wider statistics.

To better understand attendance figures for autistic girls specifically, we used a freedom of information request to obtain national attendance data from the Department for Education, broken down by autism, sex, and school stage. This allowed us to examine attendance patterns across 5 to 6 million pupils in state-funded schools in England each year, and compare attendance for autistic girls, autistic boys, and girls and boys with no identified special educational need.

Rates of absence from primary school have also increased.
Rawpixel.com/Shutterstock

These figures, however, only tell us part of the story. They show how many autistic girls are missing significant amounts of school, but they cannot tell us why this is the case, or what might be making school increasingly difficult to attend.

We know from our previous research with autistic children and families that difficulties with school can build up over time. Autistic young people describe sensory and social pressures, difficult relationships with school staff and school environments that do not always understand or respond to their needs. Over time, these experiences can make school increasingly difficult to manage, and can affect whether young people feel safe, supported, and that they belong.

Our ongoing, as yet unpublished wider research with autistic girls and their families has demonstrated that, for many, difficulties with school attendance stemmed not from a lack of motivation to attend or learn, but from their experiences at school and the associated emotional impact. One girl explained to us that teachers “just thought I was just another kid who wanted to bunk lessons and didn’t want to go to them, but it wasn’t the case. Like I wanted to go to lessons. I wanted to get an education”.

Attending school might be more challenging as children transition to secondary school. Pupils must manage bigger and busier environments, different subject teachers and classrooms, changing friendships and larger academic and organisational demands.

For autistic girls who may already be struggling and hiding their difficulties to fit in, it may not always be obvious to others how difficult they are finding school. By the time attendance starts to become a serious concern, the difficulties affecting their attendance may already have been building up over months or years.

Hanna Kovshoff has received funding from the British Academy/Leverhulme.

Chloe Eddy receives PhD funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.

Sarah Parsons receives funding from the British Academy / Leverhulme.

articles.title: The curious history of the huntaway, New Zealand’s unusually loud sheepdog
articles.summary:
The New Zealand Huntaway sheepdog. Tonia Kraakman/Shutterstock

Sheepdog trials don’t always take place in a field. Some take place in a pub.

Across New Zealand, “bark-ups” are a common sight at pubs and agricultural events, and feature a home-bred invention: the New Zealand huntaway dog breed. The aim of the bark-up is simple: find the dog with the best bark.

To outsiders, the spectacle raises an obvious question: why would anyone hold a competition to find the sheepdog that barks the loudest? The answer lies not just in the sheep stations of New Zealand where the huntaway was developed, but in the colonisation of New Zealand, for sheepdogs are breeds of empire. It’s something I explore in my new book.

The modern sheepdog was a Victorian invention. Queen Victoria herself was a fan of the collie, buying the best from shepherds on the England-Scotland borders. Those shepherds were at the helm of the emerging sheepdog trialling scene at the start of the 20th century.

In the process, sheepdogs came to embody Victorian moral values. The ideal dog displayed discipline, intelligence, restraint, obedience and industriousness, and perhaps most of all, silence while working – qualities that were equally applicable to the shepherd.

Organisations such as the International Sheep Dog Society reinforced these ideals. Under its influential honorary secretary, James Reid, the border collie was invented not merely as a useful farm dog but as the pinnacle of canine improvement.

Exported throughout Britain’s settler colonies, it became a breed of empire, carrying with it particular ideas about good stockmanship, moral character and agricultural modernity. Reid went so far as to describe the sheepdog as the foundation of the pastoral economy, whose intelligence and labour underpinned the success of the British empire.

Scottish settlers had already taken their sheepdogs to New Zealand in the mid-19th Century. But it would be a Northumbrian, James Lilico, who would transform New Zealand’s sheepdogs. Arriving in 1894 to work as a shepherd, he immediately sent home for his dog Captain, disappointed by the “useless mongrels” he had been given to work.

So started half a century of importing the finest sheepdogs he could source, usually championship winning trial dogs, earning him the title of the “collie king of New Zealand”. Lilico imported sheepdogs that had been bred with the quality known as “eye” (herding using an intense stare) that had become highly valued among triallists. Breeding them, Lilico championed the superiority of what he called “border dogs” in his weekly column in the New Zealand Farmer periodical.

Lilico’s actions were not universally welcomed, in particular his criticism of the sheepdogs and shepherds who worked New Zealand’s high country. For the shepherds of these regions, Lilico’s strong-eyed dogs were too slow, too delicate and insufficiently forceful. In their view, sheep needed to be moved, not mesmerised.

Their alternative was the huntaway. What marked out the huntaway from the border collie was its noise. Without fences and across wide open country, noise had become a valuable tool for shepherds. Before setting out to muster sheep, shepherds gathered their dogs and instructed them to bark. This bark up – just like those now seen in pubs – guided sheep from a distance, so by the time shepherds arrived the sheep were already on the move.

Read more:
Your dog may be wilder than you think, according to canine sleep research

If its bark united the huntaway, their appearance did anything but. Old photographs reveal a variety of different appearances and types: from small and fluffy to larger looking collies. But as sheep farming expanded from the South Island into the hill country of the North Island, the huntaway began to evolve.

To make the huntaway more powerful to deal with stubborn Romney sheep, its voice got louder. Breeding experiments involving mastiff, rottweiler, labrador, hound and other breeds sought to improve its barking power. A bigger huntaway became more common, but even now the huntaway defies standardisation beyond its capacity to bark all day.

Crucially, while the development of New Zealand agriculture was part of a scientific “grasslands revolution”, these scientists had little to do with sheepdogs. The huntaway instead reflected the spirit of farmers, as a “practical dog for practical men”. Scientists and breed societies were kept well away in fear of ruining the dog.

The Huntaway.

Recognition and uncertainty

In 2013 the huntaway was recognised as a unique breed by the New Zealand Kennel Club, but its origins were still uncertain. Recent genetic studies show that it is related to the border collie, and other breeds imported in the 19th century. Genetic traces of the breeds used for power are harder to find, reinforcing the mythology that surrounds the breed.

It may also be that its defining feature – the bark – is not simply a New Zealand invention but an echo of its past. Back in Scotland in 1935, James Reid had given a lecture celebrating the border collie conquering all other breeds of sheepdog. Its popularity had meant that other barking sheepdogs used across Wales and southern England had no place, consigning them to history.

When James Lilico wrote about the huntaway in one of his three books, he received a letter from a shepherd in north Wales suggesting that the Huntaway sounded no different to the dog known as ci hanos, a dog that used noise to drive sheep onto the hills in the springtime.

Lilico had planned on importing one of these as part of a breeding experiment. Such an experiment might be more valuable today as the huntaway gene pool narrows: the closure of large sheep stations in New Zealand is making breeding selection a challenge. In doing so, it raises existential questions about sheepdogs themselves, because without sheep there will be no sheepdogs.

Gareth Enticott receives funding from the Welsh and UK Government.

articles.title: Panic buying? Gradual stockpiling makes for better ‘prepping’ without emptying supermarket shelves
articles.summary:
Drazen Zigic/Shutterstock

Soon after the government launched its “Be Ready” campaign, supermarket shelves were empty where the bottled water usually sits. Torches quickly went out of stock too.

Two days before the campaign launch in October, one of us (Sayed Elhoushy) argued at a Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology roundtable that households need a clear standard for what being prepared means, including how to build supplies gradually. The “gradually” is key.

In the ten days following campaign launch, sales of essentials surged. According to retail research firm Worldpanel, sales of tinned food rose by 37%, bottled water by 67% and hand sanitiser by 83%.

The Be Ready campaign asks households to stock three days of supplies, including water, tinned food, medicines and cash. It tells people what to buy, but little on when. Without guidance on timing, many households may all act on the same advice at the same time.

When shelves emptied before the first COVID lockdown, researchers at the Institute for Fiscal Studies showed the higher demand came from more households than usual buying storable goods. Shoppers can still strip a shelf, even if they all buy little amounts, at once. The anticipation of empty shelves can then raise urgency and fear. That urgency and fear change how people shop.

Where fear falls short

The past few years witnessed a series of unprecedented, concurrent and consecutive disruptions. Cost-of-living crisis, heatwaves, droughts and geopolitical tensions created uncertainty in peoples’ daily lives. When people feel unsafe, they buy more, and shortages follow, real or imagined. Research with US shoppers during COVID found that fear can override good intentions: people who wanted to shop responsibly still stockpiled when they were afraid.

Scarcity makes products more desirable and pushes people to seek more, within short notice. In the pandemic, the risk of store closures created panic. People rushed for staples, driven by fear of missing out, social conformity or herd mentality.

Scarcity makes products more desirable and pushes people to seek more, within short notice.
gopixa/Shutterstock

People do not make the best decisions when pressured. They look for short-term, smaller gains, at the expense of longer-term, better ones. Feelings of urgency shortens decision making time, but can also cause post-purchase regret. Fear of missing out, triggers anxiety and panic buying. Social media intensifies such emotions.

Who can be ready?

Prepping, or getting ready in anticipation of disruptions, can favour the privileged. Research shows that adjusting to changes takes extra space, time and money, just when rising prices are squeezing budgets. Prepping can be gendered, reflecting the already disproportionate share of domestic and care work in households.

The Be Ready checklist suggests 36 litres of drinking water for a family of four. Carrying 36kg home is an enormous challenge if you do not have a car. In minimising disruptions, and attempting to empower, it is critical that plans do not exacerbate existing vulnerabilities during crisis situations.

The UK Public Survey of Risk Perception identifies that 29% of respondents consider costs as limiting. A quarter do not want food to go out of date and end up in the bin.

Stockpiling however, does not necessarily mean more waste. Italian households bought more food during lockdown, yet waste was low, as they mostly bought non-perishables. UK households self-reported 34% less food wastage, as people planned meals, froze leftovers and cooked from what they had.

How a sense of control helps

If fear drives buying, a sense of control calms it. Research shows that shortages weaken people’s sense of control, which fuels panic buying. Uncertainty can also fuel people’s anxiety, making panic buying more likely. When many households act on the same advice in the same week, they can create the very empty shelves that unsettle others. A clear plan gives that control back.

Advice to build up supplies over a month, adding two or three items to each shop. Start with water and tinned food, then add medicines and batteries. This spreads demand for retailers, spreads the cost for households, and gives people a clear plan to follow. Information should also be provided in multiple languages, across modalities, to increase awareness about risks while making them ready.

Food literacy should come to the fore. Consumers need to understand how to look out for expiry dates and use products on a first in, first out, basis to minimise waste, engage with food preservation.

Preparedness should start at school too. A review of 61 studies shows that disaster education in schools works, but many countries do too little. Programmes work best when lessons involve families and the wider community. Children then bring the plan home, resocialising their households towards joint actions.

What the public posts online also matters as much as what government says. A study of UK shoppers during COVID found that photos of empty shelves on social media increased uncertainty about stock; many responded by buying more. Those photos can signal fear and lead to panic. Retailers can help too. Setting allocation mechanisms such as maximum purchase quantities per customer can support with matching demand and supply.

articles.title: Poland continues to support Ukraine militarily, but economic relations are strained
articles.summary:
Poland recently announced it would transfer two MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine in exchange for anti-drone technology. The agreement comes at a time when Russian drones and missiles are wandering into Polish airspace on a regular basis.

The latest incursion occurred on November 20. Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Polish airspace was violated three times during Russian attacks on Ukraine that day. The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, called the incidents “intentional provocation” by Russia.

Poland has been a staunch ally of Ukraine since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. It has already transferred 14 MiG-29s to Ukraine, as part of a plan to move Kyiv away from older Russian fighters towards western jets. Poland has also provided over €4.4 billion (£3.7 billion) in aid, and has donated over 350 tanks and 250 infantry fighting vehicles to Ukraine.

The other prominent assistance rendered has been in welcoming Ukrainian refugees to Poland. Over 1.5 million Ukrainians fled to Poland in 2022 and official registration rolls suggest around 868,000 remain in the country. This has caused strain on Polish public services, with the population of the south-eastern city of Rzeszów swelling by more than half in the first months of the war.

However, at that time, there was a need to expand Poland’s labour force. Poland’s unemployment rate dropped to 5% on the eve of the war, reflecting a strong demand for labour. The influx of Ukrainians has provided a boon for the Polish labour market, with a UN High Commission on Refugees report suggesting they provided a 2.7% boost to Poland’s GDP in 2024.

A Polish soldier helps Ukrainian refugees carry their belongings across the border in 2022.
DBrownPhotos / Shutterstock

However, the economic relationship between Poland and Ukraine is nuanced. The first major step to increase economic ties between the two countries was the free-trade agreement Ukraine signed with the EU in 2014.

This was agreed after Ukraine’s Maidan revolution that same year, which resulted in the removal of pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych.

Since then, the Polish and Ukrainian economies have become more intertwined. The removal or lowering of many western trade barriers with Ukraine through the free-trade agreement has benefited Poland immensely, as it remains a key source of goods for the Ukrainian market.

From 2014 to 2021, Polish exports to Ukraine doubled from €3.1 billion to €6.3 billion. This number has more than doubled again since the war began, to over €14 billion. The trade balance has been in Poland’s favour for several years, hitting a new high of €9.7 billion in the first half of 2026.

Ukraine’s ongoing adoption of the EU’s Acquis communautaire, the body of EU legislation all member states must transpose into national law, is also forcing its businesses to adapt to EU standards.

Its poultry industry has already surmounted the hurdles that come with exporting to the EU, and continuing harmonisation with EU standards may make it easier for Ukrainian firms to export to Poland. With such a large diaspora there, there is a ready-made market.

An uneasy brotherhood

But there are critics within Poland of deeper economic ties with Ukraine, in many cases aided and abetted by provocateurs sponsored by Moscow.

Agriculture is and will remain a problematic point. Farmers are a powerful lobby in Poland and have agitated against Ukrainian imports as being too cheap and produced with less stringent standards.

In fact, it has been agricultural trade above all which has strained the political relationship between the two countries in recent years. Poland has imposed bans on Ukrainian grain imports, and farmers have staged repeated blockades of the border, disrupting grain crossing over from Ukraine.

Far-right Polish politicians have also struck back at the presence of Ukrainian immigrants, portraying them as not pulling their weight and benefiting from the hard work of ordinary Poles. Violence against Ukrainians in Poland – although at a low level overall – increased by 30% in the first months of 2026.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, has further exacerbated tensions by resurrecting historical grievances with Poland – including by naming a branch of his country’s special forces after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).

The UPA was a partisan force during the second world war that fought against basically everyone, including massacring Poles in eastern Galicia and Volhynia. Zelensky’s move has only provided ammunition for far-right populists in Poland to cast further doubts on the benefits of closer integration with Ukraine.

In reality, Ukraine and Poland’s defence ties are built around the shared goal of defeating Russian military aggression. Unfortunately, the errant views of Polish politicians and powerful lobbying forces in Poland continue to complicate this goal through poor economic policy and trade restrictions.

Sovereign nations will always have disagreements, and the historical relationship between Poland and Ukraine is fraught with difficulties. But the elevation of protectionist sentiment comes at a time when the countries need more solidarity against Russia, not less.

Perhaps the most important effect the protectionist impulse may have is weakening Poland’s governance instead of strengthening its economy. Ironically, Ukraine pursued a similar path for years after its independence, resulting in dependence on Moscow, rampant corruption and subpar economic growth.

Poland should learn from Ukraine’s experience and focus on continued economic liberalisation and military assistance. With a strong Poland backing Ukraine, the Russian invasion will be easier to defeat.

articles.title: Technology for ‘printing’ steel could help extend the life of ageing bridges and buildings
articles.summary:
The UK has an enormous amount of steel in service across critical infrastructure. Yet every day, millions of people cross bridges without giving much thought to the structures beneath their feet.

Many of these structures are far older than we might imagine, and they survive under demands their original designers could hardly have anticipated. But ageing infrastructure cannot be taken for granted.

As a recent report from the Royal Academy of Engineering warned: “The need to act is urgent. Many of our ageing assets are approaching a critical state where they risk compromising the reliability of the services they provide.”

Addressing this requires extending the life of steel structures in their primary functions. This may involve using additional steel for repairs or replacing part of the structure.

Steel production – including low carbon methods – and steel recycling are both carbon-intensive, so there’s an impact on the climate. The question is therefore not whether we need to intervene, but how best to intervene.

In the UK, around 300 million tonnes (Mt) of iron and steel are embedded in buildings and what’s known as mobility infrastructure: the systems that support the safe and efficient movement of people. If life extension allowed just 1% of this stock to remain in service instead of being replaced, 3 Mt of steel production could be avoided.

Even when using greener methods of steel manufacturing, such as scrap electric arc furnace production, this would correspond to approximately 2.1 million tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent (MtCO₂e) and 8.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) of steelmaking energy. In a future where low-carbon steel production competes for constrained supplies of clean electricity, hydrogen and carbon dioxide from carbon capture, the tonne of steel that uses fewest resources is the tonne we do not produce.

Yet repairing structures often requires disproportionately extensive, costly and disruptive interventions – and comes with its own carbon cost. What if instead we could encourage purpose driven innovations that extend the life of ageing structural steel for generations to come?

Layer by layer

Imagine an old steel bridge with a section weakened by fatigue cracks. Traditionally, engineers would reinforce the damaged region by attaching additional steel plates or replacing part of the structure.

Today, additive manufacturing allows us to restore deteriorated steel precisely where it is needed, without replacing entire structural components. It is a process where three-dimensional objects are built up layer by layer from a digital model.

The German company Siemens and US-based Fastech, already offer additive manufacturing for the onsite repair of, for example, steam turbine rotors or the rock-wheel trenchers used to grind through concrete.

Newcastle’s Tyne Bridge and Swing Bridge over the River Tyne at sunset.
Sergii Figurnyi / Shutterstock

To restore steel, a thin metal wire is fed into a controlled laser beam, which melts the wire as well as a small region of the existing steel surface. This allows new metal to bond directly to the original metal. By moving the laser across the damaged area, we can build up material only where it is needed. This technique is known as wire-fed laser-directed energy deposition (DED).

This concept builds on weld cladding, used for decades in safety-critical marine and nuclear applications. However, laser-DED enables more localised and controlled addition of new material with a lower heat input.

The electrically powered process makes unusually efficient use of materials. Jason Hutt, director of UK and international business development at Fastech, says the process allows degraded steel to be restored “precisely where material has been lost, potentially extending the life of an asset without replacing the entire structural component”. It could enable shorter interventions and reduce disruption caused by the work.

Safe lifetime

So why isn’t similar technology used to extend the life of vital UK infrastructure? The key question is how long the repaired structure will remain safe. Bridges are subjected to millions of loading cycles as vehicles pass over them. Even when the stresses are well below those needed to break steel, the repetitive nature of those stresses can open up cracks and then cause them to grow.

This phenomenon, called fatigue, is particularly important in steel bridges, because a repair that looks sound today must remain safe for decades. Independent evidence confirms the genuine potential of wire-fed laser DED for the repair of steel structures. In tests, wire-arc deposition arrested existing fatigue cracks beyond nine million cycles, compared with failure at 0.95 million cycles without repair.

A related but distinct technique called laser cladding also shows promise. Studies to evaluate it show that it restored more than 90% of fatigue strength – the maximum stress steel can withstand over a given number of load cycles – in artificially damaged modern steel.

But much of the scientific evidence comes from small specimens of modern steel that have been artificially damaged. Real bridges may contain century-old steel with different chemical compositions, accumulated fatigue damage and defects from decades of service. Laser deposition also changes the microscopic structure of the steel around the repair.

Engineers need to understand how the old material and the new interact, so that they can assess how much additional safe life the repair provides.

Climate benefits

Bridges also provide a tremendous immediate opportunity to mitigate carbon emissions. A recent study found that interventions using UHPFRC, a high-strength construction material, could save 1.7 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent across just 800 bridges, rising to 7.7 million tonnes across Switzerland’s federal network of 3,903 bridges.

The UK has 16,000 metallic railway bridges alone. When they were surveyed in 2004, 80% were already over 50 years old and half were over 100. The environmental benefits of preserving infrastructure extend beyond the steel itself. Bridge closures can mean weeks or months of diverted journeys, increased congestion and emissions while disrupting public transport, businesses and communities.

Bridge closures can mean weeks or months of diverted journeys and congestion.
John Whitney

Focused renovation can produce 84–93% lower emissions than replacement – even before accounting for indirect emissions from diverted traffic – while reducing the time taken for the intervention and allowing bridges to remain open.

The economic value is equally colossal. The European Commission’s Sustainable Bridges project, set up to increase the use of the European railway network, estimated that a modest 2% increase in residual life across European railway bridge stock could generate savings of the order of €1 billion (£832 million).

And for historic bridges, retaining the original steelwork can protect architectural and cultural heritage that replacement would permanently erase.

We have become accustomed to thinking of technological progress as building something new. As our assets age, extending their safe lives becomes an increasingly important part of the transition to a low-carbon economy.

Offshore wind turbines, industrial facilities and other key structures rely on enormous quantities of steel. Many operate in corrosive environments where replacement is costly and technically challenging. Some of the most important innovations of the coming decades may be those that allow us to preserve what we already have.

Barbara Rossi does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Be Ready stockpiling advice is missing something vital. You can fix it, today
articles.summary:
shutterstock Baranov Oleksandr/Shutterstock

Just hours after the UK government launched its Be Ready campaign in October, Storm Austen struck, shortly followed by Storm Boelo. Winds exceeded 80mph, causing power cuts that affected around 838,000 people, some for days.

Less than a month later, on November 12, a major Microsoft outage disrupted access to Outlook and other services for almost 24 hours, leaving hospitals, schools and workplaces in disarray.

In today’s complex world, we can rarely pinpoint the timing, impact or form of a disruption. It can happen without warning, making initiatives like Be Ready – which advises households to keep a three-day supply of food and drink in case of emergencies – a necessity.

But the Be Ready guide is, in effect, little more than a shopping list. It does not mention behaviour or actions, and is missing something just as important as stockpiled tins and bottles: a firm, agreed plan.

My research focuses on preparation for the “inevitable but opaque” disruption that we have seen in the last few months. We know that there will be disruption, but not when, what form it will take, or how bad it will be.

When families visit a busy theme park or festival, they often agree a rule like “if we get separated, meet at the entrance”. Few realise this kind of accepted information has a name: common knowledge.

When everyone hears the rule together, each person knows the others also know it. Nobody wonders whether the others will turn up, and nobody is left guessing.

A blackout is like getting lost in a theme park, except there’s no tannoy and no phone. With a quick text or call off the table, the rule must be in place before you need it. We therefore need to stockpile common knowledge, just as we stockpile water, food and medicine.

Read more:
What’s your apocalypse skill? Finding a future-proof hobby can bring fulfilment today

Why guessing fails

In the late 1950s, American economist Thomas Schelling asked people where and when they would meet someone in New York City with no way to communicate. Many picked noon at the information booth in Grand Central Station, showing that guessing can work when one place stands out.

For households, the problem is the opposite: they have too many obvious options. On any given day, a family may be split across work, school and home. What seems obvious to one person may not be obvious to another.

A stockpile of food and water won’t help you find your loved ones in a blackout.
norikko/Shutterstock

If disaster strikes, one person might wait at the office while another stays put at home. Both might then go out looking for each other. Without common knowledge, neither has any idea where to go or what to expect.

How to stockpile common knowledge

The good news is that building a stockpile of common knowledge is quick and easy. Here are four key points your plan should take into consideration:

Meeting place and time: Home is the obvious first choice, but you need a fallback location if it could become unsafe (due to flood risk, for example). This should be somewhere walkable and less reliant on power, such as a community building.

It is crucial to set a time rule. If by an agreed time you haven’t met at home, go to the fallback location.

Phone times: If the power fails but the networks stay on, every bit of battery counts. If you need to talk to someone regularly, agree to turn phones on for 10 minutes every three hours.

Choose an easy pattern so you can all remember it, even under stress: at midday, 3pm, 6pm and so on.

Pickup plans: Schools will wait for an adult, so decide who will collect children or other dependants. Agree in advance to prevent both of you from turning up, or worse, each assuming the other will go.

Write it down: Most important, agree on these things together long before anything goes wrong. It doesn’t need to be a formal crisis-style talk – doing it over dinner, for example, can make it less alarming for children.

Once agreed, write your common knowledge down on card, not a phone or laptop. Keep copies in key places such as school bags, briefcases, on the fridge and in the car’s glove compartment.

While tinned food and bottled water are essential in a crisis, common knowledge is what makes any plan work when stress and confusion are likely to peak.

Versions of this already exist: Scotland’s advice, for instance, already includes meeting places, but neither it nor the UK’s checklist explains why agreeing together matters, or covers phone-on times and a time rule.

There is also not not a one-size-fits-all solution. Some households will find this harder than others, but the underlying principle can be adapted.

My plea is therefore a simple one. Sit down with your family this week, and agree your plan. Follow the government’s stockpiling advice, of course, but add one thing to your checklist: a plan that everyone already knows.

articles.title: New Year’s resolutions: starting small today could work better than waiting until January
articles.summary:
Sergey Mikheev/Shutterstock.com

Every year, millions of people promise to start the new year by losing weight, eating better and exercising more. January feels like a natural moment for a fresh start. But big resolutions create a lot of pressure and are hard to keep up.

By February, motivation has often run out and many of us have given up. A new year doesn’t make change any easier. A survey found that only 17% of people stick to their resolutions for four to six months, with another 9% maintaining their goals over six to nine months, and 6% keeping their resolutions until the end of the year.

There is no need to wait. Every day is a chance to start moving more, which can lower your risk of diseases such as cancer, diabetes and heart attacks. Motivation tends to be highest around the time we decide to change.

Starting straight away uses that boost to build momentum, leaving less time to put things off or talk ourselves out of them. If you are reading this in late November, waiting for January 1 means several more weeks of second thoughts.

Healthy habits take time to form. One study found it took 66 days on average, though the range was wide. Starting now gives you a head start, so the routine is already beginning to bed in when January arrives.

January is also a hard month to begin. People return to work after a break, pay day is weeks away, and the next Christmas is 11 months off. Mood often dips, and cold, dark weather in the UK – or extreme heat in the southern hemisphere – can make being active harder.

January is a hard month to start.
Kmpzzz/Shutterstock.com

Small changes are easier to stick to. Our psychology is wired to respond to rewards, and small changes bring several mini-rewards each day. These help keep confidence up, while too much change at once can feel overwhelming.

Research suggests that even a few minutes of activity, plus small changes to what and how you eat, can help build healthy habits. You can start today without a gym membership, equipment or a complicated diet plan. Small changes may lead to bigger ones when you feel ready.

Simple hacks

Here are a few small changes you could make today to improve your health.

Add short “snacks” of activity to your day. A few minutes at a time is fine, such as climbing stairs at work or doing squats while the kettle boils.

Break up long spells of sitting, for example, with leg raises at your desk or bunny hops (a short jump made with both feet together and knees bent) during television ad breaks.

Cut out a couple of sugary foods or drinks each day. For instance, you could try to replace sugary drinks with water, and swap a sugary snack for fruit.

Try to go to bed a little earlier. Shorter sleep is linked to eating more sugary foods and drinks.

If your goal is to lose weight, here are a couple more tips.

Keep portions a little smaller if you can. Using smaller bowls and plates can help, and try to serve yourself once so you can see how much you’re eating without going back for more.

Say no to food you are offered when you are not hungry. And when you feel full, stop eating. Save the leftovers instead.

The appeal of a fresh start is powerful, but waiting until January 1 to launch big, all-or-nothing goals probably won’t work. Start now, with small changes, and keep going all year.

Amanda Daley receives research funding from NIHR and is a Clinical Research Advisor with Second Nature

articles.title: Readers of fanfiction have a lot in common with 18th- and 19th-century fiction lovers
articles.summary:
Forbidden Books by Alexander Mark Rossi (1897)

When Archive of Our Own , the world’s largest fanfiction archive, announced that it could be unavailable for weeks following a “security incident”, many readers reacted with some distress. Across social media, fans half-jokingly talked about experiencing withdrawal symptoms and mourned interrupted reading schedules.

The reaction may seem uniquely digital. Yet, readers waiting for the return of Archive of Our Own have more in common with 18th- and 19th-century readers than they might realise.

Many fanfiction writers publish stories chapter by chapter, often releasing updates according to a regular schedule over weeks, months, or even years. This allows readers to follow narratives in real time. The result is a shared experience of suspense, discussion and speculation.

Long before online archives existed, popular fiction was also often consumed in instalments.

Improvements in printing technology, together with rising literacy rates and expanding commercial networks, enabled books, periodicals and newspapers to reach larger audiences than ever before. Books nevertheless remained relatively expensive commodities because of the costs associated with paper, printing and binding. One early solution was to issue works in instalments, or fascicles, which were separately published instalments of a book or other printed works. This approach allowed publishers to spread production costs, and the related financial risk, over time, reducing the upfront cost for readers. Whether by design or accident, serialisation also served to create a culture of anticipation as audiences waited for the next part of a story.

A shared activity

Serial publication is only part of the story. Some modern fanfiction communities are characterised by a high degree of interaction between writers and readers. Readers comment on chapters, speculate about future developments, offer feedback, and sometimes even influence the direction of a work as it is being written.

While the technologies are different, this kind of participatory reading culture would have been familiar to 18th- and 19th-century authors. Samuel Richardson, for example, encouraged and embraced interactions with readers, and was notoriously attentive to their reactions. Discussions with friends, admirers, and critics shaped his thinking about Pamela (1740); while reader response influenced the development of its sequel, Pamela in Her Exalted Condition (1741). Although increasingly dismissive of reader feedback as his career progressed, Richardson also revised later editions of Clarissa (1747 to 1748), altering aspects of the text in response to feedback from his readership.

Reading in the 18th century was also rarely a solitary activity. Books circulated through friendship networks, generated extension discussion among readers, and even performed texts aloud.

As an avid reader and frequent correspondent, many of Jane Austen’s surviving letters reveal the innate sociability of 18th-century literary culture. On February 9 1807, for example, she tells her sister Cassandra that “We are reading Clarentine, and are surprised to find how foolish it is. I remember liking it much less on a second reading than at the first and it does not bear a third at all.”

Her novel Northanger Abbey (published posthumously in 1817 but written earlier) offers a vivid depiction of this culture. The friendship between protagonist Catherine Morland and Isabella Thorpe is cemented through their shared enthusiasm for gothic novels, particularly the works of Ann Radcliffe. Chapter six sees the two girls avidly discussing Radcliffe’s 1794 novel The Mysteries of Udolpho, with Catherine declaring: “I am delighted with the book! I should like to spend my whole life in reading it.”

Readers having their say

If Richardson and Austen capture the formation of literary communities, the reaction to Sherlock Holmes’s death demonstrates the power such communities could wield.

When Arthur Conan Doyle killed off his famous detective in 1893, more than 20,000 readers of the Strand magazine, which published the stories, cancelled their subscriptions and others wrote letters urging the author to reverse his decision. Long before readers could leave comments on fanfiction chapters or express their dissatisfaction with a book’s conclusion at an author signing, literary audiences were already seeking to shape the futures of the fictional worlds they loved.

Holmes’s eventual resurrection has become one of literature’s most famous examples of readers refusing to accept an author’s final word.

Richardson also dealt with his fair share of this. Lady Bradsheigh and Lady Echlin were two readers who were so deeply invested in the fate of Clarissa’s heroine that they suggested revisions and alternative endings to Richardson that would have changed her tragic fate. Although Richardson ultimately resisted such changes.

If a writer can’t be moved to make changes then readers can write their own stories.

One of the most well known tenets of fanfiction is its revisitation, revision and expansion of existing fictional worlds. Fans write alternative endings, explore paths not taken by the original author, and create sequels, prequels and parallel narratives that expand fictional worlds beyond their canonical boundaries.

Take Ali Hazelwood’s 2021 romance novel The Love Hypothesis, which was adapted from her 2018 Star Wars fanfic Head Over Feet. Originally published on Archive of Our Own under the pen name Ever-so-reylo, the story imagined an alternate universe to the Star Wars sequel trilogy (Star Wars: The Force Awakens,2015; Star Wars: The Last Jedi, 2017 and Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, 2019) in which enemies Rey and Kylo Ren (Ben Solo) become unlikely lovers.

Read more:
The Love Hypothesis and the rise of romance adaptations: how readers became part of the marketing machine

We can see similar engagement with existing worlds in 18th-century works too. For instance, Poems Occasion’d by Reading the Travels of Captain Lemuel Gulliver (1727) was a response to Jonathan Swift’s Gulliver’s Travels (1726) most commonly attributed to Alexander Pope. There was also John Kelly’s continuation of Pamela, Pamela’s Conduct in High Life (1741) and Henry Fielding’s satiric parody Shamela (1741).

So the desire to continue stories, debate characters, recommend favourite texts, or imagine alternative endings endures. What has changed is the speed with which these responses can be shared, the size of the communities that can form around them, and the number of people able to participate. Modern fanfiction is not a break with literary culture so much as the latest manifestation of some of reading culture’s oldest habits.

This article features references to books that have been included for editorial reasons, and may contain links to bookshop.org. If you click on one of the links and go on to buy something, The Conversation UK may earn a commission.

Amy Louise Blaney is an Associate Member of the Royal Historical Society, a member of the International Arthurian Society, and a member of the British Society for Eighteenth-Century Studies.

articles.title: Boots is moving into medical cannabis – will pharmacies make it mainstream?
articles.summary:
Edward Bauer / Shutterstock.com

Medical cannabis has been legal in the UK since 2018, but for most patients, it is still a private treatment, not an NHS one. Now, a household name is entering the market. Could Boots help bring these medicines into mainstream healthcare, or will they stay out of reach for anyone who cannot pay?

In November 2026, the pharmacy chain launched its SureLeaf clinic, which offers private assessments to adults aged 25 and over. It covers conditions including generalised anxiety disorder, insomnia and chronic pain, such as fibromyalgia, arthritis, cancer-related pain and endometriosis.

Patients must have tried conventional treatments without getting enough relief. Those who qualify are assessed by a specialist, have their case reviewed independently and receive regular check-ups if they are prescribed cannabis-based treatment.

The launch comes eight years after UK law changed to let specialist doctors prescribe cannabis-based products for medicinal use. These medicines contain compounds from the plant, mainly cannabidiol (CBD) and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). THC produces the well-known psychoactive effects of cannabis, while CBD does not cause a “high”.

But changing the law did not make the medicines widely available. For most unlicensed cannabis-based products, the first prescription must come from a specialist doctor with expertise in the condition, although GPs or pharmacist prescribers can manage repeat prescriptions.

On the NHS, guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends cannabis-based medicines for only a few specific conditions.

The result is a huge gap. Private prescribing has risen rapidly, from about 350,000 prescriptions in 2023–24 to more than 830,000 in 2024–25. In 2025, the NHS issued just 70 prescriptions for CBD.

There are several reasons for this gap. Many of these products are unlicensed, meaning they have not been through the full approval process required for licensed medicines. Questions also remain about how well they work, their side-effects and their long-term safety, so NHS prescribers and policymakers tend to be cautious.

Cost is the other barrier. Private treatment can be expensive, so access often depends on what a patient can afford.

Does medical cannabis work?

So how strong is the evidence, and who is most likely to benefit? Cannabis contains compounds called cannabinoids that interact with the body’s endocannabinoid system, which helps regulate pain, mood, sleep and appetite. But cannabis-based medicines are often discussed as a single group, when the evidence varies a lot between products and conditions.

The clearest benefit is in some severe forms of treatment-resistant epilepsy. A review of clinical trials looked at two rare, severe forms of the condition: Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. It found that patients taking purified CBD had about 20% fewer seizures a month than those on a placebo. That was enough to support approval of Epidyolex, an oral form of CBD, for these conditions.

There is also evidence for nabiximols (Sativex), a mouth spray containing THC and CBD, for easing muscle stiffness (spasticity) in adults with multiple sclerosis.

For chronic pain, one of the most common reasons people seek medical cannabis, the evidence is far weaker. Some patients report small improvements in pain, but the benefits appear modest. A large review of chronic neuropathic pain concluded that cannabis-based medicines do not provide substantial relief for most people.

Evidence for alleviating neuropathic pain is less strong.
PerfectWave/Shutterstock.com

The picture is even less certain for anxiety and insomnia. Some small studies suggest possible benefits, but recent reviews have found little evidence that medical cannabis improves sleep quality or duration.

Evidence for mental health conditions more broadly, including anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder, is also limited. That makes widespread prescribing hard to justify.

These medicines carry risks too. Common side-effects include dizziness, drowsiness, vomiting, impaired concentration and changes in mood. Products containing THC can cause intoxication and may lead to dependence in some people.

CBD can also interact with other medicines, including some antiseizure drugs, blood thinners and antidepressants, and change how they work. That is why careful assessment and ongoing monitoring are essential.

The mixed evidence and the risks help explain the cautious approach of NHS policymakers and doctors. The Boots service is private, so patients will still pay for consultations and prescriptions, and its launch does not change national clinical guidance or guarantee wider NHS access.

Even so, it shows how visible medical cannabis has become in UK healthcare. A well-known high-street name may prompt more conversations about these medicines between patients and health professionals. What it cannot do, on its own, is close the gap between those who can pay and those who cannot.

Dipa Kamdar does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
